Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can you explain the concept of strong and weak suits in the card game Bridge?
Answer: Bridge is a trick-taking game. When you evaluate a suit, you should ask: Each bridge deal can be played in either a trump or a notrump contract. In a trump contract, extra long-suit cards in your suit will only turn into tricks if it becomes the trump suit, or once all trumps have been played. If a player can play any trump card on your non-trump “winner,” your card is no longer a winner. Here’s the strongest possible 3-card suit: A K Q. A long suit like A 9 8 7 4 3 2 is potentially a good suit, but by itself is a “weak” 7-card suit. Q J 10 8 7 3 2 is a much stronger suit. Yes, you’re missing the top two cards, but your length may allow you to knock them out with your Q J 10, after which the rest of the suit may be good. In general, top honor cards make a suit stronger, and connected honors make it even stronger. K Q J 8 5 is a much stronger suit than K Q 9 8 5 because the Jack strengthens your KQ holding. A suit headed by K 10 9 is a decent suit, but not a “strong” one. That falls in the intermediate range of suit quality. 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 is a potentially nice suit - 8 card suits don’t grow on trees - but it’s a very weak suit, as you need to knock out five higher cards. Of course, if your dummy holds K Q 10 in the suit, your combined holding is extremely strong. Play the King to knock out the Ace. The Jack will fall either on that trick, or when you get back in to play the Queen. The catch is that your long suit has no entry. You will need a side entry in your hand after knocking out the Ace and Jack, and “clearing” the suit by playing the Ten. Only then can you use the side entry - probably an Ace or King - to enjoy the rest of your eight-card suit. If instead your suit was A 8 7 etc., with Q J 9 in the dummy, you can knock out the King with your Queen, get back in to cash the Jack, and then play the 9 to your Ace to enjoy the rest of the suit. Note that it would be a mistake to lead the Queen for a finesse through your opponent’s King; you probably need the Ace later for transportation.

Question: If I want to sell a video game created with Visual Studio 2022, do I need a Microsoft license or can I sell it anyway?
Answer: You do not need a Microsoft license to sell a game (or any product) created with Visual Studio or other Microsoft tools. Those tools are productivity frameworks, not platforms for reusing copyrighted content. If you made a “serious game” that taught players how to use Visual Studio, and included that product inside your game, you would need a license to incorporate it. That’s the only case I can see in which you would need a license. If, instead, you taught programming, and required players to license their own copy of Visual Studio, you would again not need a license to refer to it.

Question: I'm a conservative father paying for his two daughters' college education. Why don't liberal men do the same instead of taking handouts from the government or putting it all on their kids?
Answer: It all depends on the means, and the priorities, of the parents. My father - lifelong liberal Democrat - was an electronics engineer with a college degree. He had good jobs, and invested his money carefully, so he had enough money to put my older sister, brother, and myself through college. And that’s just what he did. Except that he also helped me get a Summer internship. They wanted me to stay, and I took a year off school to keep working. Dad asked, “Well, since you have your own money now, why should I keep paying for your college?” I agreed there was no particular reason, so I paid my own way - including housing, food, etc. - my senior year. This was in 1976–1977, as is probably obvious to any parent trying to put three children through a University education today. I made about $12,000 in that year, enough to pay all my expenses, and come out with enough savings to cover a year at a highly-rated state university (UC Santa Barbara). My son went to the same school 30 years later. His tuition and expenses came to about $25,000 a year, $100,000 for four years. A few years after that, my niece got accepted into Cornell. That Ivy League school cost closer to $100,000 per year. Nobody is paying for that from a Summer job, nor from excess earnings after working for a year. None of us could afford those costs, so my father stepped in again, and helped put his grandchildren through college. Liberal or conservative never entered the equation - The ones who could afford to pay for education did so, because we all believed that education is important. My daughter-in-law didn’t have well-off parents or grandparents to put her through school. As a result, she worked multiple part-time jobs while attending school, went to a less-expensive junior college before switching to UCSB, and later UC Berkeley, where she got a degree. And she still had tens of thousands of dollars of student debt, which it took her ten years to pay off. That’s what “paying for college” is like today. Now tell me - Where does political alignment come into any of this? It does in one respect - White men are much more likely to be able to cover their children’s college education costs than are Black men, Latino men, or single mothers. That’s one of the markers of “white privilege” that I’m sure you’ve heard about from “liberals” like me. I’m 99% sure you’ve benefited from it, and 100% sure that I have. But I don’t put down those of less privilege and means if they’re unable to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars to put their children through a good university. I respect any who try.

Question: Can you get negative points in the card game Bridge? If yes, how and why would anyone play like that?
Answer: Originally, in rubber bridge, there were no negative points. There was a horizontal line across the scorepad. Anything written below the line were points that contributed to “making a game,” and everything above the line was a bonus or penalty that could not be used to score a game. But the penalties? They still were not negative numbers. If you went down 3 in an undoubled, non-vulnerable (you haven’t yet scored a game that rubber), the 150 points were added above the line on your opponents’ side of the scorecard. As another answer mentioned, in modern tournament scoring, there are both positive and negative points. That’s because each player (in an individual event), pair, or team has their own score. If the opponents score a game with an overtrick for +450, your score will be -450. If you go down 150 as above, you’ll get -150, and the opponents score +150. It’s just a convenience. And -150 might be an excellent score if other pairs are scoring -450.

Question: How can you learn to play contract bridge effectively without a partner that plays well enough not to need bids and conventions (or at least not many)?
Answer: Play with and against the “robots” on a site such as Bridge Base Online. There is a free robot tournament every day, and you can also play in casual practice games. The robots aren’t perfect, but they bid and play much better than the typical total novice. After the daily tournament, compare your results on each deal with others in the field who played the same deal. Try to figure out what you could have done better. You should also read a couple of beginner bridge books. I started out (some 50 years ago) with “Five Weeks to Winning Bridge,” by Alfred Sheinwold. It’s still an excellent first bridge book. There’s also the “Club series” by Audrey Grant, and many other good books that will help you learn the game.

Question: Are we close enough technology-wise to the point of say a solo game developer utilizing AI to help them make a game?
Answer: People are now using AI to help with many sorts of creative activities, games included. This doesn’t mean that AI can write a great book, or screenplay, etc. But it can rapidly generate prototypes that a skilled writer, screenwriter, or game designer can use to help inspire ideas. There’s a Facebook page devoted to AI images based on my Quest for Glory games, and some of the images there are amazing. But the best ones require substantial tweaking in Photoshop, and many iterations of the text prompts, before they become great. There is a danger of using AI tools to create prototype art, music, or text - They can stifle creativity if used too literally. After looking at hundreds of AI images, our brains can fool us into thinking that the most recent ones are finished products. If used that way, AI stops being a useful development tool.

Question: What are the reasons for people voting for the Democratic or Republican party? Has the difference between the two parties diminished over time?
Answer: The differences between the Republican and Democratic parties have greatly increased in recent years. When I supported the Libertarian Party circa 1980, it was common to refer to people in both major parties as “Republocrats.” I still hear that sort of thing today, but it is far less accurate now. Most bills in Congress passed with some degree of bipartisan support. There would be dissenters and supporters from both parties. It was a matter of pride to have the legislation introduced by members of both major parties. Today, virtually every important vote in Congress is completely on party lines. If your party “whip” tells you to vote a certain way, almost everyone in that party falls into line. Meanwhile, the other party whip is demanding their party members to vote the opposite way. Only when a few partisans “cross the aisle” to vote with the other party, does anything important pass. Worse, many bills are completely blocked by the majority leader, who can prevent issues from even being brought to a vote.

Question: Why did my top performing employee quit after write up?
Answer: I was “written up” at one job by a senior manager. The comments included my failure to get a particular feature working on schedule. When I told him that I had not been assigned that task, and that my (direct) manager was doing it, the senior manager said I was just making excuses. Another complaint was that I had come in weekends to work on a feature that I thought would improve the project, instead of spending that unpaid overtime working on assigned tasks. I was livid. I didn’t quit because I had just bought a house near the company. But I basically fell apart, and my work quality dropped dramatically. The kicker was my re-review three months later. The same senior manager complimented me on toeing the line and doing exactly the tasks I’d been ordered to do. He rescinded the warning. So I quit on the spot. *I* knew that my work had become substandard. It was even worse being complimented for bad work than being criticized for good work. There was no way I could have stayed at the company after that. Moral: Don’t write up *anyone* without being really certain. Talk to them, talk to their co-workers. Find out what - if anything - is going on. Find out if they’re at fault, or if they’re being managed badly. If there’s an external issue, try to help the employee resolve it, or try to make allowances for it. But never do a writeup unless you plan to fire the person, and need to start the paper trail for that.

Question: In game development, do in-house/contractor musicians show a few song concepts so that the studio chooses which one to develop?
Answer: The musical composition process for a game is usually a back-and-forth between the game designers (or the project creative director) and musicians. The designer will ask for a piece with a particular style and feel. Sometimes they will reference a composer who has done good work in that style. Then the composer will create several “musical ideas,” and present them to the designer. The designer will either pick one, or have further discussion and suggestions about what they want. Once that’s locked down, the composer will complete the piece, then send it to the designer, who might request additional changes. Other things they will discuss together include the length of each piece, whether it plays once or “loops” to make it seem longer, etc. Another common discussion is how musical themes should interact. For example, a certain section of the game might have several melodies inspired by Slavic folk music. Or a particular character who plays an important role in the game might have their own theme that will be repeated with variations. All great game development is collaboration between team members in different roles. A programmer assigned to a game scene might request custom animation from an artist in order to make the scene stronger. An artist might here some of the in-progress music, and modify art or animation to support the feel of the music. And, of course, the game designers, director, and producer all oversee the process, and make sure that everything melds seamlessly and beautifully.

Question: How likely is it for a bridge player to make a contract by inferior play?
Answer: Can a bridge player make a contract by inferior play? Sure, it happens all the time. You “fall asleep at the wheel” and play a 3NT contract as if it was 4S. You wake up around the time you “ruff a loser,” except somehow an opponent collects the trick. And you realize you just discarded one of your winners instead. But once the dust settles, you find you have 9 tricks in the bank, and you just made 3NT. You would have made 10 or 11 tricks without the error, but you had enough raw power to overcome your mistake. I got a top on a board earlier today. I was in a bad 4H contract on a 7 card trump fit, with the opponents having a strong spade suit. I knocked out a missing ace as they shortened my trumps with spade ruffs. Then I held my breath and played my last trumps. The opponents each had 3 hearts, and I made 12 tricks for two overtricks. But if the hearts had split 4–2, I’d have been down 2 or 3. There was probably a safety play that wouldn’t have required the luck… but I got a better score by not taking it. Victor Mollo wrote a great series of “Bridge in the Menagerie” books. One of his characters was The Rueful Rabbit, who was a terrible player who frequently lost track of the hands… but somehow managed to make apparently terrible plays that turn out to be the only way to make the contract, or set the opponents in theirs. Bridge is a game of percentages, and a game of mistakes. If you regularly play contracts with a 70% chance of success, you’ll do very well. But 30% of the time, you’ll fail in the good contract. Similarly, you can play a 5% contract that comes in that day - Inferior bidding with a great result.

Question: What if indie game developers had the financial resources of major studios?
Answer: What if indie game developers had the financial resources of a major studio? That would depend on the developer, as well as a considerable luck factor. If they’re talented business managers - a completely different skill set than being talented game developers - they might be able to build a larger studio out of their indie operation. Alternatively, they might be smart enough to hire skillful executives. Examples of small companies that became big and successful include Microsoft, Blizzard Entertainment, Sierra On-Line (back in the 1980s-90s), Mojang Studios (Minecraft), and others. Small companies that acquired more resources, and failed miserably? Far too many to count. It’s very common to become overly ambitious, and exceed whatever budget you have. Again, I could name numerous examples, but you probably already know some of them.

Question: In game development, at what point is a game no longer considered a clone of a previous game that has similar mechanics?
Answer: Many games have similar mechanics. If they look alike and play alike, the later one is a clone. But it’s quite possible to create new and original games that have similar mechanics to a previous game. At Sierra On-Line, each King’s Quest tells a unique story, and has different puzzles, even though they all have similar mechanics. My own Quest for Glory series uses the same basic interface as a King’s Quest game, but my wife and I added role-playing concepts such as character attributes and skills that improve when used, and combat based on some of those attributes. Each of those games has a different setting, and tells a different story. They’re related to each other, but not clones. My Castle of Dr. Brain game also uses the same engine as King’s Quest, but it’s a wildly different game. There are no characters walking around, no conversation, but lots of puzzles and challenges. Island of Dr. Brain is a sequel by a different author, but it isn’t a clone. It uses the same interface and mechanics as Castle, but has its own storyline, and unique graphics and puzzles. Wizardry was an excellent early CRPG. Its graphics consisted of monochrome outlines of corridors and rooms. Dungeon Master is a very similar game, but it added wall textures, a different spell and combat system, and semi-real-time monster actions. If you try to just sit there and think about what to do next, a monster is likely to come around the corner and attack you. The key to making a new game that’s similar to an older one without being a clone, is to change the story, characters, and visual and audio feel of the game. Just as there are millions of different tabletop RPG campaigns, the market has room for many different CRPGs. It can even handle multiple games with the same rules - See, for example, the Gold Box series of D&D-based games. Or the Wizardry games. Or Might & Magic or The Bard’s Tale. They’re all similar, and share some mechanics, but each is a unique game. No clones need apply!

Question: What is the biggest waste of electricity you've seen in a home you visited, were a guest in, or even in your own home?
Answer: My Mom always liked the house much warmer than I prefer. When she was on hospice, and confined to bed, I put a small space heater in her room to keep the temperature up to about 74 degrees. We live in Southern California, so this was only a few degrees warmer than the rest of the house. The following month, the electricity bill shot up by about $300. I bought a new, supposed energy-efficient, space heater. The next month, the bill went up another $300, to about $800 total. Mom also had a continuously-variable air mattress, which might have contributed to the bill, but I think it was mostly the small space heater. Running the gas furnace and heating up the whole house would have been cheaper. Question: If I put a game on Steam for $5, will I get $5 for every download?
Answer: No, Valve pays you 70% of the amount a player pays for your game. If it actually sells at $5, you will get $3.50. In practice, very few Steam units are sold at the list price. Most of the time, you will have to participate in one of the Steam sales to sell many copies of your game. Suppose the actual average price for your $5 game is $3. Then you will average $2.10 revenue per sale. Many of the sales are even deeper. You might average a retail price of $2 or less, bringing you $1.40 or less in revenue.

Question: Atheists, which argument for theism do you think is the strongest?
Answer: There are some very valid arguments in favor of theism. One is community. It’s well known that people who have close friends, and an active social life, live longer and are healthier than those who don’t. When I was in my late teens, I attended church regularly, and we had all sorts of fun social events. Most of them did not involve religion directly, but the church provided structure that made them possible. As an older atheist, I have some acquaintances, but I don’t have the regular rich connections that being an active church member provide. Another mental health advantage is the confidence that you are not responsible for all of your own decisions. God is taking care of most of what matters. That can help reduce feelings of inadequacy, which in turn can lead to depression. Church attendance can also help nurture job opportunities and client relationships. I knew someone who was a closet Satanist, but continued attending his Catholic church, and was a high-ranking Knights of Columbus member. He was a successful accountant, and most of his clients came from those two “clubs.” In general, being a church-going theist provides structure and certainty to your life, and can open opportunities that are less available to atheists. Note that these are not reasons for a belief in a god or gods; they are the result of belonging to organizations that nominally require you to have such a belief, or at least pretend to have it. It’s probably more comfortable to take advantage of those opportunities if you actually have a sincere belief.

Question: What techniques do game developers use to create inordinate amounts of visual combinations? Say I had 8 characters of different sizes / shapes, 4 styles of armor, and 12 armor materials. Would I have to individually make all 384 possible models?
Answer: Mostly they would avoid specifying a project like that. Or they would specify it, then fail. I worked on a project with similar specifications. The 3D engine wasn’t fast enough to render the characters in real time, and PC’s of the day didn’t have enough disk space or memory to store them all as pre-rendered models. The project was cancelled. Today, you might be able to get away with it. You would model the different shapes, then use algorithmic scaling to handle the sizes - You need that anyway to imply characters being closer or farther. The rest is a set of 2D textures that get applied to the models at runtime. But better design is to reduce and simplify your expectations to something you can build, will look good, and that will fit in the resources you have available. Those resources include both target hardware and artist hours.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: As a person who likes game design and animation making, should I move to NYC or LA?
Answer: Both are very expensive cities. I suggest you find a job before you move. Another good possibility is San Jose, or another San Francisco Bay Area city. Boston, Massachusetts and Austin, Texas also have good opportunities in both game development and animation. As a caution, game design jobs are extremely competitive. They are rarely available for entry-level applicants - Most game designers work their way up from another development or testing position. My saying is that, “Ten years of designing best-selling games and $6 will buy a latte at Starbucks.” It won’t necessarily result in a new game design job. The economics on a AAA game are that it might have a team of hundreds of developers, one lead game designer, and maybe a handful of other game designers. The good news is that maybe half or more of those developers are artists and animators, so there are many more opportunities as a skilled animator. An appropriate college degree will be a big help.

Question: If one person was a democrat and become a republican, does it mean he makes a huge transformation as a person and he is the 2.0 version?
Answer: No, it means they took the five minutes to change their voter registration. They might have made that decision for any of a number of reasons. It certainly doesn’t mean that they suddenly became a vastly different person. For instance, when Ron Paul was running for President as a Republican, a Libertarian friend convinced me to vote for him in the primary. I switched parties to Republican, voted for Ron Paul, and continued to otherwise vote for the most qualified candidates. Once I realized that most of the best candidates were affiliated with the Democratic Party, I changed my registration again. In California, it doesn’t really matter how you’re registered, but I lived in a small, heavily Republican, town. I didn’t want to make the statistics look even worse than they were.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What expenses, and how much, would I need to open a video game development studio (even if I outsource the work online like Upwork) like rent, computers, and video games development assets?
Answer: Figure about $100,000 per year per full-time employee for salary, insurance, and other overhead. That’s somewhat below market, but you can find competent developers at that level. All other costs are secondary. Game development is all about skilled labor. A typical indie team of 20–30 developers for a couple of years will cost about $5 million. You can develop on a shoestring budget for less, but it won’t be under $1 million. Don’t forget to include yourself and any partners in the developer cost. You have to eat and pay your own rent. As for an office, you probably don’t want to make that level of commitment until you’ve been in business for a few years and produced some successful games. Let people work at home until then.
