President Reagan was more interested in giving huge tax cuts to billionaires. Incidentally, “Biden” - by whom I think you mean the current President of the United States - doesn’t give anything to anyone. The U.S. Congress votes on appropriations, spends several months debating and amending the appropriations bills, then hands them off to the President for a ceremonial signature. The Maui disaster is recent, and the government assistance for it will take time. I have no idea what this “$700” refers to; it makes no sense. President Biden has promised assistance both to Hawaii to help with the fire damage, and to Florida to help with damage from the recent hurricane. But the President doesn’t decide how much goes to whom. FEMA handles that in the short term, and Congress in the long term.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What game engine lets you make the best quality game at the fastest speed as a beginner?
Answer: Paper, pencil, and a good eraser. Make many paper prototypes, playtest them, get friends and family to playtest them. All great video games start out on paper (or virtual paper in a computer) before they become video games. Designers work out the game balance in spreadsheets, specify the story, characters, and gameplay in text documents, etc. Artists draw storyboards and character concepts long before they start modeling and skinning them. Of course, many great games never make it onto a computer. Monopoly, Risk, Settlers of Catan, Dungeons & Dragons, and thousands of other classic games are played on a tabletop. If you want to be a great game developer, make fast prototypes, and not need programming experience, paper is definitely the way to go.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I want to start a video game company but I don't know how to make video games.How do I find coders and programmers?
Answer: First, get some funds. You won’t be able to find an investor with no track record, so you’ll need to be wealthy yourself, or have some very indulgent friends or relatives. Starting a company is easy. You don’t even need a lawyer. You can find appropriate forms for your state or country on the web. So do that. Now advertise for developers. Incidentally, “coders” and “programmers” are the same thing. You’ll need several programmers in different specialties, several artists in various specialties, at least one composer/musician/audio developer, someone to manage the teams, testers, etc. Make sure everyone has clear assignments - That’s often the hardest part - and be prepared to spend a lot of money getting games developed. A small indie project can cost $100,000 or more, and a full-scale game designed to compete with those from major publishers will run many millions of dollars. Just kidding - It’s impossible to compete with the major publishers. But if you spend enough on a high quality game with substantial production values, you may be able to sign a contract for them to publish the game for you. If you don’t do that, expect to lose almost every penny of those thousands or millions of dollars. There’s another path. First get a job for a big game developer. “First first” you’ll need substantial expertise in a game development field - programming, art, animation, or management. There’s also marketing, but that isn’t a good entree into development, and music/audio, which has so much competition, you’ll have a hard time finding full-time work. After ten years or so, you might learn enough to start your own studio, and you’ll have some contacts to help you do it. There is no magic wand to avoid spending years of hard work and/or millions of dollars developing the expertise and funding you will need to start a successful game studio.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I believe a game developer cannot develop application software (only using game programming skills) but someone who does can make games. What do you think?
Answer: There is no significant difference - on the programming side - between developing “application software” and developing games. A decently educated, competent programmer can do either. A game is application software, and the techniques for developing one are similar to those used to develop others. Both games and other apps need to be user-friendly and easy to use. They need to be reasonably attractive - games more so. They need good performance, again more for games. If you can program your piece of an MMO with thousands of players, you can certainly participate in developing application software. Incidentally, neither product category is created by a single developer these days. Both have teams of dozens to hundreds, or even thousands, depending on the scope of the application. I started out in application and systems development - smart terminals, inventory control, word processing and desktop publishing apps, and even a piece of the file system portion of a computer operating system. I also played bridge, D&D, and other games. Between all that, I was able to transition successfully into game development. I know a number of top game developers who have made successful transitions in the other direction, and now develop non-game applications. You’ll find some of them here on Quora, where they talk about preferring to have a roof over their heads, and feed their families, to being underpaid game developers.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How do game designers create worlds that are so immersive and addictive?
Answer: It’s a team thing. The games you’re thinking about are gigantic, and have huge teams. The lead game designer or director oversees a team of designers, each responsible for certain world locations or aspects of the game. They in turn communicate with dozens of programmers who turn their designs into code, and with dozens to hundreds of artists who paint every detail of the world, model realistic characters, and so on. My first game was Hero’s Quest, started in 1988, and released in Oct. 1989. We had about a dozen developers total on the team. The development budget was under $250,000. That was a AAA game in the late 1980’s. Today a AAA game typically takes a team of hundreds of developers three to five years to create. They aren’t sitting around playing games, at least not most of the time. They are spending the $100 million budget making sure that every leaf, every stone, every weapon, every character feels real to players. Meanwhile, the director, producer, and other managers make sure that everything fits together, and feels consistent. Even then they make mistakes, but on the whole, that massive team effort creates a much more immersive experience than any individual or small team of developers could manage. It’s similar to huge budget films such as Star Wars or Spiderman, that have teams of hundreds or thousands working behind the actors to make a seamless and immersive film. Bottom line for anyone wanting to work in the industry: Prepare to WORK. Long hours over and over again until the project ships, then some more to fix post-launch issues.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do so many people resent health insurers making money, but seem to have no problem with auto, life, and fire insurers making profits?
Answer: All insurance is bad. It’s inherently inefficient. You pay money to the insurance company every year, much of which goes into salaries, building overhead, advertising, and so on. Some of it goes into a pool of funds. Both you and your insurance company fervently hope that nothing will ever happen that causes you to make a claim. In the meantime, they profit from all the people who buy insurance, and never get value from it. When there is a real disaster, such as the town of Paradise, California being destroyed by wildfire, the insurance companies are in trouble. They’re designed to collect modest amounts from many people, then pay out slightly higher amounts to just a few claimants. When suddenly there are thousands of people facing the loss of everything they owned, there isn’t enough money in the pool to pay all of them. This why my homeowner’s insurance in the mountains near Yosemite Park used to be under $500 a year, then jumped to $3,000, then had the “fire loss protection” stripped out as it went to $5,000. The chance that the insurance company would have to pay out more than it brought in was too great. So now let’s take that to health insurance. Most people are basically well most of the time. They (or their employer) buys health insurance. And if they get seriously ill, the insurance covers part of their cost. It’s a well-designed system to handle rare and somewhat serious illnesses such as broken bones. It starts to break down when too many people make claims, or the claims balloon into gigantic expenses (think long-term cancer treatment). It’s just a really dumb way to finance healthcare. Before becoming covered by Medicare, my monthly health insurance bill was $2,000. As a semi-retiree, that had me on the edge of bankruptcy without ever becoming seriously ill! It’s even dumber for what most people need, which is a visit to the doctor once or twice a year for a checkup. Why should everyone have to pay a massive amount for basically nothing? If a system works poorly (except for insurance company profits) when nobody gets sick, and bankrupts both sick people and the insurance companies when too many people get seriously ill, that isn’t a good system. It’s also terribly inefficient, with millions of people hired mostly to say “No,” instead of providing actual healthcare. A single-payer government system works better, because a federal government has vast resources to smooth out low and high claim spikes. There’s still inefficiency due to government bureaucracy, but at least they don’t have to worry about making a profit from sick people.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why were not many Notable video game developers/designers born in the 1940s compared to other decades?
Answer: I guess Will Crowther doesn’t qualify, as he was born in the 1930s. And Don Woods was on the other side, born in the 1950s (as I was). I was already in my 30s when I entered the video game industry in 1988. That was considered quite old - most developers started in their 20s, some as teenagers. I already had a ten-year career in software development, and only switched to game development (at a huge pay cut) for my health. Sierra On-Line was based in the foothills of the Western Sierras, and I could breathe there. There were plenty of 40-year-olds in game companies, but they didn’t start at that age. Richard Garriott is six years younger than I, but started making games eight years before I did. So really, it just comes down to video games being a relatively young industry. It was in its infancy in the 1970s and 1980s, and still young in the 1990s. By that time, people born in the 1940s who were creative enough to make games already had good-paying jobs in other industries.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why not invent a videogame that is combined with health technology? Is there an inventor that has access and can? Pure air machines with smells for your videogames? What do you think?
Answer: I imagine there are some. I know there have been videogames designed to aid mental health. There’s an entire category of videogames known as “serious games” which tie into real world issues. Some of these are simulators. Some relate to healthcare. My wife once proposed a project where medical data would be stored on flash cards in ID bracelets. Whenever you visited a doctor or hospital, they could retrieve data about your past care, then upload details of that visit. We weren’t qualified to work on a project like that, but we still think that someone should take it on. Changing doctors or hospitals - at least in the U.S. - results in a lot of lost information that could improve healthcare. I don’t think we put any thought into gamification of that process even though we’re professional game designers and developers.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it true that more than 20 million people in the USA are millionaires based on the dollar?
Answer: Yes, it’s likely true, but… A million dollars doesn’t buy what it used to. I graduated college in 1977, and had aspirations of someday becoming a millionaire. But the target keeps moving. Today you would need at least $5 million to have the buying power of $1 million in 1977. Housing is even worse. You can easily spend $1 million on a house where I live, and modest starter homes run close to $500,000. A home like that would have cost under $50,000 in 1977, or the equivalent of $250,000 in today's dollars. If you had $250,000 then, you could afford a home. Today you’d need $1,250,000 to afford a similar home. Around 3,600,000 households in the U.S. have combined net worth of $5 million or more, which is today’s version of a “real millionaire.” Some would set that definition at $10 million. There are far fewer individuals at those levels than at the $1 million level. 84% of households with at least $1 million net worth have under $2.5 million.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How do you make money off of game development?
Answer: Get a full-time job for a major game developer. You could be a programmer, artist, tester, manager, or other role. You’ll get a regular paycheck until the inevitable layoffs, not as much as doing the same work for a non-game company, but reasonable. Don’t try to start your own game company. That’s a path to bankruptcy. The few people who succeed at it mostly worked 10–20 years for a big developer before going indie. And most of the experienced developers who try the indie route still fail. It turns out that marketing a game is really hard!

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What can an atheist respond when someone says "I'll pray for you" intentionally suggesting that even if the atheist does not believe, God exists anyway?
Answer: One correct response is, “Thank you.” Another is to say nothing. It doesn’t hurt me if someone prays for me. It hurts me if they persecute me for not believing as they do. Incidentally, many of my best friends are religious. Although there are many horrible people who profess religion, there are also plenty of very nice ones. Even many Christians are perfectly nice people with whom I’m happy to be called a friend.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If everyone is fully armed while walking in the streets, would it really reduce crime?
Answer: Of course not. Crime would increase. We read all the time about road range incidents. In a recent case, someone was slow in the drive-through line at a fast food restaurant. The person behind them aimed his gun at them. If people are openly armed while walking around, you can safely assume that some of them will fire their guns. Crime will increase. Actually, that’s just common sense - If you’re armed, and see someone else who is armed and looks dangerous, the sensible thing is to shoot them before they shoot you. When I see an armed person in public, I assume that I could be a victim of their rage at any time. It’s better to take them out first. Fortunately, I don’t carry firearms in public. But I don’t want to see anyone else armed around me. It takes just a momentary adrenaline surge for someone to lose control. It’s better if they’re unarmed when it happens.

Name: Corey Cole
Answer: When I lived in a rural area, I never locked my house doors because that would have inconvenienced me more than a burglar. All they’d have to do is break a window to get in. Or push hard enough on the front door to bypass the flimsy lock - a bear did that once. If we weren’t home, the house could easily be entered, with or without locks, and with or without guns. Why would someone break in? The number one reason for break-ins is to steal guns. My guns made us much less safe than not having any. Suppose we were home. Any “bad guy with a gun” could knock on the door. When I answered it, he or she could point a gun at me, and I would have no way of fighting back. Even though I owned guns, I would never open the door brandishing a weapon! In 30 years in the home, every visitor was legitimate, or perhaps a Jehovah’s Witness. Aiming a gun at a handyman, neighbor, or fire marshal is poor optics, and more likely to get me arrested than to protect me. So my guns would be locked up in the event of a home invasion, not in my hand for self defense. As another answer mentioned, look how well answering the door with a gun worked for Breonna Taylor’s boyfriend. So yes, I felt very safe in my home, but less safe because I owned guns. As soon as I moved to a city, I donated my weapons to the sheriff’s department. My 95-year-old mother would not have appreciated me bringing weapons into her house, and they would have made all of us less safe. Incidentally, you “freedom loving Americans” with guns frequently shoot your loved ones, are injured in gun accidents, or commit suicide with them. All of those are more common than home invasions, and *vastly* more common than home invasions successfully prevented with a firearm. You are far less safe owning guns than if you did not own them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Atheists, are you firm in your atheism? If so, how when there are billions of humans who believe very strongly in God, claim to have felt His presence, and have testified that He has changed their lives through the power of the Holy Spirit?
Answer: Sure, no problem at all. I’ve read the Bible (several times). And parts of the Qu’ran. And the Bhagavad-Gita. Also Lord of the Rings, Harry Potter, and Asimov’s Foundation trilogy. All of them were much more enjoyable than the religious works. I prefer to read works that entertain me than ones that are a slog. Not too surprising, really. I had a hard time getting through Don Quixote, and it’s considered a classic. I used to call myself a Christian. Then I had quasi-religious epiphanies, and switched to Ayn Rand Objectivism worship. Spent some time in the Temple of Set, and hung around Pagans. Eventually I realized (or decided) that all of them were spouting nonsense. But yes, there are many people who believed in Ahura Mazda. Most of them are long since gone. Billions of people swear by the Qu’ran, but somehow I don’t think you’re ready to change your religion to Islam. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and you aren’t ready to change to any flavor of Christianity. How do you propose I magically “find” faith for a religion that’s full of nonsense? I see no reason to do that, and couldn’t if I wanted to. You don’t magically “believe” in something; it either speaks to you, or it doesn’t.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: For those people who happily voted for the current president, I have just one question. How better off you are now then when president Trump was in the office? Name calling is not the legitimate answer.
Answer: That isn’t quite the right question. I personally am much better off than I was under Trump, but that’s just personal circumstances. Many women are less well off than they were when Trump was President, because now they’ve lost many of their healthcare rights (not just abortion). But that was due to an obscene action by the Trump appointees on the Supreme Court, not to any action of Biden’s. And that’s the real problem with the mindset that led to the question: Politician actions often take months, years, or even decades to affect most people’s lives. Another Trump action that is starting to have a bad effect now is the “tax cuts for the richest Americans and for large corporations” law. That greatly increased the National Debt, and it has a continuing effect on the deficit each year. Republicans in Congress are trying to gain leverage by raising the debt ceiling, which means that they don’t want to support laws put into effect by Republicans during the Trump administration. It has nothing to do with the current budget, and a lot to do with the lowered federal income from the Trump tax changes. I am impressed by the Biden administration’s focus on environmental issues, infrastructure, and equal treatment of all Americans. I should think that any true conservative would love those policies. Which is to say that the Republicans in Congress who are currently trying to hold America hostage to policies that will make people’s lives worse are the opposite of true conservatives. We have a different word for people like that - You can choose it between “bully” and “terrorist.” They are un-American.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Would you prefer to earn 10 cents every minute for lifetime or instantly gain 1 million dollars?
Answer: At first, it seems like a close call. The 10 cents a minute comes out to a bit more than $50,000 a year ($52,560), or more than $1 million in 20 years. Then you keep making another million dollars every 20 years. But the $1 million up front can be invested up front, and will double in value every (roughly) 10 years after taking out capital gains taxes. So it’s $4 million in the time you’d have made $1 million from the 10 cent deal. Over the next 20 years, your 10 cents will bring you another million, but you’ll have doubled your original $1 million twice more in that time, so it will be close to $16 million. If you’re a good investor, clearly the up-front million dollars is a much better choice. Looked at another way, $52,560 a year is a decent living wage by many people’s standards, or at least it was twenty years ago. But it won’t be so great in another 20 years. From the initial million, you could take out $50,000 a year for living expenses, and still have a substantial investment. Even if you took out a ten-year advance of $500,000, the remaining $500,000 would double to $1 million. So you’d have regular income, and still all of your initial principal. If you did that on the 10 cents a minute, you’d only have $2,560 per year left to invest. Over 40 years, that might double four times to about $41,000. Not close to the million you’d still have on the initial $1 million plan. I haven’t even accounted for the bookkeeping nightmare of earning 10 cents a minute constantly. :-) Let’s take the million and run.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What should a 16-year-old be doing from now every year to become a millionaire by the age of 30 and a billionaire by 50?
Answer: Inherit $100 million or so from your parents, as Donald Trump did. Instead of blowing it on questionable real estate investments, put all of it (except for a modest $1 million a year for living expenses) into mutual funds, such as an S&P 500 index fund. At an 8% annual growth rate, your money will double every nine years. In the 34 years between age 16 and 50, it will have doubled three times, and almost a fourth. Call it 14 times the initial investment, or $1.4 Billion. Nice work for doing essentially nothing! The catch may be taxes on your gains, but I think the gross return might be closer to 10% than 8%. That will make up for any capital gains tax.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If a company’s annual income is 2 million dollars, at what average how much should the CEO be earning (CEO who owns the company)?
Answer: If that’s the gross revenues, you first pay all the bills, and pay fair salaries to all of your employees and contract workers. From what’s left, a fair CEO salary might be half of the net income, the rest being retained or invested to help build the business. I would not take more than a $100,000 salary in that situation. If the company has no net revenues, the CEO might take a token salary (presumably debt-financed), but not taking any salary is also common for independent business owners.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How hard is it to make around 2000$ a month, being a beginner solo game developer?
Answer: You’re far better off finding a job at a large game development house. There you might make anywhere between $4K and $10K a month. But as an indie developer? The odds are massively stacked against you making any money at all.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can game developers make millions?
Answer: Sure. But if you become a game developer, you won’t make millions. Some do, but they are the most dedicated, no life outside of gaming, people. If you need to ask the question of how much you’ll be paid, then you aren’t a hard enough worker to spend decades struggling before maybe having a small chance of finding a pot of gold.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I wrote down a new mobile game I wanna release, would it be better if I code and develop it myself or should I get developers to help since I have no experience in building games other than drawing arts and making soundtracks?
Answer: You should do it yourself. The difference between an indie game with no budget, one with $100K budget, and one with a $1M budget; is largely whether you only lose your time, lose your time and tens of thousands of dollars, or lose your time and hundreds of thousands of dollars. Only get a team together if you’ve managed impressive results by yourself, and you want to raise the stakes. Just remember that the most likely outcomes are there in the first paragraph. Very few indie games ever break even, particularly when counting unpaid labor from the developers as a cost.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Which one is the best profession for the next 10 years, game development or software engineering?
Answer: It all depends on what you like to do. Here’s my “programmer art” Venn diagram of the two specializations. Game programmers often make such simplistic “art” to serve as stand-ins until they get “real” game art from game development artists. Software engineering is an important subset of game development, just as game programming is a subset of software engineering. You can be a software engineer and a game developer, or either one without the other. A game development team consists of artists, programmers (software engineers and content scripters), level designers (who are a cross between game artists and game designers), technical designers (cross between programmer and designer), and hundreds of other specializations. The work a software engineer does at a game development company is largely indistinguishable from the work they do at a commercial or industrial software development operation. It’s challenging brain work in any of those environments. If you love to program, and have deep understanding of hardware, technology, operating systems, compilers, drivers, and/or other “engineering” systems, then you’re a software engineer wherever you work. If you love games, well, actually that doesn’t matter. As a software engineer for a game company, you’ll work so deeply on systems that you won’t have much to do with game play. If you like to play games in your off hours, nothing is stopping you, wherever you work. I put in 60 hour weeks making games at Sierra On-Line… but I did the same thing when I developed publishing systems and an operating system at previous jobs. Traditionally, game companies pay you less for longer hours of work, but I don’t think that’s universal today. Do what you love. If you don’t love to program, you probably won’t do well as a software engineer anywhere. If you don’t love playing video games, that might or might not make a difference in an engineering job at a game company.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can game programmers afford to buy houses and Tesla cars? People say game programmers are underpaid, but how much underpaid are they?
Answer: Game programmers for large corporations such as Activision Blizzard, Electonic Arts, and Microsoft are much better paid today than they were 30–40 years ago, when I was in the industry. Unfortunately, most of them are living in areas where nobody can afford to buy a house. They probably do make enough to get a car loan to buy a Tesla. Despite the fact that I took a 33% pay cut when I joined the game industry, I was able to buy a house. Oh, it wasn’t from my salary. It was from my wife’s royalties - She’s never been a programmer, but got royalties (in lieu of salary) for designing games. Luckily, her first game - Hero’s Quest: So You Want To Be A Hero - was a bestseller, so we could afford to make a down-payment on a house. On a dirt road in the country. A few of the top programmers at Sierra owned houses, but most rented. Many game programmers come from upper middle class families. Some of them have enough of a head start that they eventually inherit a house, or get help from their parents to make a down payment on one. That’s how I bought my first house, but all of the proceeds from the sale went to repay that loan. The second came from that one royalty check, and I lived there for 30 years.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: For game development, do I need to create a new email address to sign up for game development apps, like to publish my games on Steam, to signup for a game engine, etc.?
Answer: You will want a new email, or several. Apple and Microsoft development licenses strongly recommend unique email accounts. It is also much easier to track income, store sales, and so on, if it doesn’t go through your personal email. You will also want a support email for players, so that your normal email doesn’t get inundated with thousands of support requests.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How do you make a video game that'll be ranked #1 in education for all ages (even if that game teaches about social science, which includes political science)?
Answer: You make about 10,000 games instead of one game. Oh, make sure you get some well-heeled backers or publishers so that every one of them is extremely high quality. It’s like buying 10,000 lottery tickets instead of one. The cost is enormous, but you have a higher chance of winning with one of them. NOTE: I don’t advise that. It’s mathematically stupid. But if you only care about having one of your games be #1, it’s the only path. You can *never* predict which of your games will become a best-seller, or the #1 educational game. All you can do is pour your heart - and a huge budget - into every game, and make a lot of them. Then one might become a winner.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What do you think the gaming industry as a whole needs to make gaming fun again?
Answer: For thousands of years, people played a small number of games such as chess, checkers, and various gambling games. Presumably they found them fun, although all of them might be mocked as simplistic and boring today. Today there are tens of thousands of games, and many people spend as much time playing games as they do working. If that isn’t fun, I’m not sure what is the definition of that word “fun.” Incidentally, I once gave a lecture called, “The Fun Factor,” at a gaming conference, so presumably I have some knowledge about fun. Any non-paying activity at which people regularly and voluntarily spend ten or more hours a week has to classify as fun. I spend considerably more than that playing my favorite games. One of them is bridge, which definitely fits the categories of repetitious and boring to many people. The other is World of Warcraft, which has far more variation, but could also be saddled with those terms… after players have already put in 1000 hours or so of (apparently) fun. So what’s fun to you? I guarantee that there are games out there that will meet your criteria, no matter what they are. Ultraviolent games, ones that challenge your problem-solving skills or your hand-eye coordination. Ones that are beautiful and have amazing soundtracks. If you aren’t finding modern games fun, you’re choosing the wrong ones for you.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do software developers age over 40 leave the industry?
Answer: When there is a layoff, companies often - possibly illegally - tend to drop their older, more experienced, employees first. That’s because, by age 40, an engineer has gotten many raises, and is likely being paid more than younger engineers. But in general, older software engineers don’t leave the industry. You might find fewer of them in small startup companies, but plenty of them in larger companies, especially government contractors. In some cases, that’s because they joined the company when it was small, and it grew with them. In others, it’s easier to find work on companies that take their non-discrimination rules seriously. Other software developers are promoted out of development. They become managers, and occasionally executives. Incidentally, job hunting is much harder for older engineers. Companies might not admit to age discrimination, but it frequently looks as though they practice it.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why is it so hard to find a software developer or an app developer?
Answer: More of a comment than an answer, but it applies to several answers here. A typical answer is, “It’s easy to find a developer if you’re willing to pay [an amount that many would consider excessive].” So you might be asking, “Why are consulting fees so high?” My father spent 20 years as an engineering consultant. When I asked him about consulting, he mentioned that he typically spent two hours looking for gigs, or otherwise not working, for every hour he worked as a consultant. Think about that… A good developer these days can easily earn $50-$60 per hour or more, reliably paid based on 40-hour weeks, all year round. That also includes benefits - paid sick leave and vacation time, health insurance, and more. If they look at a risky, and likely short-term, project, they need to factor in their idle time. Suddenly $50 as a full-time developer looks more like $150 for the hours they’ll actually work, along with nothing for the hours they’re not working, looking for work, or working but not getting paid. It’s pretty common for an underfunded startup to not pay its contract developers. My company doesn’t pay developers enough to justify the risks, but we have people who come to work for us for other reasons. And we *never* miss a payment; we put that ahead of keeping lights on in the main office. If one of our projects runs over schedule, many of them will leave. It isn’t because they’re greedy. It’s because they need to keep a roof over their heads, and feed their families.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: In the game of Bridge, how do I respond to an opponent's bid if I have 19-24 points?
Answer: Usually start with a Double. Your partner will expect it to be a typical takeout double. That usually shows shortness in the opponent’s suit, support for the other suits, and opening hand values. Partner is obliged to respond, even with zero points, unless she has a stack of the opening bidder’s suit. But your next call changes the message. Suppose the auction starts (1D) - Dbl - (Pass) - 1S - (Pass). Normally you are expected to pass with a minimum hand. Partner showed her suit as expected. Instead of passing, suppose you bid 2C or 2H. That changes the original message to say that you have a very strong hand - usually 18 or more points - with length in that suit. A jump in another suit means you have a monster hand and a very long and strong suit. (Double jump, such as to 4C in that auction, is something else. That’s a splinter, showing short clubs, good spade support, and interest in slam if partner has any values.) Or suppose you bid 1NT or 2NT. Now you’re saying that you have a strong, or a very strong, hand. And you have a good stopper (usually 1.5 or more stoppers if the opponent opened in a major) in the opener’s suit. Or you can “cue bid” the opponent’s suit. That shows a very strong hand, probably with shortness, or at least no stopper, in their suit. Partner will initially assume that you have support for their suit, but you can clarify that in later bids. Partner must never, ever pass your cue bid in the opponent’s suit. If they have a stack in that suit, they can bid NT. You can raise partner’s suit. A single raise shows about 16 to 18 support points. A jump raise shows that 19+ point hand. A jump to game means you have a rock-crusher opposite partner’s known support. Remember that they could have zero points, since your double forced them to bid. It all starts with the Double, which means, “I think we should compete,” and implies that you have at least near-opening values. But you also could have a monster hand. There are a few other specialized choices, depending on your agreements. Typically those show a 2-suited hand, and will initially be taken as weak bids. When you make one of those, then bid again, you’re “correcting the message” to say that you actually have a very strong hand.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If I want to break into game design, should I seek employment at an existing team or try to assemble my own team?
Answer: Breaking into the game industry as a game designer is incredibly hard, almost like winning a lottery. After helping design multiple best-selling games, I had no better luck finding game design jobs. A typical modern AAA game has a few game designers among its hundreds, or even thousands, of developers. Almost all of those designers have multiple previous titles in their CV. The lead designer almost certainly has made multiple games in lesser design roles. How do you get around this? Make yourself extremely well qualified. Get a degree in creative writing or write a successful novel. Learn some programming on the side, especially using scripting languages. Study Unity and Unreal engines so that you can converse with other team members about using them. Develop some art skills, at least the ability to make simple drawings to illustrate your designs. Read a few books on game design and level design. Few people have all of those skills of course, but those few are much sought after. Learn a few of them, and you’ll be ready to contribute in multiple areas. Don’t try to be the lead designer at first. You’ll do better by working up the ranks from a related position such as level designer or technical game designer. If you’re coming more from the art and architecture side, you’ll do well as a level designer. If you're more technical, and have some coding skill, you might do well on the technical design side. It will still be very hard, but there are game design jobs out there. Just make sure that you have the skills, and eventually the experience, to make them want to talk to you.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can we create a good game with just free materials (sprites, objects, music, etc.)? Can you give an example of a game created following that way?
Answer: Yes, a well-designed, well-balanced game can be excellent with expensive bespoke assets, and can still be great with free ones. In fact, there have been some very good games with no graphics at all. If you’re making a close to zero budget indie game, I’d recommend using free assets. Graphics can be the most expensive part of a game.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How does a Texas Holdem Game poker game end? If it ends at the showdown, then that would make no sense since there is already a destined winner when the cards are dealt so there would be no reason to fold.
Answer: “Destined winner” is an interesting, and totally incorrect, analysis of Texas Holdem. The results are determined only after they happen, even though the betting does not change which cards will be dealt. That’s called “post priori” - knowledge after the results are in - vs. “a priori” - the knowledge you have before the board cards are shown. Did you know that flipping a coin any number of times has a “destined winner” in the same way as you assign one to Texas Holdem? All I have to do is write down the results of all the flips, then declare the “destined” result. After the fact, all probability-based events have a post priori probability of 1 - i.e. what happened is what happened, a tautology. Or “What happened is what was destined to happen.” But a priori, you don’t have that information. Similarly, Texas Holdem is not about the winning hand once all the cards are dealt. It’s a game of maximizing value by correctly betting and sizing bets. Here’s a simple heads-up example: One player has AA, the other 72 offsuit. The “destined” board ends up with KK2 on the flop, followed by two more deuces on the turn and river. The “destined winner” is the player with 72, as he ends up with a full house (222 KK) vs. his opponent’s two pairs (AA KK 2). You don’t have to use both of your hole cards in Texas Holdem, otherwise 72 would still win with trips vs. 2 pairs. Now was that the “destined” result? Only if one or both players are idiots. The player with Aces should be betting on every street, although he might be nervous about his opponent having a King in the hole. The player with 72 should fold at the earliest opportunity to minimize his loss. Over 100 hands with those same hole cards, the AA is a big winner. Now if this was a stacked deck, the 72 player will make a lot of money vs. the Aces. Probably he’d make more by making it a less-dangerous flop - 10 6 2, or even J 7 2. But if he doesn’t control the deal, or have a working crystal ball, he should get away from that 72 asap.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do some people insist on declaring variables at the start of a block rather than delaying declaration until where they are first assigned a value or just before their first use?
Answer: It’s cleaner to declare everything at the start of the block. If you declare variables “as you go,” and make changes to the code later, you might accidentally reference or assign the variable before it’s declared. Always declaring variables at the start of a block cleanly documents the scope of the variable. Later developers aren’t left guessing whether a variable they find in the code is global or local. It’s also easier to tell whether the variable is properly assigned a value before it’s referenced. In languages such as C, an uninitialized variable has no default value. Even in languages that default it to 0 or NULL, that might not be appropriate. The earlier it’s declared and assigned a value, the safer, and easier to read, is the code. That’s also why developers like to put comments at the start of a block. A later developer won’t have to study every line of code to discover the intended functionality of the block.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do indie games have smaller maps than AAA games?
Answer: TLDR; AAA game developers can accomplish more with hundreds of millions of dollars than indie developers with budgets in the hundreds of thousands of dollars… or less. Games are designed and developed within constraints. The constraints on a AAA game might include, “This must be released by this specific date in order to take advantage of the hundred million dollars we are spending on advertising and bribes (aka “co-marketing funds”).” Another is that each game must feel epic in scope, visual and audio quality, etc. That includes making gigantic, detailed maps representing a huge world. If there aren’t enough artists and level designers on the team to make all the maps, the developer gets more funding from the publisher, and hires more people. Indie companies have constraints too. For example, “We must complete this game within four months to stay within our tiny budget. And we only have four programmers and eight artists with which to do that; we can’t afford more.” That’s for an established indie developer. A smaller one might have one programmer and one artist, and a similar time restriction. AAA game developers can make huge maps because they can afford to allocate dozens of people just to making maps. The map team is often larger than the entire development team at an indie studio. Their studio mission is to make huge, epic-feeling games, and they will devote as many resources to that as it takes. Indie game developers don’t have the budget or manpower resources to both make gigantic maps, and provide innovative game play or heart-warming story. Since they need to distinguish their games from 10’s of thousands of others, they focus on well-crafted smaller experiences, rather than going for huge scope. Trying to do that results in mostly empty areas; there isn’t time nor budget enough to fill them in. To see what an indie developer can do with a $1 million budget, check out my team’s Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption. This is a hybrid role-playing/adventure game similar to Skyrim, but developed under a much smaller budget. We accomplished that by not using voice acting, and by restricting the action to a castle and some underground areas. It isn’t a *small* game. It’s as large as the AAA games I made in the 1990’s, such as Quest for Glory: But we don’t pretend to have the scope of a modern AAA game. Our mantra might have been, “Build better, not larger.” In actuality, it was, “Focus on the character relationships and unique skill systems, rather than trying to do everything at once.” The result is a highly-rated game that didn’t need hundreds of developers to create.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How can Biden be stopped for putting us to war with Russia? Keep in mind he is the president, not Trump. Now that he has sent tanks to Ukraine, we are at war with Russian.
Answer: This is actually one of the simplest things in the world. All you need to do is get Vladimir Putin to withdraw his forces from Ukraine - including Crimea - and acknowledge its sovereignty. When Russia leaves Ukraine, so will the U.S. and other NATO states. The U.S. has no forces in Ukraine, only military and humanitarian aid. Russia and the U.S. are not at war with each other. Russia would not be at war even with Ukraine had they not chosen to invade a neighboring country. Prior to the invasion, Putin could have gotten away with keeping Crimea, while staying out of the rest of Ukraine. Now that he has cost thousands of lives and billions of dollars, and disrupted millions of other lives, nothing less than total withdrawal from Ukraine - including Crimea - will be acceptable to the rest of the world. It is true that Putin would have fared better with Trump, or possibly another Republican, in office. They’re surprisingly cheap to bribe and buy.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What are some ways to get a job in the game industry without making games?
Answer: How do you get a job in the game industry without making games? It’s easy. At least as easy as developing serious expertise in some industry-related skill. Game companies do all of the things other companies - especially those that develop non-game software - do. They need to fill a wide variety of non-development roles. For example, game companies have payroll, licensing fees, etc. They need bookkeepers, accountants, and clerical people to handle all that. Game companies have offices. They need janitors and facilities managers. Game companies need serious computing “firepower.” They need expert computer technicians, people to run backups, people to maintain company libraries, and many other non-game personnel to keep the computers and other development tools running. The way to *not* get a job in the game industry? Assume you should get such a job just because you want one, without taking the time and effort to become great at one or more skills that a game company needs. But those skills don’t have to be in game development.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If you have an idea for a board game but never go through with publishing it, is it legal for someone else to make a copycat version?
Answer: Of course it is. You can’t copyright or trademark an idea. You can copyright a work based on an - or in practice, many - idea(s). You can trademark the title of the work. Even if it’s been published, it’s perfectly legal for someone to make another game with the same ideas. If you haven’t published it, what are they copying? You’ve done no work, and you have nothing to show. Do you really think you’re the only person who has ever had your particular idea? Professional game developers have thousands of ideas, and have to pick and choose which ones to use in each game. Often, they reuse a few of those ideas in multiple games. I came up with a “practice makes perfect” skill-based character development system for my (and mostly my wife’s) game Hero’s Quest. The four sequels use that same idea. So does our more recent game, Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption. None of them are “stealing” from their predecessors. It’s a very general idea that can be used in many ways in different products.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How can someone pitch a video game idea to a large company like Electronic Arts (EA) or Activision Blizzard? What are some things these companies look for when considering new games from unknown developers/designers?
Answer: Anyone can pitch a *game* to those companies. Get a loan or private investment, build a team in a development studio, create a solid prototype of your game that includes at least one completely finished and functional vertical slice of the gameplay, and you can pitch it. I’ve been told that such demos regularly cost several million dollars to develop. You can’t pitch a “game idea” to a major publisher, nor to a minor developer. For one thing, it’s lazy. You haven’t done the work, nor spent the money, to prove that your ideas can be made into a fun and addictive game, so no game company would want to hire you to do what you’ve already shown you can’t do. They’re also concerned about being bogged down in spurious lawsuits. Let’s say you went to Activision Blizzard ten years ago, waved your arms around, and said, “I’ve got this amazing idea. Players will be superheroes in a post-apocalyptic world, and they get to fight each other.” Meanwhile, Blizzard has been quietly developing Overwatch for a year or two, with a huge expenditure of funds, and doing their best to keep it under wraps. Will they even listen to your presentation? Of course not. If they do, you might come back with a lawsuit stating that they stole your idea to make Overwatch. No matter how ridiculous that is, it’s a waste of time, money, and energy for them. If you instead come in with a solid resume in multiplayer game development, 3D graphics, and so on, they might well hire you. There you’ve shown that you know how to do something, and can do the hard work required to do it well. But they have no interest in yours, or anyone’s, “ideas.” They have plenty of those from their current employees.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have 50k in USD to develop a video game as a Kickstarter. I want to make a simulation game about writing, producing, and pitching shows to networks. How should I go about it?
Answer: That’s an interesting game premise. With that small of a budget, you’re talking about a 1–2 person project. I might go with a “presentation board” interface. Possibly a multiple choice interface for each stage of preparation and pitching. I’d give players some text entry boxes that help them plan and describe their show. These will later be shown in the pitch presentation, but otherwise won’t be parsed by the game. Keep your graphics limited and simple - possibly use royalty-free clip art. Whenever you’re tempted to do something complicated, such as an action sequence, kill that thought. Keep it simple if you want to complete a game with that budget.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What are the chances of an aspiring game designer getting hired if he/she doesn't know how to code and has no intent of learning it either (at least at first)?
Answer: Their chances are slim, but not because they don’t know how to code. The issue is that game development requires very few game designers, and a whole lot of people in other roles. Competition for the few game design positions is fierce. Many game designers do not know how to code. I started as a programmer, but my wife had no coding background when she led the design of one of the bestselling game series of the 1990’s - Quest for Glory. Lori’s background was in teaching, creative writing, and art. This combination of skills turned out to be perfect for a “game director” position at Sierra On-Line. Lead game designers at Sierra were also expected to lead disparate teams of programmers, artists, and composers. We sometimes referred to the challenge of that as, “like herding cats.” A schoolteacher was a perfect leader for keeping everyone on the team pushing in the same direction. You don’t need to learn to code, but saying that you have “no intent of learning it” is a red flag. A successful game developer does whatever needs to be done to make great games. They don’t say, “I can’t draw, so I won’t even make sketches to explain my amazing ideas to the team.” They don’t say, “I don’t know how to code, so I won’t take the time to learn about the flags, variables, game loops, and tree structures that are needed to bring my game to life.” Instead, they learn enough about every aspect of the process to work with the specialists who will turn words and ideas into fun games. Brushing them off with, “I refuse to learn anything about that,” means you will never be able to communicate your design to the people who will turn it into a game. At one of my first programming jobs, several production workers called in sick one day. I helped out on the production line, soldering components into circuit boards. Was I an expert on that? No. But it was a small company, and everyone contributed whatever was needed to get products out the door. There was time enough to return to software development when the production line wasn’t stalled. But even with expertise, willingness to learn, and a wide breadth of knowledge and skills, it’s still extremely difficult to land a job as a game designer. As a novice, it’s nearly impossible. The better route is to start out in a less competitive game development position - coding (which can be as simple as using a scripting language to translate a game specification into something playable), art, animation, music, or even quality assurance. Once you have your foot in the door, you might have a better chance of moving into one of the rare and coveted game design positions. Nothing worthwhile is easy. You will have to work hard *and* be very lucky.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If someone made a video game on an original and unique theme and storyline yet has features and made it in a style and manner similar to other popular video games, would it be subject to copyright?
Answer: The clue to “copyright” is in the name - It’s about the right to copy. You may not copy things from copyrighted works. Don’t use their graphics or significant amounts of text. A few words are fine, but not complete dialogue, etc. Millions of games are made in the style of other games. It’s only when you copy actual assets from a game that you’re in trouble.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What genre of games is the easiest to program?
Answer: Text adventure games. You don’t need to worry about how to display and interact with graphics. Text-only games can be immersive, and they’re easy to create and test.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Hey can you share with me that story you had about how you dropped out of college to learn programming on your own and become a successful programmer?
Answer: Well, sort of. It was the mid-1970’s. Computer science barely existed as a discipline, so I majored in mathematics in the College of Creative Studies at Univ. of California, Santa Barbara. My father worked with Gus German, President of Geac Computers of Canada, and introduced him to me. Gus hired me for a Summer internship. When I did well at that, he offered me a full-time job. I took a year off from university to work for Geac. I could have kept working there, but instead chose to return to finish my degree. After graduating, I took a new job at an immediate 50% raise. I went on from there to become a successful programmer, and later, a game designer as well as game programmer. So, yes, I dropped out of college, and learned a lot at my internship, but finished school before continuing my career. That was also a different era in which a temporary job could help pay for college. I started at $10,500 annual salary, got a raise to $12,000 when I went full time. Besides covering my living expenses, I saved enough to pay for my final year of university. Today, that might cover a month of school.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it true that there is no such thing as an "atheist" (by definition), and that it is a lie (a made up word, a false designation, a false word, and a contrivance)?
Answer: All words are made up. They evolve over time to suit current understanding. All religions are made up. They, too, evolve over time because they give some people comfort. I assume you’re a Christian of one of its thousands of contradictory flavors. That’s a completely made-up religion that bears little resemblance to its roots, and even less to the thousands of religions that came before it. Your “Bible” is a complete work of fiction. It’s an assemblage of writings by hundreds of people, hundreds of years after the lives of the people it talks about. A group of scholars got together, picked over thousands of “religious” writings, and chose a set that would make up their “holy” book. It’s completely made up, and has only passing resemblance to actual events. Much of it is clearly fantasy, and not as well written as, say, Lord of the Rings. The difference is that Tolkien clearly labeled his writing as fiction. Why aren’t you following Zeus, or Bacchus, or Odin? Those gods have roots much older and deeper than yours. Incidentally, the Bible is clear that Jesus wasn’t a god. He was an ordinary person who tried to get people to live moral lives. That’s a pretty good life lesson, but it hasn’t much to do with gods. Do you know what the Bible says about the coming of a prophet? “He shall be called Emanuel.” Um, so who’s this “Jesus” guy? Not the same person. In any case, what passes for religion these days has little relation to anything in the Bible - Old Testament or New. It’s a bunch of self-serving people enriching themselves on the gullibility of others. There are some of them who actually believe what they’re preaching; that just means that they started as the gullible followers of the hucksters who came before them. Christianity as the New Testament claims Jesus created it was a communal gathering of people who wanted something to believe in. Christianity as it evolved is a massive hierarchical organization that transfers money from the poor to its self-proclaimed preachers. It’s an abomination, even if the Bible wasn’t a made-up fantasy novel.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What techniques are used by professional poker players to maximize their chances of winning?
Answer: Pro poker players don’t maximize their chances of winning. They minimize their losses when they lose, and they try to win more when they win. It’s money management, not odds management.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have a lot of game ideas in my mind. I don’t have knowledge about programming or business. How should I make a successful game?
Answer: Describe your game in detail with text and illustrations, to the point that a stranger can read it and feel as though they could play it as a game. Make sure you specify all of the game locations, how movement works, how any action sequences (such as combat) work - including spreadsheets to show how effective each unit type is against other units, etc. Be explicit and detailed about *everything*. If you get good feedback from people you show it to, expand the concept into a tabletop - board and/or card - game. Get friends, family, and acquaintances to help you playtest it. Improve anything that gets negative feedback. Look for a professional tabletop game publisher to market it for you - It’s really hard to reach players as an indie developer. You should probably stop there. If you’re thinking video or computer game, you might want to rethink it. It’s an incredibly crowded and difficult field even for people with long track records such as myself. A typical game costs millions of dollars to develop. You’ll need to sell over 150,000 units at $20 retail to break even on a $1 million budget, and most commercial games need higher budgets than that. The average indie game on Steam sells 2,000 units. Only a tiny fraction manage to recoup their development and marketing costs.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Have there been any games created where NPCs behave in ways that even the programmers could not have predicted?
Answer: Yes, that happens all the time in game development. If the results are inappropriate, usually the developers find the issue before release, and put in a workaround. If they’re especially silly, the developer may release a “blooper reel” of some of the craziest behavior. This is referred to as “emergent behavior.” A game developer typically creates a series of “rules” for NPC behavior. These can include things such as, “Try to follow a player who gets within 20 yards, following terrain, unless the NPC moves more than 100 yards. In that case, return to the original path,” or “Follow this patrol path, using terrain, until another rule tells the NPC to leave the path.” Inevitably, a few of these rules will come into conflict. How the game AI resolves the conflict is often too complex for the programmers to predict. Often this has an unpleasant result, such as the NPC getting stuck in a corner, or blocking a door. Other times, it leads to a temporary glitch, but the rules soon return to normal behavior. I wrote a PASCAL compiler using IBM 360 assembly language in a college class. For extra credit, we could add error handling to the compiler. I ran the test program through the first version of my compiler to determine where to put in the hooks for error reporting. To my surprise, it generated a well-formed error report before I added code to do that. It turned out that my program structure caused an erroneous program to hit built-in error handling on the 360 that coincidentally gave a meaningful response to the error. It was emergent behavior “gone good.”

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What makes a good game programmer different from other programmers? What are some tips for being successful in the games industry as a game programmer?
Answer: Great game programmers understand the importance of performance and interactivity in every piece of code they write. They make sure that the game never gets into a loop or other form of slowdown that impacts player experience. Game programmers learn a number of techniques and tricks to maximize game performance. A website can get away with a one second, or longer, response. A game needs to respond in milliseconds, or player experience is damaged. This is all while the game is handling massive amounts of data in real time - drawing backgrounds, animating the action, and so on. In multiplayer games, programmers also work out, or learn, techniques to make the game fun and realistic when player experiences don’t match. For example, suppose Player A shoots a nerf gun at Player B, who is moving. One player has a 50 millisecond latency, and the other 100 milliseconds. The information from each player needs to reach the server, have calculations made, then reactions sent to each player. Player A might be totally convinced that his shot hit Player B, while Player B is equally sure that she got behind cover in time, because it takes at least 150 milliseconds for the shot to reach where she had been at that time. The server will be the final arbiter, but it needs to make a decision that is reasonably satisfying to both players. One possible solution is to treat the shot as a “glancing blow,” awarding minimal points. Another is to manipulate the graphics so that it clearly hits - or misses - to both players. 150 milliseconds may seem trivial, but it’s a long time to action players. And this problem isn’t a new one. It had to be solved by early online games when the latencies were measured in seconds rather than milliseconds.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If a game developer used a pirated program or one without a commercial license to make a game asset, how, if at all, would anyone catch it after it's published? (We're assuming the program leaves no watermark)
Answer: That’s quite an assumption - Most of them do embed hidden information that can be used to track their source. In theory, you could be caught. In practice, you probably will get away with it. Would you be prosecuted for using stolen software to make your commercial game? Probably not. The world of gaming is too vast for more than a small fraction of criminals to get caught. It’s likely that even the largest, richest game developers use pirated software or assets at some point. They probably aren’t even aware that some of their developers bend or break copyright and intellectual property rules. If you’re an indie developer, the odds of bringing a game to market successfully are vanishingly small. If your game doesn’t become a best-seller, nobody will check on you to see if you developed it with stolen tools. By “successful,” I mean AAA level - millions of units sold. The average indie game on Steam sells fewer than 2000 copies over its lifetime; those developers have no pockets, and aren’t worth suing.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: For those of you over 40, what is it that confuses you the most about young people?
Answer: I’m not at all confused by young people. I’m impressed! My son watched my wife and I work 60 hour weeks developing games for below-market salaries, then get laid off with no compensation. For some strange reason, even though he loves both tabletop and video games, he decided that he had no interest in working in the game industry. He married his college sweetheart, and like us, waited until after 30 to have a child. In the meantime, they take vacations at least twice a year, have traveled extensively, and fill their lives with experiences. Somehow they also manage to hold down good jobs. They are now in their mid-30’s. They rent an apartment, and have decided that they will never be able to afford their own home. I offered them ours - out in the country - and they said, “No, thanks.” They like city life. In other words, they have a sensible balance of work, family, travel, and play. They will have no regrets about missed experiences when they’re older. Their friends seem to balance life similarly - Some of them are well off, some are struggling, but nobody has given up, and none of them have subjected themselves to working endless hours at meaningless jobs. Young adults in my area seem to have a similar sense of work-life balance. They recognize that everyone has challenges, and that you work to overcome your challenges. They all seem happy. I’m impressed by the young people I know.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What happens in a game of magic if both players run out of cards and there is an indestructible creature on the field?
Answer: The first player who must draw, but has no more cards, loses.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can anyone be an indie video game designer/developer if they're willing to invest time into it?
Answer: Yes, with the small caveat that they are also willing and able to learn new things. I think that’s just about everyone who is willing to work hard, aka “invest time.” My wife and I have been designing and developing games for 35 years. We never stop learning. When we went from a big company - Sierra On-Line - to making our own games, we had to wear many more hats. Lori spent half her time for several years learning Photoshop so she could make promotional materials. We both researched crowdfunding, publicity, how to work with a remote team, and much more. Now I didn’t say that anyone can make as good a living as an indie game developer as they could working for a big game development company. Most indies lose their shirts. But if you spend thousands of hours learning the trade, creating a game, and polishing it into commercial quality, you can be a game developer. Just don’t expect to pay your bills that way.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: When you spent money in a video game, what was it, what convinced you, and how much did you spend?
Answer: My wife and I have played many, many hours in Heroes of the Storm from Blizzard. That game has an option to “buy gems” for real money. Gems can be used to buy cosmetic looks for your characters, or to get a boost to experience. Because we get so much enjoyment from the game, we’ve bought gems a few times just to say “Thanks!” for our fun. We hoped that would encourage Blizzard to keep supporting the game. Unfortunately, they decided it wasn’t bringing in enough income for them to continue updating it. But they still keep the servers running so people can play it, which is good enough for us! Previously I “bought gold” once to purchase a “fast flying” mount in World of Warcraft for my wife. Back then, 5000 gold was very difficult to get, and the fast mounts are a big quality-of-play upgrade. Of course, we also pay Blizzard regularly via our subscription fees. Since we spend a big part of our lives playing, we’re happy to do that. As Lori has pointed out, if we weren’t playing WoW, we’d be frittering away our time on other hobbies. But as those go, WoW is a very affordable one.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can gaming development be automated, so a person will get an easy time creating a video game? How triggered would game developers be after knowing that?
Answer: Let’s call that “90% no, 10% yes.” As for triggering, the only emotion triggered will be laughter. The “10% yes part” is that the core of every game shares common elements. There is a central game loop, an event manager, graphics manager, and so on. These are frequently copied from game to game, or developed using templates. It’s a waste of time to reinvent the wheel for every game. But what makes a game special is invariably hand-crafted, and involves an enormous amount of creative - as well as routine - work. That can never be automated, because it’s what makes each game unique and worth playing. This part takes at least 90% of the schedule, and is often responsible for causing the game to go over schedule and budget. But without it, every game is alike, and boring.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Elon Musk is making liberals' heads explode while he gets rid of lazy employees and keeps only the best ones, those willing to work hard towards his vision. Will liberals try to break up Twitter when his strategy makes them hugely profitable?
Answer: I’ve been through a number of these “purges” in the tech industry. In every single case, most of the people who leave are the smartest, most talented, most capable people at the company. The ones who stay are the “lazy” employees. They pretend to work long hours, while playing games and shopping from the office, so that they can continue to bring in an easy paycheck. The best and brightest leave at the first sign of management idiocy. Why not? They can write their own tickets anywhere. Possibly they’ve already done their jobs so well that Twitter no longer needs them. There are, after all, several phases in a tech company - invention and creation, expanding for scalability, and maintenance. Twitter can probably be “maintained” for a long time by only modestly capable workers. But never fool yourself that top management can magically eliminate the weeds from an organization without throwing out much more of the good produce. Sweeping layoffs nearly always sweep out more of the gold than the dross. In Atlas Shrugged, John Galt was the first to leave when his bosses at Twentieth Century Motors began to make stupid decisions. That’s exactly how it works in the tech industry.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I'd like to see a list of Dems whose PPP loans were forgiven. I’m definitely NOT a Trumper but I know it has to be a two way street here unless all Dems declined. I've searched Google for this answer and came up empty. Anyone have that info?
Answer: Well, mine was declined. I had a very small workforce - and a very small PPP loan - that was declined because I used independent contractors rather than full-time employees. The loan helped us through a period when our project was delayed due to Covid-19 challenges. We now have to repay it in full. Many of the companies you’re reading about got *huge* PPP loans, even into the millions of dollars. They seemed to get pretty much automatic forgiveness. For a tiny company like mine, I had to jump through hoops on the application, then spend dozens of hours going through the forgiveness process, only to end up having to repay it all.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: When will the radical Democratic supported far left-wing realize that they have a fight on their hands before they take control of the U.S.?
Answer: There’s no fight involved. There is a democratic process of electing government representatives to serve everyone in the country - left, right, and center. No fringe group has ever done well in U.S. elections. We tend to pick the centrist, compromise candidates who are at least acceptable to people across the political spectrum. Whoever gets the most votes - with a few caveats involving districting and the electoral college - wins the elections and gets some power. None of them get enough power to “take control of the U.S.”

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How could the FBI have said Trump left with classified documents when as a president he’s allowed to classify and declassify items?
Answer: I’m President of a small company. It’s my job to make hiring and firing decisions, make sure everyone on my team gets paid regularly, and handle government and other paperwork responsibilities. In my first year of business, I didn’t do that last part very well. I kept careful records, and at the end of the year, worked with my accountant to file the appropriate tax records and the corporate income tax. After all, that’s how I’d done my personal taxes for decades. But businesses have more stringent requirements. Even though I paid everyone’s employment tax, I did it at the end of the year instead of every quarter. I unknowingly broke the rules, and ended up being fined thousands of dollars. The President of the United States works under far more stringent rules. That’s one of the reasons he has a huge West Wing staff to help him follow those rules. If it isn’t done right, the President is the one who is finally accountable. Yes, a President, while in office, has the right to follow procedures to classify and declassify documents. This involves a lot of paperwork, communication, and rules. In Trump’s case, he didn’t follow any of the rules, so there is absolutely no paper trail of him declassifying any of the documents he illegally removed from government offices. That’s called theft, and potentially also espionage, and potentially treason. Just because you’re the President of the United States does not give you license to break laws that defend the security of the country. Worse, Trump compounded the crime by lying under oath to NARA and FBI investigators. He first said that he had no government documents at Mar-A-Lago. Then he provided a few boxes of them, said, “Oh, well, we found these. There aren’t any more.” The FBI received creditable evidence from a Trump staff member that there were other government documents in a Mar-A-Lago storage room. They went through all the hoops - remember those challenging rules and regulations - and eventually executed a search warrant. There they found many more government documents, some marked Classified, others Secret, and some Restricted - so secret that they were only allowed to be viewed by “need to know” people in a secure safe room. If anyone but a former President had done a fraction of these misdeeds, they would by now have been convicted of espionage, and possibly treason, and be in jail for life. Trump gets some leeway because he’s an important political figure, but sooner or later he will have to pay for his capital crimes. Bottom line - the President is popularly elected, but then becomes a bureaucrat. He is under even more intense regulation than people in lower appointed and elected positions. If he fails to follow the rules, he’s just as much a criminal as anyone else who breaks them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What is the relationship between artists and video game designers? Can an artist also be a video game designer?
Answer: Artists and video game designers work closely together. Designers have a vision in their head as to how the game should look. They collaborate with the art team to get the spirit of that vision, while going beyond it with superior visual creative skills. It’s quite common for an artist to move up to a game design position. It’s also common for them to feel out of depth when they get there. :-) The best way to handle this is, during your apprenticeship or art production phase, listen carefully to the game designers to understand how and why they make decisions. Once you’re a designer, talk with your team about ways to make the game better, then make your own good decisions. A game designer who starts as an artist will likely see games as a mostly-visual medium. They will typically describe game action in sketches and storyboards. This can be a great way to communicate with the team - Always play to your strengths. Ask for help where you need it, but the final decisions will have to be yours. In your copious spare time - hah! - do a lot of reading, practice creative writing, and learn a little about coding and team management. Every game-related skill you get will improve your ability to lead a development team. Yes, you may have a Producer as your official team leader, but in creative matters, it always comes back to the lead game designer.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What do video game developers do if a player finds an error in the game?
Answer: They thank the player for their report. Then they try to duplicate the error in a controlled environment - Some errors only occur because the player has non-standard hardware or add-ons. And some errors are pretty random. I diverge to a tale from my first job as an intern. My code was acting strangely, so I tried to zero in on the error by inserting “print to console” commands. The bug went away. I took out the debugging code, and it came back. A real head-scratcher. After a completely unreasonable amount of work, I discovered that my code was self-modifying; it overwrote the value of a constant used by the program. (Think “5” behaves as “1”.) Once located, the problem was easy to fix, but the fix was completely unrelated to the code that appeared to fail. Debugging can be hard! Once the problem is isolated, and the developer starts looking at possible solutions, their manager asks, “Is this a game-killing bug, or just a silly annoyance?” If the latter, we’ll probably leave it in, because every bug fix risks breaking something else. If it’s a real problem, we’ll fix it along with other major problems, and eventually distribute a patch to players. What we *never* do is treat the player with anything less than respect. All reports are looked at, and resolved either by fixing them, or by explicitly deciding not to fix them. Player reports are treasured, because there are many more players than in-house game testers, so they can find issues that everyone on the team missed.

Question: Back in the 1970's there was a black and white horror movie that in one scene a woman is captured and they affix a cage to her face and release a rat to attack her. Super scary. That's all I can remember of the movie. What movie was it?
