Name: Corey Cole
Question: What are the best starting hands in Bridge?
Answer: If you’re playing for money in a rubber bridge game, the best starting hands are those that are locks for a high-scoring contract. Maybe all thirteen spades, or AKQ AKQ AKQ AKQJ in the four suits. But most competitive bridge these days is played as duplicate contests. Whatever amazing starting hand you get, an opponent has the identical hand at another table. In a matchpoint contest, *every* opponent sitting in your direction gets the identical hand at some point. Given that, 234 2345 234 234 is an equally good starting hand to the rock crushers I gave in the first paragraph. You have to play it, but so do your opponents at other tables. A truly great starting hand matches your abilities. If you are a mediocre player, a hand that “plays itself” for the same result at every table is a “win” for you. If you’re a great player, a hand that is challenging to bid to the best contract, or one that requires highly skillful play to make that contract, will pay you tremendous dividends. If you and your partner are stronger on defense than the rest of the field, you’ll want to defend more often. Let your teammates take on the generally easier task of declaring. Strong players hate easy, routine hands, because any duffer can play them as well as an expert. They thrive on borderline, challenging, difficult hands that require expert bidding and play.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Does bridge or poker require more mental math?
Answer: No Limit Holdem Poker is a much more mathematically complex game than bridge. There is no betting in bridge. When it’s played for money, the stakes are fixed - a certain amount per point and per rubber won. In poker, you need to consider the pot size and possible bet sizes at four stages of play. For example, if there’s $10 in the pot, and somebody bets $100, it’s almost never right to call, unless you have the nuts. In which case, it still isn’t right to call - You should reraise. In Texas Holdem poker, you initially know two cards out of a deck of 52. As the board comes down, you need to decide whether to bet, raise, or call knowing only five, six, and finally seven of the 52 cards. In bridge, during bidding, you know 13 of the 52 cards. After dummy comes down, you can see half the cards in the deck. There are still calculations and inferences to be made, but often ad hoc heuristics are sufficient. Information reduces the role of chance. At each trick in bridge, you learn more about the two hidden hands, increasing your available information. That’s also true with each board card in poker, but there is still far more unknown than known information. I worked briefly with poker champion Chris Ferguson. When asked about a decision, he goes to the whiteboard to work out the pot odds, and discusses likely holdings based on the opponents’ bidding. Of course, he doesn’t use a whiteboard at the table, but he uses similar principles for every decision. There’s mathematics in bridge too, but as a player of both games, my opinion is that bridge mathematics and decisions are simpler than those in no limit poker. Limit Holdem is more comparable to bridge complexity, but is a less popular game.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I gave my pixel artist a little information about my game and then they ghosted me. What if he steals my game idea? Or am I just paranoid?
Answer: You’re just paranoid. “Stealing a game idea” doesn’t make creating a game from it any easier. Why would someone spend many months or years of work to make a game from someone else’s idea unless that “someone else” is paying them to do it? No thanks, I’ll make games from my own plentiful ideas instead. Besides, if you and the artist both make games from the same “little information,” you’ll end up with two completely different games that nobody would recognize as coming from the same ideas. Those ideas have little value. Hundreds of man-months of work - That has value.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What should I do? I have a Unity game I'm developing for several systems and want them both to have the same content but with some important differences (like input)? Should I create 2 different projects? But what if I want to change both projects?
Answer: You should keep it as a single project, but encapsulate each system-specific section. All input should go through an input engine, with perhaps device drivers for each possible input device, or at least a subsystem for input from each hardware system. When I converted Sierra’s internal SCI game engine to work on the Atari ST and other 680x0 based systems, everything stayed in one repository. I completely rewrote all of the assembly language code for the different architecture. I created macros for working with numbers and addresses. For example, 0x1398 on 80x86 architecture would be swapped by macro to 0x9813 on 680x0, since Intel architecture used low-endian numbers, and Motorola high-endian. A 16-bit address on DOS or early Windows architectures was added to a base address to create a proper 32-bit address for the ST. Coming back, the base was subtracted to allow the offset to be stored again as a 16-bit quantity. But it stayed in a single code base, compiled with a compiler switch for either DOS/Windows, Atari ST, Amiga, or Macintosh. Creating a second project is a way to ensure that bugs only get fixed in one of them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do game developers still make games for Windows only? even though almost all game engines have good multiplatform support for now.
Answer: There are a number of reasons to at least start with a Windows-only game. First, it’s by far the largest PC game marketplace. A game that sells 100K units on Windows will be lucky to sell 10K units on MacOS, and far fewer on Linux and other PC systems. Console sales are high, but it’s very difficult to convert a PC game to play well on consoles. Each one has a different operating system and requirements. There are no keyboards, while PC games are usually optimized for keyboard play. Developers have to come up with completely different control systems. In addition, non-Windows hardware manufacturers put additional obstacles and costs in front of developers. Apple charges hefty developer fees, and requires that developers “codesign” their games on an Apple device. It isn’t sufficient to develop on a Windows PC using Unity, then flip the switch to output a MacOS build. Testing requirements multiply by each additional platform. You can’t be assured that your Mac build will work, unless you test it thoroughly on all variations of Apple hardware. It’s much worse for consoles and handheld systems, each with different control schemes and input and output devices. We developed Hero-U: Rogue for Redemption “simultaneously” for Windows, Mac, and Linux. That basically meant we spent 95% of our time testing and optimizing the game for Windows. We got a few backers to help us test the Mac and Linux versions. After launch, we were approached by a company in Poland to convert Hero-U to Nintendo Switch. They spent many hours translating our movement and control systems to work on both the touch screen and joypads on the Switch. Other than that, they probably mostly flipped the Unity toggle - I almost said “switch” - to make a Switch build. But then they jumped through the hoops of getting approval from Nintendo, getting publicity from Nintendo Switch specific websites, and so on. We pay them a hefty percentage of each sale, and it’s money very well spent. We would have no presence at all on the Switch without their help. Could we convert our game to run on Playstation, XBox, etc.? Sure. But we don’t have the resources to do that, and we have no clue how to publicize the game for those markets. Big developers spend tens of millions of dollars advertising and publicizing their console games. We have no budget for that. Our current game, Summer Daze: Tilly’s Tale, is once again running well on Windows. We’ve done only cursory testing on Mac and Linux, and I expect we’ll get a lot of problem reports when we start testing seriously on those platforms. The Switch launch will, once again, be handled by Silesia, and won’t even start until we’ve ensured the game is rock-solid on Windows.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What next big thing video games disappeared overnight?
Answer: The “next big thing” of Full Motion Video was the Holy Grail in the 1990’s, then mostly vanished from the scene. It turns out that FMV is contradictory in nature to player interaction and immersion, which is what makes video games a medium distinct from film.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have written a video game script, but I do not know which company/developer would accept/should be trusted, can any recommend?
Answer: You did that in the wrong order. First you get a contract with a game development company to write a game script, then you write it. It’s impossible to do it in the opposite order, because every game company has their own internal standards on game design documents, and one you write without knowing those standards won’t be usable to them. Incidentally, I don’t think any of them uses the term “video game script.” We use various types of scripts in game development, but they’re a subset of game design documentation. Much of the docs are concerned with player interaction - “What happens when the player presses the A button in each of multiple contexts?” They are very unlike TV and movie scripts, which specify what happens without regard to how players interact with it.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If Atheists can't recite the Pledge of Allegiance or swear on upon the Bible, what makes them think they are American Citizens?
Answer: We Atheists can of course do all that. Personally, I’m a bit of a hypocrite. When I recite the Pledge of Allegiance, I do so in its original form, omitting the words “under god.” They don’t belong there. At an event I regularly attend, after the Pledge, we all sing, “God Bless America.” I sing that without omitting anything, because it wouldn’t scan properly or make sense if I left “god” out of the song. But, like swearing on a Bible, it means nothing. I rather like the song, and enjoy singing it, so I do. That doesn’t mean I’m suddenly divinely inspired. It means that someone wrote a pretty good song that mentions some god or other. It wouldn’t actually hurt me to say the Pledge of Allegiance including the offensive phrase, “under god,” but a pledge is a promise, so I don’t do that. I’m not as big a hypocrite as the people who insist that our secular nation is somehow “Christian,” against the express wishes of the founding fathers.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Where can I find an experienced game designer?
Answer: Assuming you want to hire one, there are many resources. I would suggest Game Developer There’s also Monster (monster.com) and many other employment sites that will help you find a professional game designer. If you don’t want to pay, forget it - Do the work yourself.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Does your solo games have to be successful in order to join the game industry? I have 5 published (but not promoted) mobile games and keep getting rejected when I apply as a unity developer to a game company outside my country. What more should do?
Answer: Getting a job in game development is largely up to luck and connections. If you know someone who works for a particular company, and they refer you, that will greatly help your chances. If not, you just need to keep trying. Think of every job application as accompanied by a dice roll. If the dice go your way, you’ll get an interview, and possibly eventually an offer. Other factors such as connections and your previous experience give you modifiers to your rolls, but you still need luck. “Outside my country” is also an issue. For a U.S. company to hire someone from another country, they need to go through hoops to get you a rare work visa. They will also expect to need to pay you relocation expenses, which makes it more affordable to hire someone local. But the job opportunities are out there. All you can do is keep trying, build some connections through conferences and online game development boards. With enough persistence, your number will eventually come up.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What should I do if I have had a video game idea in my mind for years and have written books dedicated to said game, (I have yet to publish but fully written them) but I don’t have experience in game design, a degree, or ties to a video game company?
Answer: Start by getting your books published. If one of them becomes a bestseller, you may be able to interest a publisher into finding a developer to make the game (or games, if the first is successful) for you. Nobody has the slightest interest in raw ideas or unpublished books. It’s a classic case of, “The rich get more, while the poor stay poor.” But substitute “the famous” for “the rich” in this case. Steven King can get games made based on his books. Tolkien has had many attempted games based on his. JK Rowling has games. I directed a game based on Sword of Shannara, by Terry Brooks, because it was a New York Times bestseller. There have been other examples like that, all based on famous books by famous authors. If your name doesn’t belong on that very short list, nobody will make a game based on your books. Or worse, on your unpublished books and untried ideas.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do video game developers have ideas for future games already in development or do they just come up with them as they go along like movies do?
Answer: Yes, video game developers always have a backlog of ideas for future games. However, which ones actually get made depend on the publisher’s needs, available licenses, and other factors. When my wife and I first proposed Hero’s Quest (later retitled as Quest for Glory) to Sierra On-Line, we proposed a four game series. We actually made all of those, as well as a fifth game in the middle. Two years after we started that series, Sierra management decided that they wanted to make some educational games (“edutainment”). Each game designer presented ten one-page proposals for games they wanted to make. They chose three, including one of mine, and one of my wife’s ideas. Those became the bestselling Castle of Dr. Brain and the successful Mixed-Up Fairy Tales. When we left Sierra for a few years, Bob Bates of Legend Entertainment again asked us for ten short game proposals. While he liked our ideas, he instead assigned us to make Shannara, based on a book license with Terry Brooks, author of the Sword of Shannara series. Our proposals proved that we were creative enough to come up with strong game ideas; then the license overruled them. The only case of “just come up with them” was Quest for Glory III: Wages of War (alternate subtitle Seekers of the Lost City). That game idea was suggested to us by another Sierra game designer, Ellen Beeman. We were concerned that our dark fantasy horror concept for the next game - Shadows of Darkness - might be overwhelming to players. So we made Wages of War as QG3, and postponed Shadows to QG4. Ellen didn’t actually “just come up with” that idea. It was based on story elements we had planted in Quest for Glory II. But we hadn’t thought of making a game around them until Ellen suggested it. Before we started making Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption, we had a half-dozen game ideas in various concept stages. We might have made the Wizard game first, or a paper Pathfinder module, or finished a novel Lori had mostly completed, or several other ideas. Later we came up with even more - a cookbook based on Quest for Glory, a series of interactive visual novels, two very different puzzle games, a board game, and more. As we haven’t the time to make all of those at once, we next created one of the visual novels. All of the other projects are in various stages ranging from concepts to art complete and story outlined. Eventually we plan to do at least a few of them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do video games have scripts?
Answer: Yes, video games have scripts. However, that term has at least three meanings in the game industry: For example, a game script might read something like: salesman.moveto(counterX, counterY, counterZ) salesman.say(SALES_INTRO) player.prompt(SALES_OPTIONS) Scripting language commands *can* be written in C++ or C#, but often use a pseudocode-like scripting language so that non-technical people can create and understand game scripts.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do game design documents contain ideas made by the game designer?
Answer: Game design documents are massive expansions and explanations of game ideas and suggested implementation of them. They can run to hundreds of pages. For example, suppose a designer has the “idea” of creating a simulation wargame based on Russia’s invasion (or special operation, if you prefer their terminology) of Ukraine. They could specify that fight directly, but more often the designer will abstract it into “a geopolitical simulation game in which countries have the ability to attack neighboring countries.” What the design document will do is to greatly expand on that initial idea. It will specify political systems that each country might adopt, and how each will affect their ability to wage war. The document(s) will specify types of military units available to each country, costs of acquisition and maintenance, and perhaps a rock-paper-scissors discussion of strengths and weaknesses of each type of unit vs. enemy units. The document might discuss terrain features, how maps should be constructed with them, and how they affect each type of unit. At this point, we might end up with something along the lines of Sid Meier’s Civilization, an old SSI board wargame, or any of a hundred or a thousand different directions. From that original idea, the designer might propose a simplistic, cartoon-style game, or a detailed political and war simulation that could be used for strategic and tactical planning by an actual government. Or anywhere in between. This is the reason that experienced game developers scoff at amateurs saying, “I have an amazing idea for a game.” Ideas become amazing when they are filled out into rigorous detail, and even then only when passionate developers manage to implement something close to that plan. Ideas matter, but they are the smallest starting points for the massive design and development efforts needed to create a great game.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If I was going to make a game inspired by Beware, would I get in trouble for using the same Soviet style for buildings and the dark orange night or would there be any "not law connected" problems?
Answer: No. You’ll get in trouble if you rip assets from another game and use them in yours. You won’t get in trouble for creating your own assets with an arguably similar style.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: In my bridge app, with a hand with a long suit (6+ cards) and fewer than about 10 HCP, the app recommends a preemptive bid of 2 in the long suit. When I play the hand, I often lose by several tricks. What is the purpose of that bid?
Answer: Excellent question. First, never do that if your suit is clubs. A 2C opening bid shows a very strong hand, not necessarily with any clubs! 2D, 2H, and 2S show the hand you describe - a 6-card suit, and typically 6–10 high card points. You don’t usually want to make a weak two bid on fewer than 5 HCP. There’s more to it than that. The points should be concentrated in your long suit, and it’s also good to have some intermediates - 10, 9, 8, or 7 - in the suit. You don’t want to have another 4-card or longer major suit, and you don’t want to have a void. This is a great 2H opening hand - K10 AQ10984 xxx xx. Much stronger and you’d open 1H. A good 2S opening might be QJ10973 x Q9xx xx. Any weaker and you’d pass, but that singleton heart argues in favor of bidding, because you make it harder for your opponents to find their heart fit, and because it adds to the hand’s playing strength. You worry that you “often lose by several tricks.” That’s fine if you’re not vulnerable, much more dangerous if you are. The object isn’t to score the most points - It’s to get a better result than you would by not bidding. Look at my second example, and suppose your partner has an average 10 HCP hand. 10+5 = 15, subtract from 40 = 25. If your opponents have 25 high card points and an 8 or 9 card heart fit, they can probably make 4 hearts. If both sides are non-vulnerable, and you will go down 3 tricks in your 2S contract, you’ll lose 150 points. But if the opponents bid 4H and make it, they’ll take 420 points. Sacrificing 150 to prevent 420 is good bridge. Think about the first example, if the opponents manage to bid to 4S, but your partner has some values. Declarer will assume your partner has the King of Spades, since you’ve shown a weak hand. You’ll probably get a heart trick, and maybe two. Your bid might convince the opponents that you’re trying to steal a contract from them. Then they overbid, and you set them. Bridge is a game of risks and rewards, deception and technical bidding and play. If you never risk making a weak two, you “let the opponents walk all over you.” If you consistently make poor weak 2 bids - let’s say J96432 K3 Q4 975 - they’ll often haul you into a back alley and beat you up. The trick is to keep them guessing, but with a quality hand that will at least score some trump tricks if they double you. And sometimes when they do that, you’ll have that first hand, and your partner will show up with the right values to let you make doubled overtricks. Not to mention the free game bonus because your 2 of a major was doubled to 4.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have an amazing idea for a 3D horror video game. I thought out the plot and endings, thought out how each charter should look, and gave it lore. I now have to make the game, what software should I use?
Answer: Warning: This project will take far more time, and likely money, than you can imagine right now. That said, making at least a prototype of it yourself is definitely the way to go. You won’t manage to attract the attention of a publisher, other developers, or crowdfunding backers until you have something significant to show. That means it will have to be visually impressive, and fun to play. I would recommend either Unity or Unreal. I think Unity is easier for a beginner to learn, and it has tons of free or inexpensive assets you can use in your games. But I haven’t worked in Unreal for a while, and I hear very good things about it as well. Either should be fine for your project.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Should I send design document examples when applying for a game designer job?
Answer: That’s a tough question. If you do that, some issues may come up: When I used to apply for game designer jobs, I gave them two things - a 1–2 page resume, and a 1-page “credits” sheet of projects I had completed. A list of character references might also be in order, although that can result in the company bothering - and possibly trying to hire - your references. If they *asked* me for previous work, I carefully curated documents I could send them without violating any past agreements. More often, they asked for short game ideas, or asked me to write something original. Of course, you always try to comply with these, as well as requests for references. When my wife and I applied to design Hero’s Quest - I was already working for Sierra - we put together a few pages with some simple drawings, mocked-up screen shots of the interface, and a marketing page. I think that was the only page they really looked at. I compared our proposed game with existing Sierra games, listing similarities that would attract existing fans, and differences that would make the new game unique. I also waved around a published fantasy game module I had written for Judges Guild, as a way of demonstrating that I could complete a publishable project. When a company is interviewing you, they aren’t much interested in you, or what you want from them. They want to know how you will improve their bottom line, and help them make great projects.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: My (white American) mother says that when she was a child there was a loaf of white bread and butter on the table every night regardless of what else was for dinner. Was this common in the 1950s and does anyone still do this?
Answer: Yes, my father insisted that a meal was *not* a meal unless it included both bread and water. We typically had margarine, rather than butter, because they had read that margarine was healthier. The bread was occasionally white bread, but more often Jewish rye or pumpernickel. The sandwiches I took to school every day (in the 1960s) were usually peanut butter and jelly or jam - I liked cherry and grape - on white bread. I think I originally insisted on having the crusts cut off, but decided at some point they were ok. As for water, my siblings and I found a giant bowl-shaped glass in a store, and gave it to my father for Christmas for his never-ending supply of water. We called it “the fish bowl.”

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How can gamers be shown that NFTs and the blockchain are not evil and can be good?
Answer: You could put a statement in the game manual, and in your publicity, to the effect that: “Making games is very costly. This game had a development budget of $X million. We have provided the game to you (at no cost / for a cost that does not cover the development expenses).” “We had many choices of how to fund this game’s development. We could have embedded paid advertising or micro-transactions in the game. We could have raised money on a crowdfunding site. We could have raised funds from a publisher or investors, but they want a reasonable expectation of some return on their investment.” “Instead (or in addition), our choice is to sell NFTs within the game. You will own a unique digital asset, but most importantly, you will support our continuing development of games like this. If we don’t sell enough NFTs, we will have to stop making games, increase the sale price, or find another way of funding the very expensive process of game development.” “Incidentally, the blockchain we use to support these NFTs is not BitCoin or a similar environment-destroying technology. Instead, we’ve chosen a “lighter” blockchain system - the costs are documented here (appropriate link) - so that you are only destroying the world a little each time you buy one of our NFTs.” Well, you probably won’t want to phrase the last paragraph that way, but unless you can prove that your blockchains are magically different from every currently-existing blockchain, expect buyers to continue to hate your use of NFTs. Better, don’t use them. They suck for players, and they won’t bring you the profits you desire.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What causes crunch in the video game industry, and is it common regardless of where you work?
Answer: Crunch is extremely common in the game industry. It’s caused by developers “biting off more than they can chew.” Either the deadline is too short, or the project too ambitious, or the managers didn’t allow enough leeway for creative tasks running late. Almost every game project has substantial unknown tasks. You can’t quantify creativity, and a great game has many original, complex tasks. In theory, you can set an average expected completion time, with some tasks coming in early, and others running long. In practice, any time a task is completed ahead of schedule, the ambitious and starry-eyed developers add more creative tasks to the schedule. A great producer will try to keep that under control, but that risks making a bad game. Usually they’ll go along with the game designers, who want to create an ultimate expression of art each time. In the past, games always had to be completed by September, or early October, to make it onto store shelves by Black Friday. Many AAA games still have that requirement. But even indie games tend to have tight schedules; at some point, there are no more funds for development. That means crunching hard to make the deadline, shipping an incomplete game, or going bankrupt. As long as games are full of creativity and hard-to-quantify tasks, there will be crunch in the game industry.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What are the advantages of using an existing game engine instead of starting from scratch?
Answer: Why use an existing game engine? It depends on your goal. Do you want to create a game, or do you want to spend all of your time and resources on creating a new game engine? This is a question that developers often get wrong. I’ve worked for at least three companies that decided to “reinvent the wheel,” and ended up spending so much time on the wheel, it greatly impacted their ability to incorporate it into a wagon. Or however you want to stretch the metaphor. :-) There are times when making your own game engine can be sensible. If you are extremely well-funded, and your goal is to create multiple similar games - or a huge, expandable multiplayer world, and existing engines don’t meet your requirements well, then it might make sense to make your own engine. That’s a lot of “if’s,” because usually you will do better to let an engine developer to maintain and improve their engine. That’s typically a complex, multi-year project. The single instance where I saw a company make its own engine, and have it make sense, was Sierra On-Line in the 1980’s and 1990’s. Their AGI and SCI engines were custom-designed for their type of games, and there weren’t any alternatives on the market at the time. Sierra spent millions of dollars - quite a lot at that time - on their engines, but they became the core of dozens of top-selling games. For a single game, just don’t do it. That’s the mistake Sierra made when they decided to “roll their own” again, this time on three separate projects for three games - Quest for Glory V, King’s Quest VIII, and Gabriel Knight III. It could have made sense if they had centralized engine development, and created a single new engine for use by all three of those games. But three different engines, each taking many months (or years), and millions of dollars, away from their respective games… That was wrong, costly, and led to multiple games that would have been better in a well-maintained outside engine.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What can my son-in-law do? He has repeatedly been confused by the police for a criminal born in the same city on the same day and they share the same first name, resulting in a lost job, calls from the police, and garnished State tax returns.
Answer: This happens frequently with collection agencies. My wife was harassed for weeks because someone with a similar (but not identical) name had used a bad credit card in a city where we once lived. We just kept saying, “You have the wrong person,” and eventually the calls stopped. Similarly, someone with a name similar to - but not the same as - my father was in trouble with a collection agency near his home. We were still fielding calls and letters on that a year after my father’s death, and neither the first name nor middle initial matched. I don’t know a good solution, other than being persistent in denying the false info.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: In the card game "bridge", was the bidding round designed as a way for players to communicate information about their hands, or did bidding systems develop naturally over time?
Answer: Bidding is an essential part of the game of bridge, along with the scoring system. Bidding is both communication, and an exercise in risk vs. reward. If I remember correctly, similar older games simply rewarded you for the number of tricks you captured. That’s basically luck. Bidding lets you “make a contract” for the number of tricks you think your side can take. It requires communication - which is strictly limited by the “language” of bidding - so that the partners can agree on the trump suit and level of risk. Risk is rewarded because there are major bonuses for bidding to the game and slam levels, then fulfilling the contract. An interesting feature about bridge bidding is that full disclosure of conventions and agreements is required. While you are communicating with your partner, you also give information to the opponents. Players who are willing to gamble will often jump to a final contract without “testing the waters” along the way. This can be risky, but can be more likely to succeed because the opponents have less information about the combined assets in declarer’s and dummy’s hands.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can game developers move a game to a new game engine or would they need to make a new separate game?
Answer: A well-written game can be moved to a new engine. The caveat is that most games are not that well written. They are complex projects, involving experimental code, developed under high pressure and short deadlines. There is almost never time to rewrite and clean up code that “mostly works.” By well-written, we mean properly structure and encapsulated. To move an actor from point A to point B, while cycling “running” animation, and finding a good path between them, should be as simple as calling a “move actor” function. That, in turn, should use several other functions for the pathfinding, cycling, etc. If it’s done that way, the programmer should be able to replace the engine-level calls with similar procedure calls in a new engine. Those are fundamental building blocks that should be supported in any engine. To the extent that the game was made with an editor that came with the engine - for example, stretching “rubber band” lines to show a movement path, or defining transitions between nodes in an animation system - it may be much harder to move the game to a different engine with different tools. The general rule is that software changes are always more difficult, and take longer, than expected. But they *can* be done. Probably a good software developer will create some “port” tools that move portions of the code into a different engine’s data structures. They would use that for anything that is algorithmic in nature, rather than hand-crafted. Parts of software engineering are rote. Others require creativity.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Are new software/games less optimal than it could be because of copyright? In other words, does copyright protect code that would be more optimal for the type of program, from being used by someone else?
Answer: No, this has no effect. Designers design games, programmers code them. That’s all pretty much a combination of reusing their past work, along with new ideas and algorithms. Most code is rework of code from previous projects, and I’ve never seen copyright have any effect on that. For example, if you’ve previously helped develop three games, you generally have access to the source code you wrote for them. A good software engineer always tries to write clean, reusable code. On the new project, they’ll use libraries they’ve previously developed, or will copy/paste code from the previous project. That especially applies to code that is mostly the same for every game, such as the core game loop, animation routines, and such.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How many unreleased details do videogame studio employees receive when tasked with making a videogame? Does the entire team know or only those who need to know about these crucial details? (eg. title, location setting, upgrades and features etc.)
Answer: Pretty much all of them. You can’t make a game without knowing what you’re making. The game designers create detailed descriptions of everything in the game, as well as overview documents that describe the setting, type of gameplay, game mechanics, and so on. Everyone on the team usually has access to most, or all, of those documents. Most of them don’t read everything, but they’ll at least get the idea of the game, as well as every detail of the design for the parts they’re building. There are no secrets within the team. They couldn’t do their jobs if there were.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How do I fix NullReferenceException in Unity?
Answer: You fix NULL reference exceptions in Unity the same way you do it in any other environment. Bulletproof your code. Every place you dereference a pointer, first check whether the pointer is NULL. If it is, log details about where the exception occurred, and either throw an error, or handle it as an exception case where you don’t dereference the non-pointer at all. All great code is written with built-in error checking and debugging. Sometimes that’s code you’ll strip out for the “final” release, but often you will choose to leave it in to help find problems from the field.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it common to earn a million dollars from a story-based indie game? I would really love to make several versions of a game based on a great story. For example, one per year.
Answer: No, that is extraordinarily rare. If you are already a NY Times bestselling author, you might have a chance of making a bestselling story-based, indie game. Even then, you would almost certainly do better - in income vs. time spent - having a major developer and publisher make and sell the game for you. Your royalties per unit would be much smaller, but they would sell vastly more units. The average indie game on Steam sells 2,000 units during its lifetime. At $5 to $10 for an indie game, expect to make $10,000 to $20,000, not a million. You will almost certainly make more net income from a book than from a game. Books don’t cost a million dollars to develop, as major indie games do.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it true that design positions in the games industry tend to attract the "crazies" as expressed by veteran designer Mike Stout of Insomniac Studios? If so, why is this (video game industry, personalities, hiring, interviewing, careers, toxicity)?
Answer: I haven’t seen any evidence that game design positions are filled by crazies, whether or not the role attracts them. Most game designers are incredibly hard workers, and highly intelligent as well as creative. If anything, they tend to be mainstream. Liberal, but among most of the game developers I know, that’s mainstream.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why are almost all indie games 2D with pixel art? I understand that they are cheaper, and Indies have low budget, but still, they are not pretty. The only game where they are is Dead Cell. I am not expecting AAA graphics, just something a bit better.
Answer: There’s a good reason, but first, my exception: We started development as 2D top-down exploded view. But the artists rebelled, and we ended up in 2D isometric, and finally in 3D. In my opinion, the result is a better game. But it also exploded the budget. We brought in $400K on Kickstarter, which left $275K for game development after fees and fulfillment expenses. The game ended up costing about $1 million, which we funded through a second Kickstarter, several generous donors, a venture capital investment, and personal retirement funds. We will likely never break even, despite our game being very successful by indie standards (over 20K units sold - most indie games on Steam sell under 2K units). And that’s why you don’t see very many games like ours. AAA games have budgets of $50 million or higher. Most indies find it a struggle to raise $100,000. With art resources the largest cost center of game development, that has to be the first thing to be cut. It’s possible to make a game with primitive 3D graphics and asset store clip art, but it won’t even look as good as the 2D pixel art games you’re decrying.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Who is unbeaten in chess?
Answer: Who is unbeaten in chess? Anyone who has never played it. Everyone who has won a significant number of games has also lost some. You can apply that to any game, sport, or other human endeavor - If you don’t try it, you won’t fail at it. Of course, you’ll also never experience success, nor do anything useful with your life. Serena and Venus Williams, Rafael Nadal, Iga Swiatek, Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer - None of them would have become some of the richest, best, and most famous tennis players in the world without losing many points, games, sets, and even matches. You can’t learn to win without occasionally losing.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: As a software engineer, how can one figure if a company is following good software development practices before joining?
Answer: Look at the quality of their products. If they’re good, it’s likely that they are created with reasonably sound development practices. You can also consider the quality of the interview. If your potential manager asks challenging, but fair, questions, then they probably understand how to challenge their team without overwhelming them. If they react badly to your request for details on the interview question, expect them to do that when you’re working there. As for once you start working at the company, stay adaptable. Rudyard Kipling wrote, “There are nine and sixty ways of constructing tribal lays, and every single one of them is right.” That applies to software development as well. Just because a company does not follow the practices you’ve been taught does not mean that their processes are bad. They can do things differently, but still be doing them well. Try to fit into the process where you work.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: The chances of rolling any one number on a 6 sided (non-trick) dice is 1 in 6. How many times do you have to roll the dice to make sure you roll every number at least once?
Answer: Infinity. It doesn’t matter how many times you roll the die. Each one is an independent 1/6 chance of rolling each of the numbers. Phrased differently, each roll is an independent 5/6 chance of not rolling a particular number. If you roll the die 100 times, there is a very high probability that you will hit all six numbers, but it isn’t a certainty. There is still a (5 / 6) ^ 100 chance of never hitting any particular number you choose. The chance that you won’t hit some number on the die is even higher, but I’m not going to work that math for you. Now that chance is very small, somewhere around 0.00000012075%, but it never gets to zero. If you roll the die one million times, there is still an infinitesimal - but not zero - chance that you never roll a particular number. Incidentally, if you roll the die five or fewer times, there is a zero chance that you will hit every number. That’s why the calculation for missing “any” number is more complicated than for missing a particular number.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Games companies have departments where they try and work out what games are going to be popular 5-10 years in the future, how do they work out what is going to be popular? Have their been any big noticeable successes in 'Future Planning' in the past?
Answer: Game companies are notoriously terrible at predicting the future. A friend once phrased it as, “All marketing does is tell us what was popular five years ago.” Game company marketers and executives have no clue about what players will want in 5–10 years. If you ask a group of gamers what game they want to play in five years, they’ll say, “I want a game just like this game that I already play, only better.” Gamers have no clue about future trends. That’s actually what large game companies do; they keep making variations on the games that have sold well for them - or for other companies - in the past. Occasionally they’ll have a brainstorming session of management, marketing, and game designers to strategize future products. But most of the time, the result is “make more of the same.” As Chris Nash mentioned, the long development cycle of modern games may give the impression that the game is somehow “looking ahead” five years, but actually they just come up with a plan, and spend years executing it. If the game is successful - probably because they also spent tens of millions of dollars promoting it - people can look at it in hindsight and say, “Wow! Five years ago they predicted what’s popular now!” But that isn’t how it works. They do things to make a game popular, and sure enough, it often is.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Where can I find some people to help me make games? I have looked on Facebook groups, I have asked around in public, I have gone on meetups and usually somebody says they will help me then never show up.
Answer: Two choices: Incidentally, that last is a lot like getting a job in the game development industry. Most of the time, you’ll be assigned to make games based on other people’s concepts and designs, not on yours.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can you hire someone who owns graphic editor software (e.g. Photoshop) license to make game assets for your commercial game product? Will it cause problem, if your company don't have the license but use the game assets made by the software?
Answer: That’s fine. Generally any assets you (or your contractors) create using a tool such as Photoshop belong entirely to you, and are royalty-free. It’s quite common for small indie game companies to use contract artists who who work out of their own homes or offices. They supply the tools they use to make assets for you.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: My parents are in their mid 60s and I am hoping that they could reach at least 90 years old. Will it be more common for the boomers to reach their 90s?
Answer: According to the chart at If your mother and father are both 65, on average, your father will live 18 more years, to age 83. Your mother will live 21 more years, to age 86. It’s possible they will reach their 90s, but it’s against the odds. I don’t have a range chart, but most likely it’s a Poisson distribution (“bell chart”) with many more people near the average, and many fewer at the extremes. In 1970, the life expectancy for men was 13.1 years, so it has gone up by five years over the last 50. Where your parents live, and their lifestyle choices, also make a difference. A 65-year-old man living in California has 2.5 years longer life expectancy than one who lives in Alabama. That likely reflects wealth, race, diet, weather, whether your father smokes, and other factors that tend to be different between those states. For example, far more Alabamans smoke, and more Californians are physically active.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: A box contains 3 white balls and 3 black balls. We are selecting two balls without replacement. On average, how many white balls will be in the selected two balls?
Answer: Pull ball 1. 50% it’s white, 50% black. So that makes 0.5 white balls towards your total. If the first ball was white (50%), that leaves 2 white, and 3 black balls. 40% of them are white. So that adds .5 x .4 = 0.2 white balls. If the first ball was black (50%), that leaves 3 white, and 2 black balls. 60% of them are white. So that adds 0.5 x 0.6 = 0.3 white balls. Since those last 2 are mutually exclusive, you can add all the partial counts together. 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.3 white balls equals 1 white ball on average. Of course, you could have solved this more simply. Take out 2 balls, and then look at them. Since there were 3 white and 3 black balls originally, it’s sensible that, on average, one of them is white. Unfortunately, “sense” and intuition don’t always work with probability, so it’s better to go through the arithmetic.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If I wanted to write a real simple game similar to Army men Sarges Heros or the original Rainbow Six how much C# would I need to know and is making your character walk and shoot a gun really that complicated?
Answer: Do it as a paper tabletop game. When you want to move a character, move its piece on your board. Create tables for what happens when a character shoots a gun, ducks behind cover, and so on. Moving characters and resolving combat on a computer is at least 1000 times more difficult.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have made several indie games and I want to work at valve how do I get hired?
Answer: You apply. Mention your games in the application and resume, but don’t place all of the emphasis on the games. Instead, talk about the skills you learned in developing them. That might be Unity or Unreal, C++, scripting, animation, etc. That’s what a company such as Valve wants to see - “Does this candidate have relevant skills for working on our games.” Ideally, check your LinkedIn and other contacts to see if you have connection with anyone currently working at Valve. Contact them, let them know you’re applying, and ask if they will help champion your application. Most game jobs are filled through contacts already at the company.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why are AAA games so mediocre and with such toxic developers?
Answer: Your first premise is wrong. AAA games deliver exactly what their players want. If they didn’t, they wouldn’t find the millions of players needed to support their multi-million dollar budgets. They are certainly not mediocre in terms of art quality, audio, and presentation. AAA games are the most realistic presentations available in gaming. These games might not deliver experiences that you and I want to play, but we aren’t typical mass-market game players. They do deliver pulse-pounding action and immersive twitch gaming. Players who enjoy following sports tend to like that style of energetic, if typically story-poor, experiences. As for toxic developers, it’s unclear whether AAA studios have more toxic individuals than in other businesses. As their games emphasize risk and adrenaline, it’s likely that impulsive risk-takers are attracted to those studios, so it’s possible that they have more toxic developers. But I can only speculate, not prove or disprove the premise.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Are text based games the easiest type of games to make?
Answer: The basic setup for a text based game is easy to create. I’m thinking, for example, of adventure games with simple parser, or even easier, menu-based systems. But good writing is hard. It only takes a few pages to specify a game like tic-tac-toe or Flappy Bird, and those games are very easy to implement. But an adventure or role-playing game needs hundreds of pages of text to handle all the things players might try. Writing that text well is hard.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it true that game designers with much experience can choose their job?
Answer: Sure, it’s like choosing a specialization in the Army. When you enlist, you can pick what you want to do. Then they’ll assign you where they have a need, most likely not where you chose. A relative signed up to the Army to become a computer programmer. The Army assigned him to be a tank gunner. In the same way, yes, experienced and inexperienced game designers can choose their jobs. Then it’s pot luck whether they get the job they chose. Even game companies rarely get to choose - Most of them are contractors for big game publishers, and most of the time, they work on the projects for which they’re contracted. There is one major exception - Indie game development. If I start my own company - I have - by myself or with other developers, we can choose what games we make. But we can’t choose to have regular meals or a roof over our head. That’s chosen by players, who decide which games to buy, and which to ignore or steal. In the case of most indie and small game companies, the games in that first category are rarely yours.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: In general, is a classic video game remembered for its story or for its gameplay?
Answer: Games are remembered for their story, and special moments. But nobody remembers games that aren’t challenging and fun to play. Poor gameplay masks good story. Both are required to make a good game. We all remember, “Luke, I’m your father,” from a certain film. Or, “We’ll always have Paris,” and “Louis, I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship,” from another. But if the rest of the film wasn’t moving, and well-crafted, with clear heroes and villains, we wouldn’t care about the revelations from those lines.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it possible to hire a software developer/engineer to modify the exe file of a videogame in abandonware status in such a way that it adds a new functionality (i.e.: a racing game has 6 gears and I want to add 7th gear) to enjoy it privately?
Answer: Can you modify a Windows computer to become a microwave oven? They both have processors and memory, so what’s the big deal? Programming is hard. It’s nearly impossible without the right tools - in this case, the source code for the game. You don’t just change a “6” in the code to “7” to add a new gear. You’d have to find the table of gear ratios, and add a new one… But that table is probably exactly the right size to describe six gears. Adding a seventh to the end of it will overwrite some piece of data or code, and will almost certainly break the program. Move everything one position in memory? Now all of the references to the other data point to the wrong place. Things will break even worse. You are better off finding the original developer and offering them a contract to upgrade the game. Be prepared to spend a bundle on that.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If I have a video game idea that I think is really good, what can I do with it (if I can’t make games), or should I try to make it?
Answer: Anyone can make a game. There are many easy-to-use free tools for making games. If you care about your ideas, take the effort to learn one of those tools, and use them. You can also make your game as a tabletop game. All that requires is some paper, maybe light cardboard - I used to cut up manila folders to make my games, and a pen. You could even repurpose a board game you already own. If you aren’t willing to do the work to make games from your own ideas, you’ll never find anyone else willing to do that for you. We all have our own ideas, and don’t even get around to making our own games most of the time.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What do you think about Trump losing his appeal in the NY civil probe and now having to testify under oath?
Answer: It was inevitable, but I don’t think it will do much good. Trump has shown himself to be completely willing to lie about anything, under any circumstances. He’ll do that under oath as well. The problem with our court and political systems might be that they assume guilty people will act guilty. True sociopaths - such as Trump - have no moral core nor qualms about anything they do or say. It’s very difficult to convict a rich White man who denies all of his crimes. There’s always just enough ambiguity to introduce reasonable doubt. As Trump himself said, he could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot someone, and he’d get away with it. Knowing that his opponents have character, and that they take honor seriously, he is happy to use that against them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Are Democrats angry about being lied to about Trump?
Answer: No, we aren’t angry. We’re aghast that so many Republicans either: And are so intent on winning, that they don’t care if their leaders lie, cheat, and steal to do that. If that was, say, 5% or 10% of Americans, I’d accept that as a quirk of statistics. But it isn’t. The Republican Party, led by Trump, McConnell, and Fox News, seems to own the hearts, minds, and souls of nearly one American in three. That’s way too many of the people around me who are willing to accept rot at the heart of the country. It reminds me of the con men who said, “You can’t fool an honest man.” I think many MAGA Republicans think that they’ll come out ahead in a crooked game. Some of them may be right, but the vast majority are being pushed further down by their chosen leaders. I feel sorry for them, and frustrated at their willful ignorance, at the same time. But I’m not angry by any lies about Trump; I think I’m getting pretty good information on his character and actions.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do game developing companies require their game developers, software engineers or level designers to follow dresscode (for example: formal clothes, no long hair, no dreads, no tattoes no piercing, shaved beard etc)?
Answer: No, I’ve never heard of a company in the game industry making rules like that. The typical clothing of employees at Sierra On-Line, when I worked there in the 1990’s, was blue jeans and a t-shirt. At least one developer in the QA department never wore shoes to work, even when there was snow on the ground. Many had beards. In fact, I think I had one when I started. Other companies might require shoes in the office, or some similar light dress code, but game developers tend to be informal. Nobody wants to interfere with their creativity by putting restrictions on them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What programming language(s) were most used to develop old console games (for example, Sega games)?
Answer: Old console games were almost always written in assembly language - basically machine commands with a thin veneer of “language” to make them slightly easier to code. High-level languages such as C didn’t have amazing compilers in the 70’s and 80s. Also, the early consoles had very little memory, so programmers needed to optimize every byte of code. For example, my PET computer had 8K bytes of memory, less than one millionth of the memory in most modern PC’s. Most consoles had 4K or less memory. Even in the late 1990’s, we still used assembly language to write code for the Game Boy Color, but it was a more sophisticated assembler with “macro” capabilities that let one line of code cover more than one machine instruction.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do you think President Biden's efforts to lower the price of gasoline have mainly been effective or ineffective in the long run?
Answer: In the Twitter age, 3 days feels like “the long run,” and 3 months feels like an eternity. Try years, not days nor even months. Then we’ll have your answer. First we’ll need to get completely clear of the Covid-19 pandemic and the Russian assault on Ukraine. Those are the main factors that are driving gasoline prices up. In the long run, we might need to remain independent of Russian oil to make it harder for them to invade other countries. If that’s the case, it’s likely that oil and gasoline prices will remain high “in the long run.” But that’s ok, because the world is running out of fossil fuels anyway, and they’re terrible for the environment and “long run” climate change. Biden’s response to those issues, as well as the war in Ukraine, may result in much lower use of gasoline. At that point, the price of it won’t matter much. We’ll use more solar and solar-generated electric power… once Republicans and Democrats owned by the coal industry let meaningful change happen.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: The Democrats say the economy is not Biden's fault. Do you believe them?
Answer: Of course. The economy is massively complex, and no one person - even the President of the United States - has much immediate impact on it. Presidential policies can affect the economy, but they take years to have much effect. Some of the current inflationary issues are due to tax changes - mostly reducing taxes of very wealthy people and large corporations - during the Trump administration. But it wouldn’t be fair to blame that for everything. In case you were unaware, we’ve spent the last two years suffering under a worldwide pandemic. That has created chaos in manufacturing, shipping, and distribution. What does “chaos” mean to the average consumer? It means that prices go up, because manufacturers can no longer rely on cheap parts from other countries. Their costs go up, and they pass them along to you. More recently, we have the Russian invasion of Ukraine. That war, and the worldwide response to it, has limited supplies of oil. Less oil means higher prices for the rest of it. It’s likely true that, if Trump were still President, he’d have let Putin take over Ukraine without contest. That would have been cheaper in the short run, and disastrous to the world economy in the long run. Personally, I prefer a little short-term pain over permanent disaster. Well, ok, maybe it’s just that I have a moral core, and don’t like the idea of letting “strongmen” bully weaker people or countries. President Biden also has a moral core, and I like that in a President. A certain recent President lacked one. Do you have a magic wand that will fix worldwide economic problems? Neither do I, and neither does any President. Biden has the additional challenge that Republicans in the Senate are stonewalling most of his policies. Even if he did have the magic wand, we wouldn’t see the results after Voldemort blocked the spell of prosperity.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What is the percentage of codes that are used in AAA and indie video games coding, that are a pre written codes from programming libraries, and what are the game engines used for most console AAA video games?
Answer: The question shows a complete lack of understanding of computer coding. A game consists of many code modules, each of which is broken down further into “functions” (also called methods, procedures, subroutines, etc.). Frequently, the code in any given function invokes other functions. In addition, games have a huge amount of data, much of it imported from various tools - Photoshop, Maya, sound editing tools, and many more. Many of the functions invoked are in the game code’s libraries, and others are in outside libraries. Those in turn might be supplied with the programming language, or might be part of a “game engine” - a very amorphous term - or any number of external libraries. But it isn’t turtles all the way down. Eventually, there has to be some code that actually does something, and doesn’t call any more functions. Some of that code is in the game, some in the external libraries, and some in system libraries. It could be in a single programming language, or in dozens of languages. C++ is popular for game development, but it’s common to use higher-level scripting languages and other tools. Those tools, in turn, are a combination of ones created by the game studio and ones supplied by other vendors. C++ doesn’t actually run on any hardware platform. It compiles the code into machine language, a more primitive “language” that directly does things in the hardware such as storing and retrieving data, doing simple arithmetic, and so on. Game code that requires extreme machine performance is sometimes written directly in machine language. For example, when I developed games for Sierra On-Line, we had our own in-house game engine. It was about two-thirds in the C language, and one-third in machine language. When we converted the engine to run on various computers, we had to rewrite all of the machine language for each platform. The C code was mostly platform-independent, but we created some macros to deal with differences in byte ordering and similar issues that varied between platforms. The games themselves used libraries in that game engine, so that all of the code that *didn’t* call a library function was specific to the individual game. Our engine “compiled” the game code into processor-independent p-code, which was interpreted at run-time to call engine functions that eventually ended up executing machine code. Any given programmer worked at a higher level of abstraction, and didn’t worry about how the system was implementing the high-level constructs at run time. So how much code is where? Nobody knows or cares. A game consists of a vast amount of code and data. Much of it is generated by the game studio, but much of it is in other tools, engines, libraries, compilers, art, music, sound effects, and more. A studio could generate all of that internally, but they’d likely never finish more than a game prototype. All of those other tools save time and money, so that the developer doesn’t need to “reinvent the wheel” literally or figuratively.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it worth having multiple game engines to make various types of games?
Answer: Of course. There is no “one size fits all” in game development. Some game engines are great for making high-frame-rate games when the environment is constantly changing. Those are perfect for space battles and flight simulators. But to do that, they have to compromise in other areas. Maybe they only support relatively low polygon counts in order to increase the frame rate. They might not be good at displaying detailed, still, painted backgrounds for adventure and hidden object games. They probably don’t support development of cell phone apps that have entirely different requirements on memory and screen resolution. Another game engine might be great for making simple 2D games with small footprints for mobile games. Another might support 3D with high polygon counts for rich, detailed backgrounds that don’t change very often - say a 3D adventure game. Unity 3D is a pretty good compromise engine that supports multiple types of games, but it isn’t necessarily ideal for any one of them. I use it for my “barely 3D” adventure/RPG’s, and it’s good. But it adds a lot of development time to get around features of the engine that we don’t need. See, for example, It’s a Unity 3D game, but designed to emulate 1990’s “2.5D” graphic adventure games. We like the additional features Unity provides, but they definitely increased our development cost and time compared to using a pure adventure game engine such as Adventure Game Studio (AGS):

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have a friend that has a lot of ideas for games and apps but he doesn’t know how to code. Is there a way for him to share his ideas with people that have those skills?
Answer: Yes, he can start by learning to code. That can be done through a secondary school or University program, or at a site such as Khan Academy. Then he can get a job working on other people’s ideas for games and apps, learning more techniques along the way. After that, he might be ready to start building his own apps, which is the only way he’ll be able to find a developer that doesn’t charge him millions of dollars to work on his ideas.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Does video game “balance” matter if a game is centered around being hardcore and realistic as opposed to the casual easy instant gratification type game? Real life is rarely balanced so would you sacrifice realism for “balance”?
Answer: Game designers constantly sacrifice realism for balance, and to make a more enjoyable experience. I gave a talk once at the CGDC, and someone in the audience called out, “But my life doesn’t work that way!” Another participant responded, “Who’d want to play a game based on *your* life?” It got a laugh, but the point was valid. If reality gets in the way of crafting a fun experience for players, then we don’t try to simulate reality. Fun, challenge, and mastery matter more than verisimilitude. In any case, we can’t fit all of reality into a game. If we did, it wouldn’t be a game anymore. We pick and choose the aspects that work in that particular game, and discard the rest. When you think about it, other media are no different. Would you watch a James Bond film, or read one of the books, and happily spend one-third of the time sleeping, and much of the rest driving to the office, reading Bond’s briefing paperwork, and so on? No, films cut out most of the realistic boring parts, and focus on the fun and exciting parts of Bond’s job. In one of the books, M chews Bond out for failing to complete his paperwork, so apparently Bond doesn’t want to play that part of the game either. Balance, and challenge that leads to a sense of mastery, make a game fun. Making players waste time on routine, boring stuff is a good way to lose players.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If I have a bowl with 20 red balls and 20 white balls, what is the probability that I would pick a red ball out?
Answer: That’s indeterminate. You might decide not to pick out any ball. You might look into the bowl and decide you like the color red, so pick out a red ball. If you meant that you are definitely picking out a ball, and doing it with a secure blindfold, the answer would be different. But it would also be trivial.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Many right wingers claim "Democrats want to remake the US into the new world order." What is "the new world order", and where is this doctrine in the Democratic platform? Is it a secret that only Republicans know about?
Answer: The “new world order” of the Democrats is following the U. S. Constitution, its amendments, and the other laws that have been passed in over 230 years as a Democratic Republic. Not all Democrats will agree with everything I’m going to write here, but I think most of these points are supported by most Democrats… and hopefully, by many Republicans. We believe that everyone should have the right to vote, and to have their votes honestly counted. Loud voices should not trump the rule of law. We believe that education, health, and other public services - fire, police, roads, etc. - are important, and are best handled by government organizations, paid for by taxes - rather than being handled by paid private enterprises. We believe that everyone who lives in the U.S. should have equal rights, privileges, and responsibilities regardless of wealth, color, ethnic background, religion, or citizenship status. That means that everyone pays taxes while they’re working, should get competent healthcare, and should eventually be able to retire. Most of us believe that the environment is in serious trouble as a result of polluted air and water, and man-caused warming effects. We believe that serious action on this should have begun in earnest 50 years ago, and that we’re rapidly approaching a tipping point where the Earth will die, and it will be too late for us to save it. It is vastly more expensive to mitigate pollution and destruction of the environment now than it was 50 years ago, but we have to make gigantic efforts now. In 50 years, it will be at least 30 years too late to act.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Given how extensive and amazing lore/story Warhammer 40k is with decades of table top game industrial experience (not to mention they are worth billions), why are they generally horrible at making good video games apart from few exceptions?
Answer: In the 1990’s, the hot idea in video games was full motion video. Developers wanted their games to look like movies… which was really shorthand for, “I want my game to make as much money as a top Hollywood film makes.” Some companies went full bore and hired Hollywood film producers to help make their games. Games got more cinematic… but they were mostly awful, and they didn’t sell well. You see, the problem with hiring an “auteur” is that they want to make a film - or a game - their way. They’re likely to ignore or mock the collected wisdom of people who have actually been making games for years. After all, if they were any good, they wouldn’t need the auteur to bail them out. So, take a company that has decades of tabletop gaming experience, and let them make a video game. Why would you expect the game to be good? It isn’t “in their wheelhouse.” The skills that go into making video games include those used for making films - visuals matter, music and sound effects matter. The skills that go into making good board games *are* applicable to video games - unit balance, strategy and tactics, etc. - but they’re only part of the equation. Tabletop game developers might or might not be good at the other aspects, but they aren’t part of their day job.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have an idea and a written game and I want to outsource it. Which are the steps I must take?
Answer: Write your idea in a design notebook or Google Doc. Draw some charts about the implications of your idea - what does it do to your story, characters, and plot. That should lead to a few more ideas. Write them down, chart them, then chart the relationships between all of your ideas so far. Start scratching out - or moving to the side - ideas that you just can’t get to work with your other ideas. When you get up around 100 ideas and the network of their effects on each other idea, you’ll start having something that looks a little like a game. Somewhere around 500 to 1000, you might have enough design for an actual game. That’s why professional game developers don’t give much respect to anyone who says, “I have a great idea for a game!” It’s only when you have hundreds of ideas, and have taken the time and effort to see how they all interact, that you’re actually ready to make a game. You can start sooner than that, but you’ll waste a lot of time reworking things that turn out to be incompatible.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can I alone make a first person adventure game? I am not aiming at great production value, I want to make it for fun. Can I do it, maybe use AI for voices of characters?
Answer: Sure. Your best bet is to make it a text adventure. You could use TWINE, Inform, Inkle, or any of a number of free development systems (aka “engines”). If you want something a little more immersive, go with 2D (or “2.5D”) graphics using AGS (Adventure Game Studio), GODOT, or a similar environment. Unity is also free, but I wouldn’t start with it - too many features, and not specific enough to adventure games - for a solo developer. After you’ve acquired some development experience using a text or 2D graphic adventure system, you can upgrade to Unity to make your game first person 3D.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I'm making a video game on Unity. How do I send it to someone for feedback without letting them change anything?
Answer: Use the Build command to make an executable version of the game. Send the executable (and any necessary data files) to your testers.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it normal for a new game designer to feel overwhelmed by the technicalities and necessities of game development?
Answer: Yes. You never get over that. One aspect of it is called, “impostor syndrome,” as in, “Should I even be here?” The truth is that feeling overwhelmed is a realistic response to the incredibly challenging nature of game development. If you don’t feel overwhelmed at times, you probably aren’t taking it seriously enough. That feeling comes when you really care about what you’re doing, and want to do the best job possible. For a perfectionist game designer (or other game developer), “good enough” is never good enough. You get through this by temporarily focusing in on a single task, or by taking the time to break down your huge monolithic game design into manageable pieces. Designing a game consists of designing dozens or hundreds of subsystems, hundreds of scenes and events, and so on. It’s pretty easy to get overwhelmed by all that, and that’s the time to get just one of those systems or events written out in detail. Get that one off your list, and move on to another. Just make sure that you periodically move back up to the bird’s eye view to make sure you aren’t neglecting the forest for the trees… or turning elegant design and writing into a bunch of metaphors and cliches as I just did. :-)

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Assume you're a game design student, who's working on a small racing game to improve his/her skills. Even then, would you still have to pay royalties to car makers if you intend to use their cars in your small game?
Answer: I don’t think any car manufacturer would come after a student-created racing game. Even though your small on-screen cars may look like their large, real ones, it’s pretty hard to prove that yours are “stolen” from their designs. You might want to use fantasy names rather than trademarked ones - Instead of Lamborghini, call yours a Super Sheep. (My first thought was “Ewe orgasm,” but… That depends on your style and audience.) Don’t use actual blueprints of their cars to make your 3D models, and it isn’t important to make them exactly identical. But unless you start selling your game, and it becomes very successful, nobody will care. If that does happen, contact automakers and offer to include their cars for a fee - that they pay you!

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What are chances of getting off a waitlist from either Tulane, UMich, or UCSB? I was waitlisted at alll 3 and am really hoping to get off of one (they are much better schools than my current options) but want to know how real my chance is
Answer: It partly depends on where you live. All of the UC campuses make a strenuous effort to accept California residents, even though tuition is much higher for out-of-state residents. A quick Web search came up with this: “At UCSB, the waitlist admission rate in 2019 stood at 10% and shot up to an astounding 97% in 2020.” That sounds pretty good… except why such a dramatic difference between 2019 and 2020? Most likely the answer is that many admitted students chose not to attend in Fall 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic, so the University was able to accept almost everyone on the waitlist. That implies that the situation might be very different in 2022. If your qualifications are excellent, you’re probably a favorite to receive an invitation. If they’re borderline, you’ll just have to wait. I haven’t looked into Tulane or UMich, but I imagine they’ll have similar hard-to-interpret acceptance ratios. Good luck! UCSB is a great school, and a wonderful place to live on campus or off.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Im planning on becoming a software developer or a game developer. When I get a job and begin working will I be told what lines of code and language im suppose to use or will I need to figure it out myself?
Answer: You generally won’t be hired unless you already have demonstrated expertise in the language and development environment they use. That might be a little silly, as good developers quickly adapt to new environments, but it gives the HR team an easy criterion for filtering applicants. You’ll generally work with one or more mentors who are very experienced with the company’s development environment. They’ll answer questions and help you get up to speed with their preferred tools. In a larger company, you’ll usually work on only small areas of the development project, and these will hopefully be clearly defined for you. At a more senior level, you’ll be expected to have more knowledge, skills, and flexibility. You might then be assigned to more open-ended projects on which you’ll need to define a strategy and do some mid-level design before diving into the code. For example, my company hired an experienced software tool developer for our game project. His first assignment was to design and prototype a “design editor.” We gave him some examples of ones we’ve used in the past, then he started coming up with ideas. His first version was elegant and easy to use, but turned out to be cumbersome for a huge project like ours. He went back to the drawing board, and soon emerged with a new version we’re still using nine years later. We didn’t supervise his work, except to test it an let him know where it could be improved. With an inexperienced developer, I’d have worked much more closely with them, possibly providing some example code, and giving detailed feedback on each prototype build.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why should you choose Unity 3D for your next game development project?
Answer: Unity 3D is free (until you release a successful game), powerful, and very well supported with tutorials, manuals, and sample code. There are many experienced Unity 3D developers you can hire as employees or contractors to help you make your game. Unity 3D is great for multi-platform development.
