We use it to build apps for Windows, Macintosh, Linus, Android, iOS, and Switch. I think it also supports some consoles.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Has anyone ever considered using the technology (and world map) of Google Earth to create the open world of a video game, no matter what genre?
Answer: Yes, many people have considered it. I don’t personally know of games that have done it, but I’m pretty sure some exist.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do you think there is a high entry level barrier in making big triple A video games? How can one developer make such a thing?
Answer: One developer cannot make a “big triple A video game.” By definition, a AAA game is a high-budget game made by a large studio. Hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of developers work on each AAA game. My company makes “small” indie games, and we still have teams ranging from 6 or more developers up to dozens. Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption had a team of 30 developers over the course of 5 years. If we had a larger budget, we’d have made it in 2 years with 50 or more developers. Good video games made by a single developer are “rare as hens’ teeth.” By definition, they cannot be “big AAA” games, and they rarely achieve meaningful - by a big publisher’s standard - sales.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Will making a successful video game with a good amount of sales be a good extracurricular to put on my college applications?
Answer: Of course, that would be impressive! But you don’t need “a good amount of sales.” Completing a game is a great accomplishment in itself; most people who start making one fail to finish it. Uploading it to Steam, and getting any sales at all - at any price - also shows commitment to finishing a project. That’s what colleges - and game companies - want to see. They want to know that you can finish what you start. Sales aren’t expected, but are a bonus. Quality is preferred, but is again a bonus. Finishing a project will put you far ahead of most industry wannabes who have ideas, but fail to follow up on them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If I have story for video game, but I don't have experiance in programming languages, are there any compnies might make this video game and sell it?
Answer: No. No game company buys ideas or stories for games. They make the game in-house, or contract out design and development to another studio. Ideas are of zero value to them. They won’t even open a letter with a game idea because they might already have a similar game in progress, and don’t want to be sued by someone whose idea they never needed.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Who will win? An AAA game company that released a bug consisting, unfinished game, or an indie game company that released a bug-free, finished game?
Answer: Both will lose. (Ok, the indie game has a small chance of being a modest success, but the odds are against it.) The AAA company spent many millions of dollars to create their unfinished game, and expects to sell millions of copies to pay for that work, along with marketing and advertising expenses. The game will sell well initially, then players will abandon it when the poor quality is reported. The game, and therefore the company, will lose money. The indie game company almost certainly spent a lot less to develop their game, but they also don’t have the marketing muscle and funds to put into advertising it. It’s possible that the game will become a sleeper hit, but far more likely it will sell modestly because most gamers will never know it exists. Most games lose money. When you hear about games outselling movies, that’s the aggregate of tens of thousands of games. Far more games are made than films, so while the total sales of all those games is immense, the market share for each game is relatively small. It’s even worse for indies, because most of those sales dollars go to the small number of heavily-hyped AAA games. If a AAA game is bad, it will lose a lot of money, but its gross sales will still vastly exceed those of any one indie game. 100K unit sales - maybe $5,000,000 at $50 each - is considered a gigantic failure for a AAA game. 20K unit sales - maybe $400,000 at $20 each - is considered successful for an indie game. But they’re both financial failures. The indie game probably cost at least $500K to develop and market. The company’s 70% share of sales - $280,000 in the example - means a $220,000 loss. The AAA game cost at least $20 million to develop, so at their sweetheart-deal 80% share - $4,000,000 in the example - means a $16 million loss. It’s a very bad idea to release a bad, unfinished game after spending tens of millions of dollars developing it.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I’m 24, is it too late for me to become a professional game developer?
Answer: I started at 33 and am still doing it at 66. 74 might be pushing it, but at 24, you barely have the real-life experience and technical education you’ll need to make games. The earlier you start, the more time you’ll have to make great games.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: A show has been running on TV and has stopped. Now I want to create a game based on it, with a different name but with a similar theme. Can they sue me?
Answer: No, you won’t need permission for that. Themes are universal and unprotected. Specific assets, such as titles, character names, art assets, and music are usually copyrighted. The downside is that you won’t be able to use connection with fans of the original series to help build a market. You can probably mention the series in passing, “Our game lets you play a lifeguard like in Baywatch.” But nothing closer than that, certainly no reference to any of the Baywatch characters or actors.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If I wanted to create a video game similar to Ready Player One (no VR), how could I do so while giving full credit to the creator of assets that I would borrow from various gaming companies?
Answer: You’d never finish that project. Each individual sub-game would require substantial work to give it the feel of the original and proper game balance. You could do it as a text adventure game with about the level of abstraction of the books - Players have to figure out the key, or secret, to each game, and enter that as a text command. If you do it that way, you probably don’t require any permission. If you include full, playable retro games in your game, yes, you would need permission from the rights owner of each game. Most likely that will be a publisher or a holding company. Don’t attempt to make any of the game before getting permission in writing for each sub-game you plan to use. Odds are you won’t be able to get permission for most of them. For example, my wife and I designed the Quest for Glory series for Sierra On-Line, but we have had zero luck attempting to purchase a license from Activision-Blizzard (the current rights-holder) to make new games in the series. Someone who had no involvement with the original development will have even less of a chance.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why are the white businesses more successful than the black businesses?
Answer: A friend who worked as an adviser to startup businesses once told me that he could almost immediately spot which ones would fail, and which had a chance of becoming successful. The #1 factor was capitalization, or initial investment. The businesses that started out “on shoestrings” almost always failed. Ones that had substantial initial capital had a good chance of success. Given America’s history of “white privilege,” businesses with White founders usually start with higher investment than those with Black founders. I’m using the “privilege” term in a limited sense - If you were born White, you are more likely to have been sent to a top University by your parents, who in turn likely attended decent schools and made a good living, etc. There’s just more money in the pool, and more wealthy contacts, for a White business founder than for most Black ones. Under-capitalization leads to failure or minimal success. Substantial capitalization often also leads to more spectacular failure, but the chance of success is much higher than for the undercapitalized businesses.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How can I earn money with a game development company? If the games you make aren't successful, you just lose a lot of money.
Answer: Use the Mel Brooks approach from The Producers. Convince a lot of investors up front that you’re going to make an amazing game, then spend less than they invested. Voila - Profit! The game, and your investors, lose money, but some of it has been transferred to you. Of course, making a profit honorably and honestly is much harder. Make an excellent game that fills a niche in the market, and promote it heavily; then you might have a chance of making money. I might recommend books by Seth Godin on how to have a massive marketing impact with a small dollar investment. Of course, every dollar you don’t spend has to be “paid for” in work effort by yourself and your team; nothing is free. I’m personally rather lazy and poor at this. Others are more successful, but from what I can see, that isn’t many of them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I sequence roll a pair of fair dice. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers is 7 or 11?
Answer: On any given roll, there are 36 possible results. Let’s say you use one white die, and one red one, to make that more obvious. Two of those results give you 11: White 6 and Red 5, or White 5 and Red 6. Six of them give you 7: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1. Those are all exclusive, so you can add them together to get the total probability. It’s (2+6)/36, or 2/9. Over a long sequence of rolls, you can expect either a 7 or an 11 on about 2 out of every 9 rolls. On any given roll, it’s either a 7, an 11, or something else, but the probabilities are not equally weighted. You can only observe the probability by doing many rolls, and recording all of them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do most people get the 80/20 wrong in software development?
Answer: The Pareto Principle states that, for instance, 80% of your sales comes from 20% of your customers. It’s been extended into a general principle that, in just about any endeavor, there is a “most important” 20% that has more impact that the remaining 80%. So why do “most people get the 80/20 wrong”? It’s because the Principle is an after-the-fact observation, not a prediction. We can safely predict that there is always a most important 20% of work, customers, etc. But we can’t accurately predict which 20% are the important ones. If a software developer chose to decide in advance what is the most important 20% of their development project, and to mostly neglect the other 80%, the project would never be finished. Just because the “other 80%” is “less important” doesn’t mean that a software project can succeed without handling 100% of the task. Besides, they’d probably be wrong about which 20% was most important. Pareto does a great job of looking backward, and a terrible job of looking forward. Once everything is done, analysis can find the most important 20%. But nobody is good at guessing that in advance. It should also be noted that a “long tail” is an important part of corporate income. If you only focus on the 20% of customers that provide 80% of your income, you’re still losing out on 20% of your income. In most cases, that exceeds a company’s profit margin.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What is the biggest threat to the video game industry?
Answer: The biggest threat to the video game industry is market saturation. There are so many games released every year that few players even learn about most of them. The game industry keeps growing, but the sales-per-title keep going down. The released games range in quality and scope from magnificent to small, but fun, to worthless crap. But until you or I play one, we don’t know whether it’s a great game, or a terrible one. As a result, most of us buy games similar to ones we’ve enjoyed in the past, and often sequels of those games. That turns most of the “unknown gems” into market failures, because you and I don’t even know they exist.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Where would I get a consent form for my game? How should I choose a gaming company to create my game if I'm in a coding club at school and would like them to not take my game idea?
Answer: If you are using assets from a commercial game to make your game, then you are probably violating their copyrights. However, no game company will bother to stop a school project; it isn’t worth their time or money. Morally wrong, illegal, and nobody cares. :-) As for your game idea, no commercial game developer will steal, or have any interest in, it. The closest I’ve seen to that is the case of an artist who created a 3D model, then found a toy based on his model on sale at Disneyland. Even that is extremely rare. Most likely someone in another country made the toy and sold it to Disney without the company knowing that it violated an artist’s implicit copyright. If you want to make games professionally after graduation, keep doing what you’re doing! Every game, or part of a game, you make will teach you techniques and artistry that will help you make better games. Pretty much everyone in the industry has made some practice games before working on major ones.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do I have to get permission to use the police in my video game? This is a racing game with the police, it is still in development. I want to use coloring (black and white, black).
Answer: If you are using “police” as a generic, abstract term, no permission is needed. If you photograph actual police officers, and want to use their image in your game, you’ll need permission.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I am making a career transition to a filmmaker from a Product/Project Manager. Should I work as a (game) producer or a product manager (non-industry specific) in the meantime? Which profession has more skills in common with a film director?
Answer: Game development has much in common with filmmaking. Your experience will be helpful in a game producer position.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: There are countless examples of great things being initially rejected. For example, Star Trek and Seinfeld were rejected by multiple studios, likely by the most powerful and wealthy and execs there. What do such rejections tell us about such people?
Answer: William Goldman (screenwriter, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, The Princess Bride, and others) wrote some fascinating “behind the scenes” looks at Hollywood screenwriting and producing. One of his memorable quotes is, [In Hollywood], “Nobody knows anything. Not one person in the entire motion picture field knows for a certainty what's going to work. Every time out it's a guess and, if you're lucky, an educated one.” Turn down a script, and you save the studio money, and you don’t fail. Nobody will know if it would have been successful. Greenlight one, and the show bombs, and you’re out of a job. Few producers are fired for saying, “No.”

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why did the Canadian Government suddenly decide to mandate truckers be vaccinated to cross international borders, when it was perfectly fine letting them do their job for 2 years? Was this done to divide us?
Answer: I wasn’t in on the decision, but most likely it had to do with the Omicron variant, which is vastly more contagious than previous Covid-19 variants. Canadian truckers who regularly travel to the United States, where many more people are unvaccinated, are likely to transmit the virus back to Canada. The decision was made to protect Canadian citizens, not to divide anyone. Note that the web pages that organized the trucker blockades were hijacked to hide the identity of the people posting them. Vaccine misinformation and attacks on Western infrastructure appear to be largely driven by Russian propaganda organizations. They are not spontaneous protests by American or Canadian citizens.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why is diversifying your portfolio necessary if you can just put all of your money into one company?
Answer: When I was younger, my broker got a “hot tip” on a company merger, in particular that the CEO had invested heavily in the new company. The broker also invested in it. I had recently read something about the merger, but didn’t remember the details. It turned out that it was about employees of the acquired company being unhappy about the merger. That should have been my clue to steer well away from the merged company. Within 3 months, its stock was completely in the tank, and I lost most of my retirement portfolio. Don’t invest in a single company. Anything can happen to it. Companies go out of business constantly. By spreading out your investments, some of them will fail, but hopefully the overall success of the market will make up for the failures. I keep it simple these days - total stock market index funds or S&P 500 index funds. They have low costs because they don’t need to do any analysis, and the market as a whole always goes up over time. Don’t try to time the market. If you try to miss crashes and catch expansions, you’ll more likely just cost yourself money. Buy and hold. It might be a good idea to spread out your purchases over time, but I believe I read a study on that which suggested it doesn’t make much difference.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it hard to get a job as a PC/console game designer if you have 2+ years of experience of mobile hypercasual game design (+ some indie solo projects)?
Answer: Yes, it is hard to get a job as a PC/console game designer with 2+ years of somewhat relevant experience. It’s hard to get such a job with 10+ years of directly applicable experience. Game designers either work their way up within a company, are rock star level famous as well as having connections at the developer, or basically get there by luck. It’s almost impossible to plan to get a game design job, and get it, without a healthy dose of luck. Of course, some of that is of the “make your own luck” variety, being exceptionally prepared for a particular opportunity, but some is just real life RNG.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is store.steampowered.com a legit site game store for a PC? What is your review about the site?
Answer: Yes, Steam Store is the biggest legitimate distribution site for indie games as well as some games from major publishers. It’s the game distribution arm of Valve Software (known for Half-Life and other games), but is open to everyone. Pretty much all indie PC game developers publish on Steam. The other major indie distributor is . It’s the game distribution division of CD Projekt in Poland. GOG originally specialized in out-of-print older games, but now carries new titles as well. The third major PC games store is the Epic Store, but I don’t have any personal experience with them. When I contacted them about distributing my games, they didn’t respond.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How should I go about publicizing my video game to online magazines (Kotaku, IGN, any gaming magazine)? Should I email the authors?
Answer: I made a mailing list based on the published contact information for authors who review similar games to the ones I make. When I have something new, I send them a press release with an offer to supply a game key and/or interview. It’s a crapshoot. Sometimes you’ll get somewhere with that, and probably a few of the sites will publish the release as-is. But it’s rare to actually get an interview or full coverage from a release like that. Still, it’s the best way I know to get publicity without paid advertising. And the latter is usually ineffective for a small developer or publisher.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How will a game look if creators say that it'll be long but the budget on this time will be $17,000?
Answer: Most likely they haven’t gone through the arithmetic to make a proper budget. One possibility is that they’re making the game as a labor of love, and the $17K budget just pays for some incidental expenses, or for specific contract work. If that’s the case, they should say that explicitly. A game that takes a long time costs a lot in developer pay. The only way to get around that is to not pay the developers. That’s either stupid or exploitive depending on who isn’t getting paid. :-)

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Are there any game designers who are also authors for books? To clarify, I’m not talking about people who write the stories for games.
Answer: Sure. Many authors of narrative games also write novels and/or non-fiction books. Raymond Feist based his bestselling Midkemia “Riftwar” books on his tabletop RPG sessions, then later consulted on the Betrayal at Krondor computer game based on the books. Bruce Balfour wrote both games and books: Jane Jensen, who co-designed Ecoquest and wrote the popular Gabriel Knight games, is also an author. Christy Marx designed games, wrote screenplays (e.g. the Jem TV series), and contributed to graphic novels. With a modicum of research, you could find dozens or hundreds of others. Start with the credits in mobygames, then check Amazon or another bookstore for their books.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Should the law require all games and software to be equipped with anti-piracy methods and the developers who didn't do that be punished/imprisoned for "failing at duty to protect intellectual property or copyrights"?
Answer: No, that would be obscene. When I started developing games for Sierra On-Line, most games included some form of copy protection. My wife and I fought those for our games. We felt that pirates would easily break any protection, while players who actually paid for the games would be inconvenienced. As an example, I bought one of the Ultima games that included a mechanic of sailing your ship into a whirlpool to be transported to another land. They apparently had some sort of copy protection tied to that, but it didn’t work properly on my AT&T 6300 PC clone. Instead, the game crashed most of the time on going into a whirlpool. As the number of ships was limited, eventually the game became unplayable. An Atari ST copy protection technique relied on a peculiarity of the floppy drives. When Atari sourced drives from a different manufacturer, that “feature” went away, and a number of games and apps stopped working. Sierra let us make our games with no copy protection, and they became some of the company’s biggest sellers. I am not in favor of game piracy, but I accept that it’s inevitable. The key is to make games that are enticing and compelling enough to get legitimate players to pay for them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Game designers: Is it better to write the story/plot first or make the game as you go along? Honestly seeking advice.
Answer: “There are nine and sixty ways Of constructing tribal lays, and every single one of them is right!” - Rudyard Kipling, “In the Neolithic Age” I used to think I constructed software top-down - start with the requirements, and gradually build up the details until you had a finished product. But in practice, I work back and forth from the details to the overview and back. For Hero’s Quest (original title of the Quest for Glory series), we started with the idea that the game would use Sierra On-Line’s SCI engine. Previously that had only been used for graphical adventure games, so we knew that we’d have typed commands, the ability to walk through environments, etc. Starting with a constraint like that is good, even if you artificially design one to give yourself some context. Our mandate was to create a computer role-playing game “like Ultima,” so we decided we would try to emulate tabletop D&D games we’d played. Our favorites of those were story- and character-heavy games in which combat was a smaller part of the game. It made sense to use that approach, given that we were using a text-oriented engine. At that point, we thought about some character archetypes that would be fun to have in the game. That was a “mechanics” concept, but ironically, was almost entirely stripped out during development. My mentor, Bob Heitman, pointed out that quadrupedal characters would have a terrible time walking up and down stairs and getting through narrow obstacles. They would also require custom animation for changing direction. But there was no budget or time for all that, so bye-bye Centaur character. The game was to ship on floppy disks, and many players did not have hard drives, so multiple character models were at best problematic. Bye-bye choice of gender, elves, and gnomes. We shortly settled on keeping three character classes - fighter, magic user, and thief - but using the same generic male model for all of them. Meanwhile, we planned out the story, which would continue through four games. We wanted continuity, so we decided players could save their character at the end of each game, and load it to start the next game with a predetermined character name, stats, and some memory of accomplishments. That was a mix of story and game mechanics. We determined the setting for each game, and based on that, wrote the story. Noting “inflection points” in the story, we were able to determine puzzles or problems where the player could help it progress. Again, a back-and-forth between story and puzzles. We decided we wanted to have some traditional RPG combat, but that we would have problems with terrain. Our solution was to pop up a custom combat window with no terrain. We based the RPG mechanics on a tabletop gaming system we had written, and that turned out to work pretty well in a computer simulation. Once we had that, we went back to the story to determine places where we would have specific combats, and where random encounters could work without breaking the flow of the story. The rest basically came down to playtesting and luck - We wrote the story elements to the best of our ability, and tried to get the game mechanics to work smoothly and be balanced, then we put all that in the hands of testers. I say “luck” because we didn’t have the luxury of enough time to make any major changes, other than parts of the game we stripped out to keep it at a reasonable number of floppies. Well, sort of reasonable; I think we shipped on 8 disks, with the company’s previous games having taken 2 to 4 disks.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What should I do? I want to develop games, more precisely, engines and mechanics, but there is a fear that in the future game developers will be able to replace AI that will be able to generate code itself?
Answer: When I did the Lifespring personal effectiveness training, they referred to questions such as yours as “considerations.” These are stories we tell ourselves because it’s less scary to give up before you start than to try something challenging and risk failure. Will you avoid getting a job as a waiter because robots might take over all the waiter jobs in the future? Refuse a job driving a delivery truck because Amazon is working on driverless vehicles to deliver packages? AI can already generate code, but it’s just helper code for human developers. AI doesn’t have the creativity, understanding, and communications skills necessary to do the very challenging work of game development. Thirty, forty, fifty years ago, game developers’ jobs were already insecure. It wasn’t because of genius-level AI, but because game companies constantly merged or went bankrupt. Five years was considered a long tenure for a game developer. There is no certainty in this world or the next. If you’re serious about developing games, do it! Your job might go away in 3 months or 3 years, but you’ll learn more from every project on which you work. As Nike likes to say, “Just do it!” If you don’t, you’ll never know if you could have succeeded.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What do software engineers consider as a failure when they are asked in an interview if they have failed at something?
Answer: A lot of people answer that question with a self-serving answer that doesn’t really show a failure at all. But everyone fails. Those who become successful learn from their failures and strive to do better the next time. I had a task that failed because I tried to push it through to QA too quickly; I should have tested it more first, even if it meant delaying the product schedule. I’ve had several projects cancelled, or stopped them when they were incomplete. I could easily talk about those, to what degree I was responsible, and how I would try to prevent cancellation of a future project. I haven’t applied to a new job for a while, but if I did, I would consider this a test of the interviewer as much as of me. If he or she reacts poorly to an honest example of a failure, then I probably don’t want to work there. Good managers know that failure is an inevitable part of the process, and learning from failure is essential to doing a good job.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do most indie games fail because they are based on bad ideas or because they lack the money to invest in marketing and graphics?
Answer: Indie game companies are almost always undercapitalized. Lack of capital is the #1 reason that any business fails. The game industry is hit-driven. A few hit games monopolize most of the sales. Players who like Call of Duty, World of Warcraft, NBA2K, or any other series almost automatically buy each sequel. That gives them reliable sales to support future game development. In contrast, an indie game is almost invisible to players, and is competing against 10,000 or more other indie games for player dollars. Unless one becomes a viral success, or the developer spends tens of thousands to millions of dollars - that they rarely have - on advertising and marketing, most potential players will never learn it exists. Along those lines, I guess I should take the opportunity to mention my own money-losing, but highly rated, indie game: I’m hoping we’ll find more of an audience with future games in the series, but it’s also quite likely that players who would love our games will never learn about them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do software engineering companies request for a LinkedIn profile when the candidate has already uploaded their resume?
Answer: Having a candidate’s LinkedIn profile shows connections between the candidate and people already at the company. That allows the hiring manager to reach out to those connections for verification of the candidate’s skills. Resumes / CV’s prove nothing. It is trivial to copy someone else’s resume, or simply make one up. Verifying that the candidate has a LinkedIn profile that matches the resume, and connections who will verify their work history, makes a much safer hire. Once you go through the steps of actually hiring someone, you not only have a harder time firing them for falsifying the application, but you have also upset, and probably lost, other qualified candidates.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Will most Alliance players, especially the night elf fans, ever forgive Sylvanas Windrunner and the Horde for the Burning of Teldrassil, now or in the future?
Answer: It is players of the Horde who may never forgive Blizzard for turning Sylvanas from an interesting, tormented character into a one note, “pure evil, do not touch” caricature of a character. Many long-time Horde players have left the game as a result. Both Horde and Alliance get to “defeat” Sylvanas at the end of the Sanctum of Domination raid. It’s a tremendously hard fight on Heroic and Mythic levels, but not nearly as one-sided as Sylvanas vs. Bolvar in the teaser cinematic before the Shadowlands expansion. Rumor has it that disgraced design director, Alex Afrasiabi, is responsible for the change in direction of Sylvanas’s story, against the wishes of other long-time World of Warcraft lore designers. As a game designer myself, I consider it poor storytelling to make a critical lore character so one-sided. Villains need complexity to be interesting.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is GOG.com a legit site game store for a PC?
Answer: Absolutely! GOG is a great site, and totally legitimate. The name originally stood for Great Old Games. They specialized in distributing updated versions of older games, modified to work on modern PC’s. Today they distribute both old and new games. GOG is the distribution arm of the Polish company, CD Projekt Red, also known for The Witcher series. When I met with one of their representatives about ten years ago, he told me that my Quest for Glory Collection was among their top sellers. My wife and I designed and directed development of those games for Sierra On-Line from 1989 to 1998. Activision, which owns the former Sierra On-Line games, receives royalties from the games on GOG. That’s about as “legit” as you can get. (No, I didn’t, and do not, receive royalties on those games, as our Sierra deal expired shortly before the games appeared on GOG.) When Lori and I created a new game, Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption, GOG told us they would love to distribute it on their site. Since releasing the game in 2018, our two major distributors have been GOG and Steam. GOG has been super helpful in helping us promote the game to find new players. They are great at communicating (and paying) on sales, royalties, and marketing events. I rate them as “totally legit.”

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it possible to become a billionaire in a year as a 3D modeler? If so, how?
Answer: No. Unless perhaps you’re talking Rials (Iran) or Dongs (Vietnam). But earned in the U.S. or U.K. One billion of either of those currencies would be about $40,000 to $50,000 U.S. That’s a realistic annual income for a 3D modeler. Some might make more. That’s ok, a few billion a year is still a billionaire.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: When did WASD replace the arrow keys for most video games?
Answer: WASD was used for game movement very early on. Most early keyboards were essentially typewriter keyboards. They didn’t have arrow keys. A second reason to use WASD for movement is that all of those keys are under the left hand. That leaves the right hand free to use the mouse or joystick, or to hit keys on the right side of the keyboard for other game commands.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Will processor architects make a video game about CPU/gpu vendors where players can make rough designs of their own processors and benchmark against other players while some players stay in software development and write the bench for credits?
Answer: Probably not, but I like the idea. A classic early video game was “Chip’s Challenge.” I haven’t played it, but my understanding is that players had to do a form of programming to win. A chip design game - if not too realistic - could be interesting. You just have to Find the Fun when designing it.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have a video game idea, how do I get started?
Answer: My standard answer would be that an idea isn’t worth much, but let’s skip that part this time. The trick to making a game is to break down the big problem into many small parts, then work your way through them systematically. It’s a bit like writing a novel, except that a game has additional facets such as interaction, graphics, sound, etc. Start with your idea. Decide what would be a good genre for it. Does it fit - and do you want to make - into a first person shooter, an adventure game, a role-playing game, a puzzle game? Where will you set the game? Who are some key characters who will be in it? What is the player’s viewpoint character? Your first plans should be “on paper” or in a combination of text files and spreadsheets. If you can, make a physical version of the game “board” and “pieces” so that you can experiment with them, and fine tune them, on a tabletop. If this is starting to sound like more work than you want to do, then you aren’t ready to turn your idea into a game. Most games take anywhere from a few months to multiple years, with a team of developers working full-time. They can cost millions of dollars to develop, although it’s possible to make a small game in some genres cheaply on your own. For example, a text adventure or “interactive fiction” story can use free tools, and just requires you to become a skilled writer, and for you to understand the conventions of those games. It will still take you a long time and a lot of stress if you want to make a good one. If you plan to have multiplayer, or extensive sound and graphics, that’s when you get up to the millions or tens of millions of dollars, big teams, and multiple years. Suggestion - Don’t do that. :-)

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why does HR play games with people when hiring for a position? HR will string someone along then get bent out of shape when the the people they are stringing along find a position. Why?
Answer: You are but one tiny minnow in an ocean filled with fish. The HR department is juggling your qualifications and availability with the hundreds or thousands of other applicants who might be suitable. If they identify eight suitable candidates, but only have one or two openings, they’ll string all of you along. They hope to get one of their strongest candidates to accept a position, then follow through. In the meantime, they string everyone else along because their first choices might decide not to take the job, or will turn out not to work out. At that point, they’ll contact a backup candidate. My father did something similar with real estate investing. He would make a dozen or more ridiculous lowball offers while looking to buy one place. Odds were that one of the sellers would be desperate enough to accept his offer, then he’d dump the rest. Or maybe close two or three deals that were profitable enough to be worth financing.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How would game publishers accept your game idea (pitch, gdd)? What are the requirements?
Answer: Game publishers will accept your game idea if it is properly presented in the form of an advanced prototype with a complete “vertical slice.” That’s a small section of the game so professionally completed that players think they’re playing a finished AAA game. I’m told that such a prototype with enough detail to impress a publisher costs about $10 million on average to create. If you haven’t already put in months of work, and millions of dollars, you won’t even get in the door of a publisher. They’ll also expect you to have a professionally-managed development house with multiple completed games in your portfolio. How do publishers find developers under such seemingly impossible conditions? Mostly they work only with ones they’ve used before. If you want to break into the game industry as a new developer, either get a job for an established studio, or make multiple low budget games on your own. Nobody wants to take a chance on an untested beginner.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can adding 'freelance writer on Quora' on your resumé increase your chances of being hired as a writer or journalist?
Answer: Any competent hiring manager who is hiring a writer will ask for samples of your work. If you’ve written amazingly detailed and powerful essays as Quora answers, by all means supply them as samples. Nobody cares what you say you’ve done. They only care about demonstrated ability and accomplishments that you actually have done.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why has it taken until the end of 2021 for developers to realize that they should take risks with games, even though a few years back nobody was willing to risk a game failing?
Answer: There have always been game developers willing to take risks with games. They go by various names - unknown, bankrupt, etc. Every once in a while, one of their experimental games becomes a sleeper hit. Then others with deeper pockets step in and make similar games. The large corporations rarely take risks. Why should they, when they already have winning products, and gamers show little interest in trying new things?

Name: Corey Cole
Question: When did pointless busywork become such an acceptable part of gaming?
Answer: From the dawn of time. My favorite time-waster used to be Klondike Solitaire. I would spend hours shuffling cards, laying them out, and trying to clear the deck. Such pointless busywork! But relaxing in one way, and exercising my mind in another. What is Chess (or Go, or Tic-Tac-Toe), but moving the same pieces by the same simple rules on the same limited board over and over? What is Tetris, but “pointlessly” busying yourself by trying to get the pieces to fall into the right places with the orientation you want? Early graphic adventure games had large areas of open space and relatively few that contained puzzles. Even those puzzles were the same every time you played - talk about pointless. Shall we go on to your day job? Odds are it’s mostly pointless busywork. Very few of us do anything really creative and meaningful at our work. Game developers are sometimes an exception, but a lot of it is still pretty rote. When I talk to my wife about giving up World of Warcraft, a game full of mindless busywork, she asks, “Why? You’ll just find something else equally pointless to spend your time.”

Name: Corey Cole
Question: When has the video game industry begun to include the use of mouse and graphic tables in game graphical and art production, in North America, Europe, or East Asia?
Answer: Do you mean graphical tablets for creating game assets? Artists used them in the late 1980’s in the U.S. when I entered the game industry, and probably for several years before that. They could have been in use as early as 1979, when rock musician and audio electronics pioneer Todd Rundgren invented a tablet for use with the Apple II computer. Ken Williams reputedly used one of those early tablets to let Roberta Williams and team artists draw graphics for Sierra games around 1980. The vector output from the tablet used very little memory, so was much more efficient than storing images as pixels on machines that only had 48K memory or less.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What do you think of Microsoft buying the video game maker Activision Blizzard, maker of "Candy Crush" for 68 billion?
Answer: I can’t speak to the valuation, but if the deal goes through, Microsoft will own a huge collection of popular games, both current and out-of-print: Presumably the main reasons for the purchase are those first three massively successful “jewels in the crown.” Microsoft can create sequels that are exclusively for the XBox, and will sell a lot of both games and consoles. But they’ve mentioned that they might want to revive some of the popular older games. Unfortunately, I doubt they’ll bring back the original authors, but there’s still a lot of potential life in those series. In a dream world, I can imagine them going on to acquire Mark Crowe and Scott Murphy’s Space Venture, to rebrand it as a new Space Quest. Then they can pick up my Hero-U series, and rebrand it as new Quest for Glory content. If only! :-)

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Wouldn't a fourth Arizona 2020 election audit urged by Dr Kelli Ward, be truly substantive if all audit staff properly interviewed voters for which signatures seemed unclear, missing or duplicated? Surely anything less is incompetent, wasting money?
Answer: We have audits for close elections. They’re done by professionals in non-partisan offices. The idea of a partisan group doing an “audit” is contrary to every principle of free and open elections. Maybe if they paid their way - Deposit $1 for each vote in the election, receive back $100 for every fraudulent vote they find, as long as it is then confirmed by the secretary of election’s office. We could fund a government department with the proceeds! None of these audits has found any serious problems. They’re fundraisers for the losing candidate and the company doing the audit. They raise publicity, which is then quietly abandoned each time the audit finds that the original vote-counting was done professionally and correctly. They aren’t good for democracy.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have a complete roadmap for a game idea and whole prototype but how can I want any company to make a partnership with me? How can I make this possible?
Answer: Assuming your “whole prototype” is fun and compelling, you need to market it to game publishers. Be prepared for a lot of rejection, because publishers see far more prototypes (as in hundreds or thousands of times more) than they can possibly publish. It comes down to marketing. You need to make a short video that shows off your prototype so that potential customers (publishers) can see at a glance what makes your game beautiful, exciting, and unique. That might mean you will need to spend money up front to improve the art and sound of your prototype, and to get a professional video made. One of the most successful prototype proposals in recent years is Star Citizen, by Chris Roberts. First he lined up some well-heeled investors. He created a well-featured prototype to the point that people who don’t know much about games might think he had almost finished the game. Then he had a polished, professional video made about him and the prototype - When I saw it on Kickstarter, I estimated that he had spent at least a million dollars creating the prototype and the video. Compare that with the rest of us indie developers, many of whom are trying to raise a few thousand dollars on Kickstarter. Roberts started with far more than that just to create a compelling funding campaign. Most of us can’t recreate the magic that has been the Star Citizen funding and development journey, but everyone who wants to get a game made has to do some similar things. You can’t just reach out to a publisher or developer and say, “I’ve got a great idea for a game.” You’ll be laughed out of the building, or most likely won’t even see the inside of it. It takes massive work, time, and likely some expense to make a compelling proposal to a potential publisher, investors (including individual crowdfunding investors), or other developers.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Does a game engine (like Unity) really make a complete game, or am I missing something?
Answer: Think of a game engine - such as Unity - as the computer equivalent of a toolbox filled with tools. It’s just part of what you need to make a game. Does a carpenter’s toolbox make a house? Not by itself. The tools are one of the three things needed to build the house: Unity provides most of the tools you need to build a game. But it still takes a very talented individual, or a team of people covering a range of talents, to make the game. A game also needs raw materials. The Unity Asset Store provides some possible materials, and you can actually make a game with mostly those assets - in fact, an infinite variety of games. In addition, some of your team members probably specialize in creating assets such as images and sounds. They’re made up of building blocks such as musical notes, color palettes, and so on, but they’re more specific to the look and feel the final game will have. Programmers and writers create assets too. They start with building blocks such as a programming language or words. Then they build layers of higher complexity that eventually end up as a game executable, text, and dialogue. The running joke in Terry Pratchett’s Discworld - and in cosmology - is that the world sits on the backs of four elephants, who in turn stand on the shell of a huge turtle. But what does the turtle stand on? Another turtle. In fact, it’s “turtles all the way down.” Why don’t we see the elephants and the turtles? Perhaps they’re invisible. But most likely, we don’t see them because the world is in the way. The process of making a game often doesn’t look at all like a game. It’s built up in layers of code, words, pictures, sounds, etc. Unity and other game engines are one (or several) of the turtles that hold up the rest. In a sense, a word processor and a spreadsheet app are other turtles - It’s pretty common to write a piece of an engine that pulls data from a spreadsheet, and uses that data to drive some of the game behavior. A modern game has a high degree of complexity. We create that complexity by building it in layers, a little at a time. A major game - think World of Warcraft, Call of Duty, or Star Citizen - has thousands of specialized developers, each building small pieces of the game. For another analogy, think of crafting a jetliner. Boeing and Airbus have thousands of engineers, mechanics, and other specialists. They work with other companies that provide specialized parts. In fact, I don’t personally know how the plates of an airplane fuselage are built - whether the airplane manufacturer orders sheets of aluminum, and cuts and forms them into shaped plates; or if a specialist supplier crafts the plates. The same is true of building a computer game. When you buy an asset from the Unity Asset Store, you’re getting pre-formed “plates” from which to build your game. Your team artist might modify them into the specific assets you need, or might start with a paint tool and a 3D modeling tool to make them “from scratch.” I put that in quotes because it’s “turtles all the way down” - Even the most basic shapes in an art program are pre-supplied - stamps, brushes, curves, boxes, etc. The artist builds new layers on top of the supplied layers to make something more useful to the game. The game engine allows an artist or other developer to display those assets in various ways. It allows scaling, rotation, animation by multiple images or by morphing, and much more. Turtles and tools let people build things. More complicated games take more steps, more layers, and more time to make.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Would taxing unrealized gains destroy the economy since everyone would just pull their money out of the stock market?
Answer: No, it wouldn’t have anything like that effect. Personally, I love paying taxes! It means my businesses are profitable. Would you rather have an 8% annual return in the stock market, then pay 50% of that appreciation in taxes… Or earn 1% in a money market fund, and pay 50% of that in taxes? In the first case, you have a 4% annual return. In the latter it’s 0.5%. When you take your investments out of the stock market, you have to put them somewhere else. It could be in real estate, or in direct corporate investment, but you’re always going to look for the highest return. If taxes reduce that return, you *still* want the highest, because your after-tax income will be higher that way.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Can a video game (business) founder be the story writer at the same time?
Answer: Sure. It’s just a question of how many ways you want to split your time and energy. I founded a development studio to make Shannara for Legend Entertainment. I found that I *could* help write and design the game, but that my attention was constantly needed to answer phones, do bookkeeping and budgets for our producer at Legend, do some of the programming, and so on. I got all of those things done, but the quality of each suffered. When I started Transolar Games to develop Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption, I resolved not to make the same mistake. As a result, my wife did most of the writing, contractors did all of the programming, and I did administrative stuff. We again got it done, but I think parts of the game suffered from having me stay away from them. If you’re a small indie developer, you pretty much have to wear multiple hats. You won’t be able to afford hiring specialists for every department, and you won’t want to give up control of the finances to a stranger. You can still write under those circumstances, but it will be hard.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What are the downsides if the tax loopholes were fixed and every billionaire and corporation paid what they owe?
Answer: Each of those “loopholes” is designed to protect a group of people for whom the base tax law is inappropriate. If you “fix” all of them, there would be more tax revenues, but some people would be massively unfairly taxed. Besides, it’s pretty much impossible. It’s like asking, “What if we had a perfect representative democracy, and everyone cast informed votes that both support their personal interest and those of the nation?” The best we can do is compromise.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I got a message on Reddit. It was a request to help beta test a game. Should I accept?
Answer: Whether to become a beta tester depends largely on your personal situation - Do you have free time? Do you enjoy seeing the inner workings of things before they’re fully polished? Do you have good tolerance for frustration? Testing a game isn’t like test-driving a car. It’s more like, “Well, we haven’t added a chassis yet, and we’re not sure if the brakes work, but give it a try.” But if you have a problem-solving personality, and like to help others, beta testing can be very fun and fulfilling. You’ll get to contribute to the final quality of the game. So on balance, I’d say, “Yes,” but don’t expect a beta test to play like a finished, polished game.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: As a software engineer, what do you double check the most at work?
Answer: Good software engineers focus on testing “edge conditions.” If a function seems to work properly for a normal range of input, how about unexpected inputs? Zero, negative numbers, huge numbers, tiny fractions, etc. In a job interview, I was given a set of inputs that were very small numbers. I saw the potential for “underflow,” losing significance because the numbers were so small. The interviewer wanted to make sure my solution could handle “overflow” when the numbers got far larger than expected. Personally, I spend a lot of time crosschecking the temporary code I write for testing my other code. Such routines tend to be written quickly, and that makes them very susceptible to error. Test code needs the most testing! At one of my first jobs, I tried to debug a problem by adding “snapshot” commands - roughly equivalent to a print statement - throughout the code. The behavior kept changing as I moved the snapshots around. Eventually I discovered that an errant piece of code was rewriting memory in the code, so adding a line either made the bug harmless, or made it worse.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Does it make sense to take up an EMBA if you're already a millionaire or billionaire?
Answer: The two are unrelated. If you’re working as an executive, and think you could benefit from more training, an EMBA course is one option. I don’t think executives think much in terms of whether a particular degree will help them get an even more lucrative job. They’ve already figured out a way to succeed in business. Being a millionaire or billionaire is a completely separate thing. It just shows that you either came from a wealthy family, or have had major monetary success. Degree programs probably won’t have much effect on your status.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Does the phrase "Let's go Brandon" offend you? Why?
Answer: No, the expression doesn’t offend me in the least. To me, it just shows the childishness of supposed adults who sniggeringly try to insult someone by not quite saying what they mean, “F*** you, Biden.” What difference would it make if they said it directly? It would still say they’re childish and immature. Screaming out an insult (or for that matter, saying one calmly) is no substitute for actual discussion of policies and results. The phrase I’d like to see is, “Let it go, Donald!” Our previous President is fixated on the idea that he couldn’t possibly have been voted out of office without fraud. The problem is that it’s been investigated over and over, and there hasn’t been any significant fraud, let alone the hundreds of thousands of fraudulent votes it would have taken to alter the election. Let it go, Donald. The 2020 election is over. You lost. You’re just showing yourself as a childish sore loser by insisting that somehow you magically won. In 2016, most pundits thought that Hillary Clinton was a shoo-in to become President, but elections are chaotic. She lost, people were shocked, but that didn’t somehow magically mean that the election was fraudulent. In 1948, many newspapers and pundits were sure that Thomas Dewey would be the next President. The Chicago Daily Tribune even announced his victory over Harry Truman. The thing is, they were mistaken, and Truman became President. Nobody can be 100% sure in advance what will happen in an election. But once it’s done, it’s time to let it go and move on.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: My sister-in-law is elderly with early signs of dementia. What does she do to hire her daughter as her live-in caretaker? Issues such as social security and federal tax payments for her daughter are major concerns? Where does she start?
Answer: I’m answering mostly as a response to Jennifer Castro’s answer, which does not allow comments. While your sister-in-law is still capable, have her sign a contract hiring her daughter. Make sure that other family members, such as yourself, are on board and approve the deal - You don’t want any taint of fraud or elder abuse to come up later. From there on, her daughter just has the normal tax requirements. The United States has a patchwork quilt of programs for family and hired caregivers, memory care, and so on. There is information available, but it’s scattered and often hard to find. In addition, every individual has different needs. Some need full-time nursing home care, some can get by with less care in an assisted living facility, and many prefer to stay at home as long as possible. Five or ten years ago, I got an urgent call from a V.A. psychologist to say that my mother needed 24-hour care. Since we don’t have real social insurance in the U.S., it would have cost $5,000 to $10,000 or more monthly for her to have 24-hour professional nursing care. The thing is, I was visiting my Mom at the time, and she clearly didn’t need that! We had caregivers who visited a few times a week to make sure she had healthy food, wasn’t suffering fall injury, etc. But she was also active and alert, participating in chair volleyball, playing a mean game of table tennis, etc. The psychologist saw one aspect of Mom’s behavior in a “mindfulness” class. It hadn’t been explained properly to Mom, who thought it was effectively an Eastern philosophy based “mindfulness meditation” class. What the instructor saw was not typical of Mom’s daily functionality. The instructor didn’t know that Mom was an avid reader, Mensa member, and far from “out of it.” But she did have an early stage of dementia. That situation changed in January 2020. Mom came down with a respiratory illness that might (or might not) have been Covid-19 before anyone knew how to test for it. She spent a few days in the hospital, then a month in a nursing home. When she came out, her mental had gone from an occasional quirk to full-blown dementia. My wife and I moved in with Mom for a month, then my brother for what was supposed to be another month, which turned into three. Lori and I came back, and we’ve been there ever since - close to two years now. For the first six months of that, Mom was close to a Zombie; then she regained some, but not all, of her mental faculties. She’s had many ups and downs since then. Dementia has wide variety. Mom can’t take care of herself anymore, but she is quite aware of her environment. She’s happy at home, and doesn’t want to move into a nursing home. My wife and I can take care of her relatively easily, although doing so prevents us from doing many things such as going out on a day trip together. Should Mom go into a nursing home at vast expense when she’s happy at home, and capable of staying here with minimal care? We don’t think so. The time will come when she needs to move to a home - or passes away - but early-stage dementia, or even fairly advanced dementia as she has now, does not mean that time has come. Everyone has different needs, and many do fine at home with family or occasional care.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Who invented video games, African Americans or the Chinese?
Answer: “Who invented video games, African Americans or the Chinese?” This is an odd question. My answer is that no single individual or group “invented video games.” The field is the combination of work by tens of thousands - possibly even millions - of individual contributors. I recall reading of a Black American engineer who contributed to the early hardware development that became an important part of video game technology. But it would be incorrect to say that one person “invented video games.” He was just one of many contributors over decades. As for the Chinese, I don’t recall them having any significant part in the early phases of video game development. Of course, Chinese games are very important parts of the market today, and many Chinese engineers and developers have contributed to the industry.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Do others think Zynga Poker is rigged? I’ve played over 50,000 hands and more than this in live poker and I am beginning to feel it is rigged to push you to purchase chips. I spoke to someone who worked for Zynga who said this is as true… thoughts?
Answer: I developed online poker software in the early 2000’s. My experience is that *every* online poker site - and probably many live games - was accused of being rigged. My boss had an answer to that: “We rely on customers trusting our software to be fair. If we lose that trust, we lose customers and money.” I’m pretty sure that every site has that same philosophy. However, players are another matter. In free and low-cost games, most players are notoriously loose. They will stay in on hopeless hands, and frequently make huge raises without justification. . You can beat those players by playing a tight game, only raising or calling when you have a great hand, but that takes enormous patience. In any case, wild betting creates huge variance. If you never call, you’ll lose out on potentially huge pots. If you call too often, sometimes your opponent will have the nuts, and you’ll lose huge amounts on those hands. That leads to you needing to buy more chips. So it isn’t the site; it’s the players. Incidentally, if you’re one of those loose and wild players, it’s your own craziness that is creating additional variance, and you’re likely to be on the losing side more often than not.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: As a software engineering interviewer conducting system design interview would you ask the candidate a generic system design problem such as designing Dropbox, URL shortener etc or would you ask to explain the design for something in their resume?
Answer: Both are valid approaches. The “How would you…” question is designed to get candidates to show their creativity and thought processes. “How did you…” is more of a reality check on whether they really did the work they claim, and how they plan projects. There are some problems with the first question, even though it’s one I might ask. When I interviewed for a position at a major international corporation, the manager told me they had recently added a feature to their operating system. How would I go about designing something like that? I did a whiteboard brainstorming and mini-lecture on it, and ended up getting the job. My first task was to build that system, which they actually hadn’t done yet. That could be considered dishonest, although to me it was just a wonderful challenge. For another corporation whose work most of us use every day, I was asked a game design question based on the previous project the interviewing manager had done. The problem with that is that he had preconceptions about the “right” way to do that task. To the extent my answer didn’t match what he had done, he was likely to have a problem with my solution. I didn’t get that job, mostly because I was so flustered by the question, I did a poor job answering it. You want to provide a warm, welcoming, but also challenging environment for candidates. Remember that they are interviewing you and your company as much as you are interviewing them. Relax expectations, and instead try to get to the essence of how the candidate thinks and answers your technical questions. It can also be a good idea to let the candidate do some of the work offline, where they have a chance to think about it more. Then have an in-person interview in which you discuss how they went about it, and what other options they considered. People with more introverted personalities can perform clearly when pressured at a live interview, but might still make wonderful candidates if given the chance to respond in more comfortable ways.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What do you think of Oregon dad, Jared Schmeck, who told Joe Biden “Let’s go Brandon” during a Christmas Eve livestreamed call, is now complaining that he’s “being attacked for utilizing my freedom of speech”?
Answer: I’d like to coin a new phrase. I’ll generously donate it to the public domain in hopes others will help spread it. The phrase is, “Let it go, Donald!” That should be the answer to anyone who smirkingly says, “Let’s go, Brandon!” Those people apparently never grew up. Those of us who have can respond with a more meaningful meme, one that reminds the former President to accept reality.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do most open world games (not all) underrepresent the true density of pedestrians and vehicles within the real world version of the player map? (eg. Grand Theft Auto: IV set in New York City, having few characters and/or vehicles)?
Answer: It’s pretty simple - Every added character, vehicle, or other potentially moving object in a game adds to its cost in at least four ways: In a game, the player is the star. My wife and I hosted a game design workshop once with everyone brainstorming ideas for the ideal adventure game. An attendee said, “Those ideas are ridiculous! They couldn’t happen in real life!” Another person stood up, looked at the first one, and asked, “Who would want to play a game based on your life?” Everyone laughed. So my question is, “Who wants to play a game in which they spend most of their time stuck in New York City rush-hour traffic?” I’ve done that; it isn’t compelling game play. :-) Realistic crowds and traffic patterns in a big city would interrupt game flow.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Am I causing any harm to game developers if I pirated most of their games?
Answer: Basically, you’re helping to drive developers out of business. The game industry is intensely competitive, with very small margins for most games. When too many copies are pirated, and too few paid, companies die. Many formerly big game companies have merged or closed shop because costs keep going up faster than sales. I started developing games for Sierra On-Line in 1988. A game that cost $250K to develop in 1989 took more than $3 million to make by 1998. Sales maybe doubled during that period, not even close to paying for the increased costs. Sierra stopped in-house development in 1999. Dozens of other game developers also closed in that ten year period. For the last ten years, I’ve been an indie game developer. When Steam strictly curated its titles ten years ago, an indie could expect to sell 50K-100K units. Today, with many more titles on the shop, Valve makes even more money, but the developers are squeezed to death. The average indie game on Steam today sells 2K-5K units. That’s enough to pay for 3 months of development by one or two people. My last game averaged 12 developers over 5 years. You do the math; it isn’t pretty!

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do so many people end up believing like religious devotees in media nonsense that flies in the face of any sort of reality?
Answer: Possibly they’re preconditioned to believe in nonsensical things by their religious upbringing? There isn’t too much difference between accepting the Bible as God-given facts, vs. believing that everything Fox News, QAnon, OANN, or Trump says is “gospel” truth. Once you’ve swallowed a few lies, the rest seem equally digestible.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do religious people and atheists argue so much?
Answer: Hmm, I’ve not seen much argument between religious and non-religious people. Generally each is secure in their own space. There might be an occasional statement such as, “You need to believe in [my favorite of the tens of thousands of religions]!” or, “Believing in a god is nonsense; there’s no evidence to support it.” The other party then disagrees, and that’s about as much of an argument as you get. I do have religious friends occasionally send me long posts about miracles, prophecies, or other things they think I should know. I either don’t respond, or give a short response which could range from, “Ok, thanks for letting me know,” to, “That doesn’t seem right to me.” The latter usually results in a few more pages of proselytizing, so I don’t use it often. What doesn’t happen often is that anyone convinces anyone else to change positions. I broke free from a few quasi-religious positions over the years, but that wasn’t because of any argument. Most religious people believe in the religion they had as children. I had an atheist father - raised Jewish - who later converted to Buddhism… Maybe, since he was an intellectual who might have been serious, or might have thought of it as a game. My mother was brought up Christian, and rededicated herself by “coming forward” at a Billy Graham Crusade. Later in life she took up various Eastern spiritualist beliefs. So I guess I could have gone any way. As my profile states, I became a fundamentalist Christian as a young teenager, spent many hours reading the Bible (mostly New Testament), and was baptized. Later I became exposed to other systems of belief including Ayn Rand “Objectivism,” Temple of Set, and modern Paganism. ToS is hard to describe - some Aleister Crowley / Anton LaVey “practical magic,” Egyptian mysticism, and using psychological techniques to manipulate others. Anyway, I eventually repudiated all of them, and realized that there were several thousand (or tens of thousands) of other religious systems I hadn’t experienced. The simple solution was to decide that every religious belief is a mixture of self-delusion and manipulation. Trying to convince others to follow your particular cult fits in the latter category. I neither practice, nor am susceptible to, that sort of manipulation.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If video poker machines are not rigged, why don’t they make the code open source?
Answer: Suppose you spent five years designing, refining, and testing algorithms for a video poker machine, and finally have a rock-solid engine that handles multiple poker variations. Would you like to profit from that? Or would you prefer to give away your code to dozens of small developers that haven’t yet done that work, or that can improve their profits using your algorithms? There’s also a potential security issue. If there is any vulnerability in your code, letting hackers examine it in detail will make it easier for them to find it. I haven’t worked in the gaming machine space, but I have designed code for online and single-player games for decades. Developers always build in code to enable testing every feature of the game. This code is often done more quickly, and less rigorously, than the actual game code. That means it’s more vulnerable to attack if revealed.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why is there an Alpha and Beta stage of game development but no Gamma or Delta stage?
Answer: At Sierra (major adventure game developer in the 1990’s, now part of Activision Blizzard), we used to joke that players who bought our games were our “Gamma testers.” (Not Charlie, that’s from a different alphabet.) No matter how much Alpha and Beta testing we did, there were always bugs in the released version, sometimes hundreds of them. Based on player feedback, we sometimes had the opportunity to fix some of the worst offenders and release an after-launch patch. So in a sense, we did have Alpha, Beta, and Gamma testing. But it would make players wonder why they paid to play the games if we publicly called them Gamma testers.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I have a master’s degree in mathematics and want to apply for design roles. Do I now need to get a degree from design school or any online certification would do? Which one can help me get a better job?
Answer: A degree in mathematics is almost completely orthogonal to game design. It’s fairly relevant to software engineering, so you might want to start there. I got a B.A. in Math., but took quite a few software development courses in my college years, including programming in various languages, operating system design, compiler design, etc. That qualified me for a Summer internship as a programmer. After graduation, I became a full-time programmer. Later I started my own business developing software for the new-at-the-time Atari ST. That led to a job at a game company, porting their games to the Atari. After a year of that, I moved to the game development side, and eventually got a chance to design some games. That might not be a typical path - every developer’s story is different - but it’s illustrative of the very indirect way you can turn a mathematics degree into a game design career. With your Master’s, you’ve probably learned enough about linear algebra and vector calculus to work on a 3D engine, or at least to use one well. That’s probably your best path to a game development, and later game design, career. Note that a typical AAA game has a few leads including a single lead designer, maybe 5 or 10 designers (level and technical), and a hundred or more programmers. You have a much better chance of breaking in as one of those programmers than going directly into design. Those design roles are mostly occupied by artists and writers, not mathematicians.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How can you find out a game's parameter when doing a clean decompilation?
Answer: You’re probably breaking the terms of the EULA when you do that. Don’t do it.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Who gets to eat the two chicken/turkey legs in a family of three?
Answer: The two who don’t prefer breast meat. As a kid through most of my adult life, I found the dark meat on turkey legs gamy and unpleasant. I was perfectly happy to eat only white meat with plenty of cranberry sauce. My sister preferred the legs, and I think my brother was ecumenical. Today I’ll eat either - and admit that the leg meat is more moist - but I don’t worry about which parts I get.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How often do independent game developers cannot run a traditional marketing campaign due to a lack of funds and resources?
Answer: Pretty much always. When most people think of a “traditional marketing campaign,” you’re thinking of huge releases such as Call of Duty. I’ve driven through Los Angeles and seen billboards for major games. You’re thinking of magazine and television advertising. This kind of marketing and advertising isn’t even practical for mid-range games, let alone indies. The rule of thumb for companies such as Sony and Activision is to spend roughly as much on the publicity campaign as you spent developing the game. That can amount to $50 million or more for a AAA game. Indie games are mostly made on budgets well under $100,000, and often under $10,000. For most of us, every penny we can scrape up goes into making the game better. In my case - not typical of indie developers - I raised $500,000 on Kickstarter, $250,000 from an investor, and put in another $250,000 from my retirement savings. That got the game finished. Where would I possibly have found another million dollars, or even half that, to promote the game on traditional (read “expensive”) media? That had a ripple effect on game reviews. Game review publications and sites claim to have independent paid advertising and review divisions, a “Chinese Wall.” But in practice, the reviewers mostly get assigned to review games that are advertised in that venue. If you don’t have an advertising budget, you don’t get reviewed. An answer might have been to make the game on half the budget, but it wouldn’t have been the game we wanted to make. As it is, for another 25%-50% of the budget, we could have added professional voice acting and more language localization. I probably would have chosen those over heavy “traditional” advertising.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Have computer game developers historically earned similar royalties as book authors (15%)? Assuming a single developer dealing with a software publisher like EA or Broderbund back in the day.
Answer: I received a 1% royalty for designing the bestselling, critically-acclaimed game, “Castle of Dr. Brain.” It stopped after two years. I had to fight for that, as other game designers at Sierra received only their below-industry-standard wages. Now that your shaking your fists in anger about that, perhaps it wasn’t unreasonable. The game design and writing is a small part of the development of a computer game, or of its market success. A game requires programming, art, animation, music, sound effects, publicity, manufacturing, and more. Maybe something like 5% is a fair indication of the game designer’s contribution to a project. 1% is pretty low even with that. Of course, game company executives then talk out of the other side of their mouth to explain how their multi-million-dollar salaries are appropriate given how they set the tone of the company’s operations. Personally, I believe that the average CEO’s contribution to a company’s success is less that that of the designer of one of its games. It’s rare to have a full team develop a game without up-front investment from the publisher. If they get 15% royalties in addition to investment, that’s quite generous. If the advances are subtracted from their 15%, that might feel pretty low, but it’s rare to find a better deal. My wife got a small monthly advance while designing and directing Quest for Glory V: Dragon Fire. By the time the game shipped, she ended up getting zero royalties; they were completely eaten by the advances. Which, as I implied, were smaller than what some of the salaried employees working on the game received. Don’t expect to get rich on game royalties. Especially given that 80–90% of games are cancelled before release.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is the video game industry currently in shambles?
Answer: The video game industry has always been chaotic. A common term for managing game developers is, “It’s like herding cats.” So you could say it has always been in shambles. Historically, most game companies have always lost money, and even the largest frequently declared bankruptcy, and were subsequently absorbed by a few huge corporations. Today, a few companies are making fortunes by making games, and thousands of others are losing money. There may be problems even at the biggest companies, but it isn’t keeping them from practically minting money. Everyone else is in trouble. Is it worse than in the past? I’d say that the large companies - even Activision Blizzard, which is currently being sued for discriminatory labor practices - are in better shape than large game developers of the past. It’s harder than ever for the small developers to succeed. There are so many new games being made every month that it’s really hard to get anyone to look at or buy your indie game. Here’s my last release, from 2018. Check it out and tell your friends if you find it interesting. We plan to bring our next game out as Early Access soon. But no, I wouldn’t say it’s shambles. Just extremely competitive, and “a hard way to make an easy living.”

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How complicated is poker (Texas Hold'em) from a game theory perspective?
