Answer: Two-player Limit Hold’em is a completely solved game, so “not too complicated” in game theory. Each additional player adds complication, and arbitrary betting as in No Limit adds a lot of complication. As far as I know, there is no complete game theoretic solution for these, but there are some very strong AI programs that will beat most human players at Hold’em, even No Limit.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How much is the tax limit that God specified in the Bible?
Answer: The Bible states, “Render onto Caesar that which is Caesar’s.” In other words, Christians are also citizens of their country. Whatever are the laws of the country, it is their responsibility to obey them. Nothing in the Bible limits the amount of tax that “Caesar” or the government may charge. U.S. law specifies that, “Congress shall make no laws respecting an institution of religion.” They won’t tell you how to worship, and your house of worship will not tell you how to pay or evade taxes. But the Bible does tell you it’s your duty to pay them.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How can you spot a programmer who was trained as a mathematician?
Answer: While I would never consider myself “trained as a mathematician,” my B.A. was in Mathematics. Maybe that counts. A friend who had a degree in European History developed an online bridge game. He had some code that looked a bit like: if (contract.strain == NOTRUMP) { switch (contract.level) { case 1: contract.score = 40; break; case 2: contract.score = 70; break; (etc.) } else . . . It drove me crazy. My code might look like: if (contract.strain == NOTRUMP) { contract.score = 10 + (contract.level * 30); } else if (contract.strain == SPADES OR contract.strain == HEARTS) { contract.score = contract.level * 30; } else { contract.score = contract.level * 20; } Or more likely: int NoTrumpScores = { 40, 70, 100, 130, 160, 190, 220 }; int MajorSuitScores = { 30, 60, 90 . . . }; if (contract.strain == NOTRUMP) { contract.score = NoTrumpScores[contract.level]; } etc. The formatting would have been prettier; that isn’t the point. The point is that mathematicians think in algorithms, and non-mathematicians tend to look at individual cases. Whenever I faced a problem, I tried to work out how I could combine as many cases as possible, rather than having a massive “if” or “switch” chain that treated each case individually. Object-oriented programmers think in terms of data and modeling the project domain space, which makes data tables especially applicable. Procedurally-oriented programmers think in terms of algorithms, then create data structures that support their algorithms. When I wrote code - I rarely do it these days - I tried to make it as short, simple, and straightforward as possible. Having good data structures helps to do that.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is a video game designer a secure job?
Answer: It’s about as secure as a carpet - It will stay under you until someone pulls it out. Unfortunately, carpet-pulling happens regularly in the game industry. There is no security. It’s quite common to lay off the entire team at the end of each project. It’s also pretty common to cancel a project without notice, letting most of the team go. I worked with one guy who had 8 or 10 companies on his resume. . . and 3 years of experience. I’ve started a new job in a senior position, only to be laid off a month later. (That one was software engineering, not even in the game industry!) Twice I’ve signed a two or three game contract, only to have it cancelled after one game. On one of those, they rehired me a year or so later.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I get asked over and over again about why so many developers fail. Is it money, experience, the right team, idea, or support? What is the most important factor in the success of the game for you?
Answer: Success in game development is largely a matter of luck combined with well-managed expectations. I’ve delivered multiple “successful” games (see ), but each new one is a crap shoot - Can we finish the game with the funds we have? Will it be good? Will people buy enough copies to pay the costs of developing and marketing? The second question is unanswerable - It’s a question of player aesthetics - but the other two are “why so many developers fail.” Finishing development of a game is really hard. It’s so hard that few developers get to the end of their projects. For every game that gets released, a thousand others die along the way. (Arbitrary statistic - It might be more or less.) Even so, with millions of enthusiastic developers trying to make games, thousands of new ones appear every year. Of those, only a few dozen - at best - earn out their development and marketing costs. Tiny minimalist games cost very little, but sell even less. Mid-sized games have trouble achieving mid-sized sales to support them. Most large, ambitious games lose even more money because players only buy a few titles each year, and most of those are sequels or expansions to games they already own. Lori and I tried to catch the lightning again with our Hero-U series. We ran a successful Kickstarter campaign, raising over $400,000, which turns out to provide about $275,000 to the actual game development. We then spent over five years developing a huge, ambitious game similar to the ones we made for Sierra On-Line in the 1990’s. Note: Five years of development using 2015-era dollars cost a lot more than developing a game in one year with 1990-era dollars. By indie standards, the game has sold quite well, maybe 10X the number of units of the average Steam game. That makes it a “success,” but a few more successes like this will bankrupt us. We and a major investor are each out about $200,000 on our experiment in indie game development. There are successful game developers, but they are few and far between. Notch made a mint from Minecraft. The developer of Stardew Valley has done very well from his obsessive work on the game. Dave Gilbert of Wadjet Eye Games has been successful by making many games relatively quickly, and with low overhead. Of those, only Notch is actually wealthy from making games. The rest of us muddle along, keep trying to make quality games, and hope to do slightly better than break-even in the long run. Most of us fail at that last goal.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Atheists, who do you choose to live if there is no God? Even if you could "advance society", none of that matters because you'll die anyways. It's like spending years playing a video game only to realise none of it matters.
Answer: Poster, why do you choose to live if nothing matters outside yourself? It’s like spending years playing a video game with no win condition. When you die, you go to the same afterlife whether you’ve worked hard all your life, or spent it drinking and partying (but after “accepting” Christ - or maybe it’s JHVH or Mohammed or Buddha or one of the other thousands of special beings people believe in). Whereas an atheist knows that we’re all on a time limit. We have only this life to do things that matter. If we choose to spend most of our time zoning out watching videos or playing games, then we’re choosing a less meaningful life. And that’s probably ok too. Most of the really famous and accomplished people in the world did their great works or research in the course of maybe ten years out of a sixty year life. (Life spans used to be shorter.) Maybe it’s perfectly ok if they rewarded themselves with leisure for the next 30 years. My wife and I did that. We grew up and went to school for 20 years. Then I worked as a programmer, and she as a teacher, for the next 10. We made a living, and maybe she improved some students’ lives, but nothing too special. Then we spent ten years making games about heroism. As far as many of our fans are concerned, only those ten years matter. We still get letters every week about how we’ve changed some of their lives, and given them the answer to your question - They found meaning through our games that you think can only be found through one of those thousands of gods. (By the way, Occam’s Razor decrees that you are almost certainly worshipping the wrong god. There are so many of them, and you’re probably worshipping the one your family taught you about when you were a child. Out of thousands, it’s probably the wrong one. Or as atheists “believe,” every single one of them is wrong.) Ten years ago, after twenty years of forced retirement from the fickle game industry, we started making games on our own. We’re much slower at it now than when we were in our 30’s, so we’ve only finished one so far. But now we’re hearing from fans that they’re finding new meaning from that one. So yay! We’ve done two decades of work that others consider important. That’s twice as many as most world-changing scientists and artists of the past. We’ll take it. For what do we need a god? When we work, we get into it, and believe we’re making something worthwhile, and we do our best to achieve that. When we play, we have fun, and know that it’s our choice, not that of some arbitrary dice roll of the thousands of almost-certainly-false deities. When we die, someone else will be born to pick up the baton we dropped.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What's the simplest video game you can make?
Answer: Ultra-simple video game? Maybe I’d create a betting game with a loop asking the player to choose: Then the game generates a random dice roll. The player’s score increases if she chose “Go high!” and it’s a 4–6, or chose “Go low!” and it’s 1–3. Otherwise she loses a point. On quitting, display the final score. My first game was tic-tac-toe against the computer. That’s actually far more sophisticated as it has to display the board and make decision for the computer’s turns. But I wrote it in a few weekend hours. It originally wasn’t much fun, since the computer always won or stalemated. It got much better when I taught the AI to make a different random mistake each game.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is Bobby Kotick trying to make his company as bad as possible or is it just a coincidence that Activision Blizzard suddenly got worse when he became a CEO?
Answer: Like any corporation, Activision Blizzard is neither “bad” nor “good” per se. It’s a collection of the attitudes and behaviors of its nearly 10,000 employees. Each part of A.B. started out as a group of enthusiastic gamers deciding to make games on their own. In general - especially looking back 30 or more years - gamers have never had a reputation as suave, sophisticated winners. At the time these companies were founded, they were mostly social outcasts. But some of them suddenly found themselves being seen as… if not actually rock stars, then at least members of popular bands. They were being paid actual money, and had fans who loved their work. It isn’t at all surprising that some of these social misfits, who in some ways were still children playing games at heart, might make poor decisions when suddenly confronted with a certain degree of power, money, and fame. Bobby Kotick came into all this as someone who wanted to make money from the success of all those nerds. He has little to do with how games are made, and essentially nothing to do with how the game makers behave. The ways in which Blizzard became “worse” when he took over have more to do with Kotick trying to squeeze more dollars out of their work than about good or bad social policies and behavior. But that isn’t what the current scandals are about. As a figurehead for the organization, Kotick is trying to set policies that will minimize the damage of past behavior, and hopefully to create rules for future behavior. But he has no real power over what a bunch of misfit nerds - and I say that lovingly, as one of them - did in the past and may still be doing. Game companies in the 80’s, 90’s, and 2000’s were not “woke” - They were barely a step up from hobbyists fooling around and having fun. Many of the mega-selling games today started out as some high school or college student fooling around with a computer. That they are considered high-end professional entertainment today is mostly because they started selling enough copies for people to take notice, and partially because companies started becoming more organized to keep the golden geese producing eggs. I coined a saying in the early 1990’s that I think still holds today: “Never assume that anyone in the game industry is actually a professional.” I occasionally added, “Including me.” Managing software developers is sometimes compared to “herding cats.” In the game industry, it’s worse. So Bobby Kotick can be blamed for many things. But he has little power over cats in heat doing what they naturally do.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: One year and umpteen recounts later, are you still convinced Trump won the 2020 election, or are you not insane?
Answer: Most people in the U.S. are at least somewhat unclear on the role of “President of the U.S.” Trump and his associates have tried to redefine it as “King” - the absolute leader of the country with dictatorial powers. That isn’t actually too far off if you use “King” the way it is currently used in most constitutional monarchies. The King or Queen is essentially a figurehead who gets respect and certain ceremonial benefits, but has little to do with day-to-day governance. A U.S. President also has that figurehead role - He (or eventually she) is the titular head of the country, and a convenient personification for the U.S. Presidents help set direction for policies by speaking about them or by assigning staffers to write about them. However, Presidents also have boring administrative responsibilities as the head of the executive branch of the government. Most of them take this role seriously and try to perform well at it. Trump was an exception. He gloried in the ceremony and role as spokesman for the U.S., but had no interest in doing actual governmental work. His staffers pretty much did that on their own, with very little direction. That in effect meant that Trump was more of a King than a President. But you rarely depose a King. Since they serve only a ceremonial purpose, there isn’t much reason to replace them every four or eight years. Those who agree with Trump that the 2020 election was “stolen” from him are basically saying that he is their King, regardless of a bunch of numbers and statistics that they understand even less than the role of President of the U.S. In other words, they simply don’t care about the election results. They’re irrelevant. All that matters is that Trump should still be King because he appeals to what they want to see in a figurehead. The idea of Biden and Harris doing actual work from the West Wing is foreign to people who only care about a symbol.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If you cloned 10,000 exact copies of Donald Trump and sent them out into the world, what would happen?
Answer: It depends. Are you starting each of the 10,000 Trump copies out with the same advantages he had? A “small” $10 million loan with which to invest in real estate? Inheritance of his father’s businesses? Those copies might turn out similarly to The Donald. The rest will likely fail, as do most ambitious people without resources.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What is the easiest way to learn a new language? Are there any applications that can help in the process?
Answer: How to learn (anything): Practice, practice, practice. Build a small app. In the old days, everyone started by writing a program that displayed, “Hello, world!” That’s all. Then make a slightly bigger one. Practice new techniques as you add features. Microsoft has a free version of Developer Studio. Unity has a free hobbyist license for Unity. You don’t need to pay for the learning tools. There are also many free videos on YouTube and various educational sites. For instance, Khan Academy | Free Online Courses, Lessons & Practice has several free programming classes.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What is the bare minimum amount of people to create a full running video game of high fidelity?
Answer: It only takes one, if that one has some art talent and uses the right scripting tools. But that one will work his or her tail off, most likely for several years.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: William Hartmann, a Republican official who opposed coronavirus vaccines, and tried to block certification of President Joe Biden's election win, died after being hospitalized with COVID-19. What do you think about that?
Answer: I used a different credential than usual, since this is actually a probability, rather than a political, question. People make “insurance” decisions all the time. Some think that the cost in time and effort - no matter how negligible - of using seatbelts is too high compared to the probability of getting in a serious accident. Strenuous seatbelt law enforcement has slightly changed this calculation, because now people need to include the possibility of a big fine in the equation. William Hartmann made just such an insurance decision. He decided that the chance of dying, or contracting a serious illness, from Covid-19 was small enough, and the potential profit from being a contrarian large enough, that it was worth it. While he was wrong for himself, that might have just been a dice roll. Thousands of other Republican politicians have taken similar positions, and haven’t yet died of Covid-19 complications. Most of the “anti-vax” politicians are cynical opportunists. By riling up their base against those manipulative vax-pushing Democrats, they rake in piles of donations. The most successful might be the truly cynical ones, because they and their staffs are vaccinated, but they push anti-vax nonsense to constituents who love that talk. “Stick it to the Democrats… and donate to my campaign so I can stick it harder,” when the people they’re really “sticking” are their constituents.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Are most video game developers billionaires?
Answer: The only “video game developers” who are billionaires don’t actually develop games. They own the few biggest game development companies, and build fortunes on the backs of their underpaid developers. See the other answers for the plight of most actual game developers. It’s a tough business, although it can be very rewarding intellectually and emotionally.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Are there any IRS crowdfunding rules?
Answer: Funding from a crowdfunding campaign is considered ordinary income. However, if you are using the funds to develop and create a product, you can postpone payment of taxes until the product is released and starts generating income. Each year, you can deduct your expenses from a pro-rata share of the income, which likely means no tax liability until you start showing a profit.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do Republican senators want to vote on defunding Biden’s vaccine-or-testing mandate?
Answer: They want to recharacterize a public safety measure as an imposition on people’s freedom. The fact that it’s a dangerous “freedom” that can result in sickness or death to the “free” people, and to others with whom they come in contact, doesn’t seem to phase them. To Republicans, it’s a clear case of not having to do what strangers order them to do. To Democrats, it’s an equally clear case of public safety - the mandate, or endangerment - fighting the mandate.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How do video game developers come up with such creative games and ideas?
Answer: Coming up with creative ideas is easy; I’m pretty sure everyone has creative ideas all the time. The hard part is convincing someone else to fork over the funds to turn those ideas into games. The next hard part is actually finishing a game. It always takes at least a little more blood, sweat, and tears than you can imagine, and often a *lot* more. Then there’s the harder part of actually making a *good* game. Even if the initial ideas are brilliant, it’s enormously hard to maintain that brilliance while teaching them to a dumb computer. Not to mention enrolling the rest of the team in your vision when some (at least) of them are just there to collect a paycheck. Then, once you’ve made a good - or a great - game, it’s incredibly hard to bring it to players’ attention, and get them to pay for it. Ideas aren’t *actually* easy to come by, but they’re far easier than the work of turning them into a successful game.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What has shocked you the most about the Kyle Rittenhouse verdict of not guilty?
Answer: It seems clear that, from now on, protestors must come to protests armed to the teeth. If they catch even a glimpse of a counter-protestor carrying a gun, they must shoot first “in self defense,” since they know that the law will protect anyone who shoots at them. I’ve often felt that way about “open carry” in public places. Since there is no way to distinguish between a proud patriot openly waving his AR-15 around vs. a terrorist about to open fire with it, the right answer seems to be to take down anyone openly carrying before they take me down. [Note: I *don’t* go armed in public, so manage to avoid this dilemma.] Or, of course, we could tighten up some laws and law enforcement to prevent anyone from bringing deadly force to a protest.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What jobs do you recommend I go into to get very rich in Louisiana?
Answer: Work remotely for a company in California or New York. Your savings from living in Louisiana will eventually allow you to become well-off, if not “very rich.” Stock options trading is highly risky, but has potentially high rewards. Less risky, but it will take longer to get rich, is to become a computer software engineer (fancy term for “programmer”).

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What did it take to make a successful indie game (at least 10k players)?
Answer: What did it take to make a successful indie game (at least 10k players)? By that definition of “successful,” Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption is a very successful game with more than 20K players. And you’re right - The average indie game on Steam sells fewer than 2K copies. In most cases with which I’m familiar, including ours, success comes from having a long track record of many other games. Obviously, most of those games did not reach that degree of success, else they’d have been made without a long track record. :-) One of the few exceptions of which I know is Stardew Valley. On that project, the developer obsessed over the game for years. His lost income compared to working for an established game company or other software developer was likely at least $500K during that time. Or the previous games weren’t indie. My fan base comes mostly from players who loved the games my wife and I made at Sierra On-Line. These were as close to AAA as the industry had in the 1990’s. All five Quest for Glory games, the remake of Quest for Glory I, and Castle of Dr. Brain sold over 100K units each. Mixed-Up Fairy Tales might have reached that mark, and certainly sold over 50K units. Our game Shannara was one of the few Legend Entertainment games to sell over 100K units. This track record led to “instant” success with Hero-U: Rogue to Redemption - over 6000 Kickstarter backers, and over 20,000 units sold over the course of the last three years. The only problem is that, knowing that all of my previous games sold over 100K units, I budgeted for a comparatively modest 50K unit sales. We avoided going massively into debt only because a few generous backers contributed additional funding beyond our Kickstarter funds. So we’ve managed about ten times the average indie game sales, but are a long way from turning a profit for ourselves or our investors. That’s likely true of most indie games, including other “successful” ones, especially if you consider the opportunity cost of lost income while making the games.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What should I do? I am a game developer and am working on a game. Frequently, I do not feel like programming it because it feels like so much work. It is not so much work. I can complete the whole game in less than 20 hours. How can I change this?
Answer: Get out of the industry. Making games takes immense effort and frustration, and you apparently don’t have the stomach for it. If you think a quality game can be completed in 20 hours, you’re wrong. If you’ve been working on a game for years, and only think it will take 20 more hours to complete it, you’re wrong. Why don’t you feel like putting in those 20 hours? It’s because you know they won’t be enough, and you don’t want to put in the necessary 2000 hours.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If a person were to work in game design or game development, does that also mean they have to relocate in order to work at the company they want to be in? And what are the chances of getting a job with these positions?
Answer: Basically any question that you ask about needing to compromise to get a job suggests you aren’t passionate enough to make the needed sacrifices. That especially applies to game development, an intensely competitive field. You might find that you can get a game development job that will let you work remotely. But if the answer matters to you, this probably isn’t the right field. Game developers are intensely passionate about what they do. Their questions are about how well they can make games better, not about what compromises they will have to make to do it.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I’m interested in getting into game development, and I’m wondering what steps one should take to get into the industry? I think I should focus on programming initially, and I could look into/try other aspects of game dev later in my career if I want.
Answer: That depends totally on your skills and interests. If you enjoy wrangling computer code to teach a dumb machine how to look intelligent, then programming is for you. You could become a software engineer in a company’s tools group, a server software developer focusing on the world content, or a client developer focusing on presentation. If you love drawing and painting, you can get into creating game art and animation. There are hundreds of specialties in game development, with thousands of sub-specialties. Find your affinity, then focus on that.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why don't billionaires have to pay taxes on their unrealized gain from stocks but people who win a car on a game show have to pay taxes on sweepstakes prizes like a car?
Answer: The keyword is “unrealized.” Let’s say I spend $1000 on stocks, and over time the market value of those stocks increases to $10,000. How much actual money do I have? That “market value” means that other people are buying and selling the stock, and that they’re willing - on aggregate - to spend ten times as much as I did. But until I sell the shares, I don’t see any of that appreciation. I’m out the original $1000 (which was probably paid from what was left after paying income tax), but I haven’t received any of the $10,000. Maybe next year those shares will tank, and only be worth $3000. I still won’t have an actual gain or loss at that point. If I sell the shares then, I’ll pay taxes on $2000 - my net profit. Billionaires are in this situation constantly. You don’t become a billionaire by earning money and putting it in a low-interest savings account. You invest and reinvest your money constantly. You keep some of your money in cash, which you can use to pay your bills. Billionaires also have fantastic credit ratings, which makes it easy to borrow money. Borrowed money is not income, so it isn’t taxable. If they constantly pay for their expenses and new investments with loans, they may never be in a situation where they pay taxes. The system is designed to collect taxes when someone is actually paid, or when they sell investment assets. The game show winner has an actual car that they received. It has immediate value; they could turn around and sell it for maybe half its retail price. And that’s what many game show winners do - They take a smaller cash award rather than the car. They then pay taxes on the actual cash they received rather than on the theoretical value of the car. If I won a car and decided to keep it, I would talk to an accountant about the tax situation. I expect I would have to pay taxes, but possibly not on the full sticker price of the car. Is this fair? I could argue either way. But it’s clear that rich people who make good investments can grow their wealth much faster than people who need their income to live, and thus pay taxes on it each time they are paid.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If you ONLY consider the work done by programmers? Which is more difficult to make a AAA game or a large website?
Answer: From a programming viewpoint, making a AAA game is a thousand times more difficult and challenging than creating a large website. Nobody cares if a web page takes a second or two to load. But if a complex video game fails to refresh 60 times a second, players get angry. If you’re shooting at an enemy, and it looks on your screen as if you hit them, the game had better respond accordingly. But that other player? On his screen, he escaped in time and ducked behind a car. If he gets hit, he’ll blow his top. He *knows* the other player couldn’t hit him. But latency is inevitable. If there’s a 100 millisecond time between when Player A acts and when Player B sees the result, odds are good that they each have a different view of reality. Programmers have to make things look as though they make sense despite the lag. There are thousands of other things that programmers need to take into account in a AAA game. There’s much less to handle on a website.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Why do Democrats act like even though Biden won, they want to make Republicans admit that he won? It makes them seem like sore winners.
Answer: We’re worried about the future of the U.S. If a third of the country won’t accept election results, how can anyone govern? How can people choose their representatives if anyone who loses can claim that they actually won, and get millions of people to believe them? It isn’t so much that Democrats “want to make Republicans admit” that Biden won the election. It’s just that we’re scratching our heads about how anyone can get so caught up in conspiracy theories that they think everyone - except their chosen talking heads - is lying to them. In 2016, liberals were shocked and disappointed when Hillary Clinton lost the Presidential election. But we didn’t act as though the election didn’t happen. And some of us worked hard over the subsequent years to prevent a repeat performance.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: I make video games and I come up with ideas. What is it called? Am I a producer or am I a director?
Answer: At one of my first jobs, I needed business cards for a show. I asked my boss, “What’s my title?” and he replied, “What do you want it to be?” So I became a Senior Systems Analyst with just one year of programming experience. If you work for a big game development company, you probably already have a title. If not, yours is whatever you choose. I’m currently the President of Transolar Games, Inc., but I could just as easily have chosen Producer or Executive Producer as my title. You say you “make” video games. Do you do everything, or part of the job? Is your work mostly planning, technical design, level design, programming, painting scenes, animating characters, testing, writing dialogue, or leading a team? A producer is generally someone who provides or arranges for funding for a project. They’re also generally responsible for overseeing production schedules, hiring or contracting resources, etc. A director is a team leader, but in the game industry, often has a creative role as well. Director-designer and director-writer are common dual roles.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is there a computer monitor and/or TV to consider when using them to design a game that would require color accuracy, as well as for using it to play fighting games that have low lag time for inputs, or whatever else should be considered here?
Answer: We try to build games for the “least common denominator” in game peripherals. Development systems tend to be high-end because some tasks require extra memory and fast processing. But we don’t want to optimize games for high-performance hardware. We try to make them playable and fun for most players. It’s sometimes a challenge to realize that our development systems aren’t typical. For example, artists tend to set their monitors to very high contrast and brightness. If they don’t check their work on more normal settings, they can end up creating scenes that are hard to “read” on an average monitor. Similarly, games tend not to support unusual peripherals that most players won’t have. We only have limited resources for testing our games, and it’s impossible to handle every combination of hardware and systems.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is "randomness" a relative term? To put it another way, can one random number be more random than another random number?
Answer: “Random” is random. If I roll a die twelve times, and get 1,3,2,5,5,5,5,5,6,2,4,3, those fives may not look random, but repeats can randomly happen. If over hundreds of rolls, I still average more 5’s than other numbers, I might conclude that the die is likely loaded, but even then it could be truly random. Games and other computer software typically use a pseudo random-number generator. These are numbers that appear random, but which can be predicted if you know the algorithm and the initial seed value. But for most practical purposes, they’re just as useful as truly random numbers.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: How do indie developers advertise the Kickstarter for their games?
Answer: This is a great question! Back in 2012, Tim Schafer and Double Fine used Kickstarter to raise funds for an adventure game. It was so successful that dozens of fans contacted me and said, “You need to Kickstart a new game!” One of them offered to lead development of the new game. What I should have done at that point would have been to call Tim and get advice. Instead, I copied his model, sought to raise a similar amount as his initial ask, and waited for tens of thousands of adoring fans to scream, “Just take my money!” (Spoiler: That didn’t happen. But I did get a few hundred mega-fans to help us get going, and with their help we eventually got a few thousand backers who barely pushed us over the all-or-nothing funding line.) I did a couple of things right. We got some nice art for the Kickstarter page, and I contacted a number of journalists who had covered previous Kickstarter projects. That helped us get some publicity, but would not work as well in 2022 as in 2012. Game sites became jaded about crowdfunding; their readers want to learn about games they can actually buy and play, rather than about a game that might or might not exist in two to five years or more. The one thing I actually did get right, whether by luck or intention, was to contact everyone on our “school for heroes” email list. We started the school around 2004, so some of the emails were stale, but many of them connected with actual fans of our games. Those fans became the core audience that helped us get some momentum with the campaign, and kept cheerleading through the end. Since then, I’ve learned that having a strong connection with fans is by far the most important thing you can do to promote a crowdfunding campaign. People assume that there are millions of Kickstarter fans who are constantly looking for the next great project to support. In reality, the successful projects bring their own audiences to Kickstarter. Besides the mailing list, we started new Facebook pages to connect with fans and promote our projects. These have been useful (and fun), but not as successful as direct email to fans and influencers. Today we have a very active Discord server. That’s proving to be the best way of having real dialogue with our players. More importantly, it connects them to each other. We have some really fascinating discussion threads on the Discord, both about our games, other games, and occasionally non-gaming topics. We still have the Facebook pages, but the interesting discussions are happening on Discord. We also do a semi-regular (every two weeks) Twitch stream that helps keep us connected with some of our most enthusiastic fans. I’m not sure if it’s cost-effective for us, but it’s fun! All of this would be very hard if we were unknown developers creating new indie games. We’re finding it’s quite challenging enough for “famous” game designers. But that doesn’t mean it’s impossible to raise yourself by your own bootstraps. The key is to build your profile organically and constantly. Provide lots of free content in the form of mini-games, YouTube and Twitch videos and streams, promotions on your website, etc. Try to get everyone to sign up for an email list, then feed that list with regular, fun content. When you’re ready to launch the Kickstarter or indiegogo campaign, reach out to your mailing list. Make sure you have permission to do that - MailChimp and other sites will shut you down in a hurry if you start spamming people who didn’t opt in to your list. The best way to do that is by making the mailing list a valuable resource before you try to monetize it. For example, Cliff Johnson - creator of The Fool’s Errand - presented jokes and puzzles in his email list for people interested in his upcoming game, A Fool and His Money. I looked forward to those monthly posts even though the game ran years behind schedule. (That’s a common problem with indie games, to which mine are equally subject.) So basically, build an audience, then launch your crowdfunding campaign. That probably means you’ll be spending a lot of your time (which in some ways means money) on promotion long before you will be able to run a successful crowdfunding campaign. I started our Facebook page a few months in advance, which wasn’t really long enough. It was our eight years of building the mailing list that really paid off. Figure you’ll need to spend at least a year building an audience before you can ask them to support a new project.

Question: Why does Michigan still have 25,000 deceased people on its voter rolls?

Question: How do game development companies teach employees to use their proprietary game engines?
Answer: Game developers are usually highly intelligent, as well as creative. They have no trouble learning a new tool. If the documentation is lacking for a proprietary game engine, the keyword is “proprietary.” The engine developers are right there at the company to answer questions for the game developers. That’s actually a major reason why companies choose to develop proprietary tools - It gives them control over the tools when changes are needed, and the developers are right there to answer questions.

Question: When someone is awarded compensation stock options and they have to exercise them, do they pay income tax on gains for that year regardless if they sell the shares or not?
Answer: My brother was in this situation about 30 years ago, so I may not quite have the story right. As I remember it, he had a choice of selling his option shares, and paying income tax on them, or of keeping them (converted to stock, no longer options). He chose to keep the stock. He had to pay Alternative Minimum Tax based on their theoretical value. A few months later, the stock tanked, going from $30/share to $7. By the time he sold it, he had lost out on most of the “value” on which he’d been taxed, as well as on the higher market value. When I was awarded options, and chose to cash them in, I paid capital gains tax based on the difference between the sale price and the base value at the time they were awarded. Again, this is an old memory, and I could have the details wrong. Check with a tax professional about your individual situation. Make sure you consider the impact both of holding the shares, or selling them.

Question: In game development how exactly would one write code to use all CPU cores the consumers CPU has?
Answer: How would one write game code to use multiple CPU cores? That’s generally handled by the programming language or environment’s run-time system. Code is written to use multiple threads, and can work on a single CPU or multiple. The run-time system allocates new threads to the least busy CPU. There are a number of reasons to use threaded code. Some actions are time-consuming, but don’t need to block player actions, so you take them out of the main game loop. Others are well suited to being done in parallel, so you put them in threads in case the system is able to allocate them to multiple cores.

Question: Why do game developers release patches for new games?
Answer: Whenever we release a game, there is always a list of outstanding bugs. Nobody has ever released a bug-free game. But there is pressure to release games sooner rather than later. A game that isn’t yet on the market costs money to refine, but doesn’t bring any in. We advertise a release date, and fans expect us to do our best to make that date. If the game is sold in stores, promotions need to be arranged months in advance for a specific date. So we release a “good enough” game, but we want it to be better. During the weeks or months of production and shipping, the team is still working on the game. Eventually that work turns into a patch. However, players don’t see that overlap. They see a game get released, and a patch come out almost immediately. That looks odd, but the alternative would be to hold the game longer before starting production and marketing.

Question: I am looking to join a small game studio. I am not yet certified professionally, but I have 4 years of personal experience. I want to be a junior 3D artist. What are the requirements?

In the case of a small game studio, that’s probably the founder. A good demo reel is an excellent starting point. You also have to be willing to work for a low salary, or on spec, because most small game studios are money-losing operations. It’s best to do that type of work part-time while you have at least another part-time paying gig. You’ll learn a lot making indie games, but it’s very unlikely you’ll make a fortune - or even a decent living - from that job.

Question: Would you support the democrats getting rid of the filibuster now if you knew for a fact that republicans would have 55 senator votes in 2022 and would impose draconian changes to voting such as requiring photo ID to vote, no mail in voting, etc.?
Answer: Actually, yes. The filibuster is a procedure for which the time is past. It used to be used to prevent or postpone a vote on legislation that some people felt very strongly should not be passed. Today it is used as a political party tool to prevent Congress from passing any legislation at all. It’s used solely by one party to try to prevent the majority party from making laws. There is no passion in it, only cold calculation. And that isn’t even calculation about the measure under discussion. It’s a blanket, “They want it, so we won’t let them have it.” I’ve known six year old children with a better sense of sharing than that. If a slim majority of 55 Senators chooses to vote for a bill, they should be able to do so. A minority should not be able to hold the 55 up for ransom, and that’s the filibuster. Question: Is it necessary for video game developers to learn how to create assets?
Answer: A “video game developer” is anyone who helps develop video games. That includes artists, animators, and composers, the primary job of which is to create assets. Game designers and programmers create assets too. All text in a game, scripts, and code are also assets. But you’re probably thinking more in terms of visual and audio assets. If you (inaccurately) restrict “developer” to “programmer,” and (also incorrectly) “assets” to “art and music assets,” programmers do not need to create final assets. They do, however, usually create stand-ins. A simple X in a box can serve as a placeholder for scene props that haven’t been drawn or animated yet. A clip of “Voice goes here!” can be used as a stand-in until you have actual voice recordings. An artist or audio engineer can easily supply those, but they’re apt to get distracted and provide more than was asked. But please - If you want to get into the game industry, first learn correct terminology. “Video game developer” includes thousands of specialties.

Question: If I saved $500 per month, how many years later will I become a millionaire?
Answer: “How many years later will I…” is a hard question to answer. That’s because future market results might not match past ones. The historical trend has been that the total stock market increases 8% per year on average over time. I can answer the easier one - “If I saved $500 per month, and invested it in a low cost total stock market index mutual fund, how many years did it take to become a millionaire?” If trends continue the way they’ve been for the last 100 years, the answer may apply to your future question. But I won’t promise that will happen. I’m sure there are better calculators on the web, but I made do with this one: Putting in $500 initial investment, $500 per month, and 8% growth rate - the historical market average - here’s what I got. After 18 years, you’ll have a little over $242,000, and after 25 years, about $479,000. That’s close enough to double “for government work,” so let’s say your investment doubles every 7 years under that strategy. That brings you to $958,000 after 32 years, which is just short of your goal. So let’s call it a million dollars after 33 years. Let’s try a small modification assuming you’ll earn more in the future. Invest $500 a month for ten years, then increase your investment to $1,000 a month for 20 years. Under that scenario, you’ll pass $1 million in the 30th year, cutting 3 years off the previous strategy. If you double the investment again after the 20th year (10 years at $500, 10 at $1,000, and 8 years at $2,000), you’ll shave off another two years, reach $1 million after 28 years, and reaching $1,228,000 after a total of 30 years.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: If paper-pushers say they shouldn't have to pay taxes because they "worked hard" for their money shouldn't construction workers be the richest people on the planet and paper-pushers be the poorest never working hard 1 day in their life?
Answer: Yes, yes they should. Wages and earnings are not determined by either hard work or skill at the job. They’re determined by how good the “worker” is at convincing other people to pay him money. I once took a job at a startup company where the manager explained to me that everyone there had taken a 25% pay cut from their previous job. In return, they would grant me stock options. I wasn’t sure I could afford to support my family on the lower salary, but it seemed the only option, so I agreed. A few months later I talked to a new hire. He mentioned they had fed him that same story, but he told them he had a family to support, and couldn’t do it. They not only paid him his ask, but they also granted him the same stock options they gave me. The only difference - we were equally qualified, and I worked there longer - was the willingness to say “No,” and hold out for a better offer. As my profile says, I once considered myself an Ayn Rand “objectivist” and libertarian. I felt that I was one of the “elect,” and naturally deserved the good jobs and pay that I commanded. Over time, I’ve realized that my success was as much a result of “White privilege” as any skill or brilliant mental ability I have. Sure, I did well in school… but I was raised in a family that took education seriously, and shared that attitude with me. My father paid my way through the first two years of college - far easier in the 1970’s than today - and helped me get my first internship. After I graduated, I went to work for his company with a big pay jump. Is an insurance salesman of as much value to society as a carpenter? No way! But the salesman brings in a lot more income. The system rewards people with connections, and those who are willing to risk rejection when they demand more.

Name: Corey Cole
Question: What would atheists do if their sane, drug-free, trusting, intelligent family member, friend, or partner said they saw god, and asked you to believe in god too?
Answer: I once had a co-worker come up to me in the break room to say, “I saw Him last night!” It was a bit out of context, but he eventually explained that he had had a personal visitation from… Satan. As I was a member of The Temple of Set at the time, liked to wear all-black, and considered myself edgy, it’s understandable that he chose me for his revelation. So how would I react if someone I knew told me they “saw god”? Much the same way as I did with my co-worker. I politely humored him, and minimized interaction after that. Now I myself have had some miraculous encounters. During high school, I attended a Christian prayer meeting and Bible study. Afterwards, I was so full of euphoria from the experience, I backed my car into a pole. Damage not serious, fortunately. I’ve always been a careful driver, watching for potential problems on the road before they happen. The ones I’ve seen the most involve cars with “Maranatha” and the like on their bumper stickers. As I was that one night, their drivers frequently seem to inhabit a different plane that doesn’t include safe driving. I had another miraculous encounter years later, during a ToS meeting. With incense fumes heavy in the air, I found myself in a fugue state. I saw Set himself float out of a statue of him. So what does it mean when a normal, sane person relates a divine occurrence? It just means that they allowed themselves to enter a susceptible state, and that our minds are very easily fooled. A random pattern on a cracker suddenly becomes a miraculous image of the Virgin Mary or Jesus. Or Elvis. It doesn’t mean that there is any real meaning to the vision. In fact, if I myself “saw god” - as I’ve related occasionally happens (shame if it doesn’t always happen to be your god) - I’d add it to the “evidence for” folder. But unfortunately the “evidence against” is always far more conclusive. Self delusion is the Occam’s Razor explanation for essentially all mystic visions.

Question: I have been on a diet excluding red meat for the past few weeks. However, I ate a burger from cookout yesterday and today I feel sick. Am I allergic to red meat?

Name: Corey Cole
Question: Is it possible to create an artificial general intelligence system, an AI/computer that is indistinguishable from human intelligence, that is as intelligent and as powerful as the human brain, while uses 20-25 watts per hour, like the human brain?
Answer: Yes, but it takes both a male and female creator - with the woman doing most of the really hard work - and 15–20 years. When they’re done, they’ll have a computer indistinguishable from a human brain. The types of AI’s we make have a different purpose. They’re equivalent to “idiot savants” with strong specialized knowledge and reasoning ability in a particular area, but near-complete ignorance in most other fields. They can make calculations and decisions much faster than a natural human brain, but they won’t have the whimsy and unpredictability of human decisions. On the other hand, I’ll take a well-trained AI over a well-trained human for things that need fast, accurate calculations. I’d want the AI to represent me in a chess tournament, for example. The very best humans can beat the best AI players at chess, but there are very few “best” human players. The AI will defeat everyone else.

Question: Is there any way someone can be a game designer without a bachelor’s degree?

There are three excellent ways to answer that question: Once you’ve demonstrated your work ethic, your talent, and your understanding of what it takes to make a great game, they’ll talk to you. You don’t need the degree, but you do need to show that you’re ready to work really hard, and that you have the skills to make a great game.

Question: Scientists have been wrong about a lot of things in the past, so how do we know scientists aren't wrong about climate change?
Answer: Yes, scientists are often “wrong.” That means they’re doing actual science instead of repeating trivial answers. The scientific process involves making a hypothesis, testing it, then rinse and repeat many times. A real scientist considers the experimental (testing) process a success whether it supports the original hypothesis or tears it to shreds. Real scientists love being proved wrong, because that teaches them (and the world) something each time. Eventually, some of the hypotheses survive repeated experiments. Those are published as “scientific knowledge.” Even then, later work may show flaws in the original experiments, or conditions under which the knowledge is incomplete. That leads to refinements and corrections. It isn’t terrible that “scientists are sometimes wrong.” It’s magnificent! Rather than stating a hypothesis and insisting it’s correct because it was stated, a scientist tests and verifies everything they do. What we’re left with, at any given point of time, is the best evidential-based knowledge to that point. That’s a whole lot better than untested opinions. A few fact checks might be beneficial in other fields.

Question: Why can't Blizzard games launch a video game successfully anymore?

It’s called “reversion to the mean.” The odds have been against Blizzard with every game they’ve launched, but until recently, they beat the odds every time. That’s somewhat self-fulfilling, as fans of the previous games are likely to buy the new ones. But there’s never a guarantee. Every time you launch a game, it’s a heart-wrenching experience of hoping players will love and buy it.

Question: How or where do I find a game artist volunteer?
Answer: You can find amateur artists many places - conventions, Facebook groups devoted to game art and fandom, etc. But if you don’t have artistic talent, and don’t know any artists, I’d look to do things a different way. There are oodles of cheap and free art assets available for Unity and other development environments. I would make my first few games with public domain art. If you start to build enough of a following that you think you need custom art, then by all means find artists… but pay them. There’s so much free and nearly-free content available, you don’t need to take advantage of a “starving artist” by getting them to work for free.

Question: Is it okay to be sad that others are better than me at the things I want to be good at and respected for doing? I’m afraid I’ll never catch up on game making or writing the next big story crazy or an artistic design. How do I get out of this slump?
Answer: Being sad isn’t a useful response. All creative people occasionally (or frequently) doubt themselves. There’s even a term for that - “imposter syndrome.” But watching talented people do amazing work should inspire, not depress, you! Talk to them. Ask about particular techniques, then later practice them on your own. 80% of artistic talent is hard work - Practice, practice! Most of the rest is having good role models, with just a little bit inherent talent. When you’re beset by writer’s block, or feel that your art isn’t good enough, there is no substitute for sitting down and writing or drawing more. The more you create, the better you get at it.

Question: If I get Medicaid, will that pay for the cost of any surgeries I might need on my knees and feet?
Answer: Yes, Medicaid pays for surgeries. However, you will have to get your doctor to agree that the surgery is necessary. Even with full insurance (Medicare plus an Advantage plan), my mother had trouble getting authorization for a knee replacement. Her doctor said he first had to order her a knee brace, and it would likely take a year to get authorization for surgery. We ended up getting it through the VA. Her doctor looked at her walking posture, and immediately decided she needed surgery. As she recovers slowly from wounds, he said that a knee brace was a terrible idea that would leave lesions. He authorized an x-ray and scan, then expedited the authorization so she could get surgery in a few weeks instead of waiting a year. Medicaid is a different system, but even more conservative on what is “necessary” surgery. If you get the surgery, they’ll pay for it; you might just have to wait a while to get it.

Question: The Washington Examiner has a story called "Democratic plan to tax billionaires could force entrepreneurs to sell businesses". If they thrived at 92% in the 60's, why would 39.6% "force them out of business"? https://tinyurl.com/nvb335pr
Answer: Only profitable businesses pay taxes, and they only pay them on their profits. The tax rate doesn’t matter much. If my company brings in $1 Billion in revenue, but has $950 Million in expenses, we only make a “scant” $50 million taxable earnings. If we then pay 10% local taxes, that’s deductible, leaving $45 million. 40% of that is $18 million, leaving $27 million after tax profit. If we become more successful, and clear $100 million after expenses, we’ll still clear $54 million after taxes. The point is that, no matter how much a company earns, it will still be profitable after taxes. And if it wasn’t profitable in the first place, the tax rate doesn’t matter. (In California, we pay a minimum $800 annual business tax even if we lose money one year.)

Question: Do indie video game developers ever hire composer for their projects?
Answer: Yes, most indie games use custom soundtracks, and we usually hire independent musicians to compose and play them. Our budgets tend to be tiny, although there’s quite a range to it. I’ve seen indie games with budgets as low as $5,000 and as high as several million. But even the high end is dwarfed by AAA game budgets that can reach $100 million. A small portion of that small budget goes to the composer. Sometimes there’s a clause allowing the composer to benefit from soundtrack sales, but those are usually trivial compared to game sales. My most recent game has sold well over 10,000 copies, and we’ve sold fewer than 100 soundtracks. There is intense competition for composers and sound designers. I get email from them constantly, and generally have to say, “Sorry, we have that handled.”

Question: I sell music for video game developers and I don’t like the idea of someone making 100x more money using my music in their work. What advice do you have for me?
Answer: Let’s see. The last video game I made cost about $1 million to develop. Suppose I pay the composer a (below-market) fee of $10,000. Suppose the game sells $1 million. Whee! I’ve “made” 100x what I paid the developer! Good times! Except, of course, I didn’t. My profit so far is zero - more likely negative after accounting for marketing expenses. It would take $2 million in sales to *actually* clear 100x the pittance I paid to the musician. That happens maybe 1 time in 100 for indie developers. Are you willing to take on risk commensurate with your ask for a larger payday? Will you accept $0 compensation until the game becomes profitable? Or look at it another way - the total man-hours that go into making a game vs. the number of hours the composer spends on it. Most of the time that’s much larger than a 100:1 ratio. A third way - Composers are a dime a dozen. Many people want to compose music for video games, but only a few are needed. If you’re charging $100K, and an equally-talented composer charges $10K, which one do you think will get most of the gigs?

Question: How do professional game developers implement a dialogue system in their games?
Answer: The most common way to implement dialogue (and other text) in a large-scale video game is to create a custom design editor. Smaller companies prefer off-the-shelf solutions, such as Excel (or csv) spreadsheets, or features included in a game engine. Direct inclusion of dialogue in code is frowned upon, as that makes it much more difficult to “localize” (translate and customize) into additional languages. My company developed its own custom scripting system. Possibly we’d have been better off with a standardized scripting language, but this worked well for us. It allowed our writers to focus on the text and dialogue without having to worry too much about the environment and code. For translation, our editor has an Export option that creates a csv spreadsheet, and an Import command that reads the translated version and incorporates it into the game.

Question: Is it the beginning of the end for the Republican Party?
Answer: A good friend of mine grew up in Cleveland, Ohio. To the end of his days, he was a staunch fan of the Cleveland Indians and the Browns. He felt betrayed when the latter moved to Baltimore (before reforming a few years later). It didn’t matter to him that both were losing teams most years, or that he moved to California and lived in the Bay Area longer than he had lived in Ohio. He was a Cleveland fan, and that was that. Republicans are much the same way. They have always been Republicans. Their parents were probably Republicans. Many of them spit on Democrats, or at least consider voting for any Democrat unthinkable. Will they switch just because some people think that the Republican Party has been irrevocably compromised. No, they have no more respect for “those people” than they do for Democratic Party candidates. Most of them will continue to vote Republican until they die, though triumph and scandal, win or lose. The question is whether the party will continue to attract new followers. They will get most of the children and grandchildren of current Republicans. But their outreach among others has been mostly unsuccessful for some years. As older Republicans pass away, the party may have trouble renewing itself. So is this “the beginning of the end”? Not really. It’s a slow, continuous process, and it isn’t clear where the tipping point will be, or if we’ve already reached it.
